Spring Framework: Core Concepts & IoC Container Complete Guide

What is Spring Framework?

Spring Framework is a comprehensive, modular Java application framework that provides infrastructure support for developing robust enterprise applications. It addresses the complexity of enterprise application development by offering a consistent programming and configuration model.

Core Philosophy: Spring enables developers to focus on business logic rather than dealing with low-level infrastructure concerns. It promotes best practices such as coding to interfaces, dependency injection, and aspect-oriented programming.

2003
Initial Release
6.0+
Java Version Support
20+
Modules & Projects

Key Features of Spring Framework

IoC Container

Manages Java objects (beans) and their dependencies through Dependency Injection, providing loose coupling and easier testing.

Aspect-Oriented Programming

Enables separation of cross-cutting concerns like logging, security, and transaction management.

Data Access Framework

Simplifies database operations with comprehensive transaction management and exception handling.

MVC Framework

Provides a robust web framework with flexible configuration and view resolution options.

Transaction Management

Offers consistent transaction management abstraction that can scale across local and global transactions.

Testing Support

Provides comprehensive testing support with mock objects, TestContext framework, and web test client.

Inversion of Control (IoC) in Spring

Understanding Inversion of Control

Inversion of Control is a design principle in which the control of object creation and dependency management is transferred from the application code to a framework or container.

Traditional Approach (Without IoC)

public class OrderService {
    private OrderRepository orderRepository;
    
    public OrderService() {
        // Control lies with the class itself
        this.orderRepository = new JdbcOrderRepository();
    }
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        orderRepository.save(order);
    }
}

// Problems:
// - Tight coupling to specific implementation
// - Difficult to test
// - Hard to change implementation
IoC Approach (With Spring)

@Component
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;
    
    // Control inverted to Spring Container
    @Autowired
    public OrderService(OrderRepository orderRepository) {
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
    }
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        orderRepository.save(order);
    }
}

// Benefits:
// - Loose coupling
// - Easy testing with mocks
// - Flexible implementation switching

Key Insight: IoC inverts the traditional control flow - instead of objects creating their dependencies, the container creates and injects dependencies where needed. This is often described as the "Hollywood Principle": "Don't call us, we'll call you."

Benefits of Inversion of Control

Loose Coupling

Components depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations.

Testability

Easy to mock dependencies for unit testing.

Flexibility

Easy to swap implementations without code changes.

Maintainability

Cleaner, more modular code structure.

Reusability

Components can be easily reused in different contexts.

Configuration

Dependencies can be configured externally.

Dependency Injection (DI)

What is Dependency Injection?

Dependency Injection is a design pattern and specific form of IoC where dependencies are "injected" into a class rather than the class creating them itself. It's the mechanism Spring uses to implement Inversion of Control. 


// Without Dependency Injection
public class CustomerService {
    private CustomerRepository customerRepository;
    
    public CustomerService() {
        // Class creates its own dependency - TIGHT COUPLING
        this.customerRepository = new JdbcCustomerRepository();
    }
}

// With Dependency Injection
@Component
public class CustomerService {
    private final CustomerRepository customerRepository;
    
    // Dependency is INJECTED by Spring - LOOSE COUPLING
    @Autowired
    public CustomerService(CustomerRepository customerRepository) {
        this.customerRepository = customerRepository;
    }
}

// Spring Configuration
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public CustomerRepository customerRepository() {
        return new JdbcCustomerRepository();
    }
    
    @Bean
    public CustomerService customerService() {
        // Spring injects the dependency
        return new CustomerService(customerRepository());
    }
}
Dependency Lookup (Traditional)
  • Component actively fetches dependencies
  • Uses service locator pattern
  • Tight coupling to lookup mechanism
  • Harder to test
Dependency Injection (Spring)
  • Dependencies are provided to component
  • Container manages dependency resolution
  • Loose coupling
  • Easy testing with mocks

Difference between IoC and DI

IoC vs DI: Understanding the Relationship

While often used interchangeably, IoC and DI are related but distinct concepts. IoC is the broader principle, and DI is the specific pattern used to implement IoC.

Aspect Inversion of Control (IoC) Dependency Injection (DI)
Definition Design principle where control is inverted Design pattern that implements IoC
Scope Broad concept covering various patterns Specific technique for dependency management
Relationship The principle or concept The implementation of the principle
Mechanism Framework calls application code Dependencies are injected into objects
Examples DI, Events, Callbacks, Templates Constructor, Setter, Field injection
Analogy: Hollywood Principle

IoC: "Don't call us, we'll call you" - the framework controls the flow.
DI: The specific way the framework "calls you" by providing your dependencies.

In Spring Context

IoC Container: The framework that manages object lifecycle.
DI: The mechanism used by the container to provide dependencies.

What is Spring Container?

Spring IoC Container

The Spring IoC container is the core of the Spring Framework. It's responsible for instantiating, configuring, and assembling beans (Java objects) and managing their complete lifecycle.

BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext

Spring Container Hierarchy

Spring provides two main container interfaces: BeanFactory and ApplicationContext. ApplicationContext is a superset of BeanFactory with additional enterprise-specific features.

Feature BeanFactory ApplicationContext
Bean Instantiation Lazy loading by default Eager loading of singleton beans
Internationalization No support Full MessageSource support
Event Handling No built-in support ApplicationEvent publication
AOP Integration Basic Seamless AOP integration
Resource Access Basic Enhanced Resource access
Performance Lightweight, less memory More features, slightly heavier
Usage Mobile devices, applets Most enterprise applications 

// BeanFactory Usage (rarely used directly)
BeanFactory factory = new XmlBeanFactory(
    new ClassPathResource("beans.xml")
);
MyService service = factory.getBean(MyService.class);

// ApplicationContext Usage (recommended)
ApplicationContext context = new ClassPathXmlApplicationContext("beans.xml");
// OR
ApplicationContext context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class);

MyService service = context.getBean(MyService.class);
Recommendation

Use ApplicationContext for almost all scenarios. It provides comprehensive enterprise features and is the container used in Spring Boot applications. BeanFactory is rarely used directly in modern Spring applications.

Types of Dependency Injection

Spring Dependency Injection Methods

Spring supports three main types of dependency injection, each with its own advantages and use cases.

Constructor Injection
@Component
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;
    
    @Autowired
    public OrderService(OrderRepository orderRepository) {
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
    }
}
  • Pros: Immutable, safe, testable
  • Cons: Many parameters can be cumbersome
  • Use when: Mandatory dependencies
Setter Injection
@Component
public class CustomerService {
    private CustomerRepository customerRepository;
    
    @Autowired
    public void setCustomerRepository(
            CustomerRepository customerRepository) {
        this.customerRepository = customerRepository;
    }
}
  • Pros: Flexible, optional dependencies
  • Cons: Mutable, object can be in incomplete state
  • Use when: Optional dependencies
Field Injection
@Component
public class ProductService {
    @Autowired
    private ProductRepository productRepository;
}
  • Pros: Concise, less boilerplate
  • Cons: Hard to test, hidden dependencies
  • Use when: Quick prototypes (not recommended for production)

Spring Team Recommendation: Use constructor injection for mandatory dependencies and setter injection for optional dependencies. Avoid field injection in production code as it makes testing more difficult and hides dependencies.

How Spring Achieves Loose Coupling

Loose Coupling Mechanisms in Spring

Spring promotes loose coupling through several mechanisms that reduce the dependencies between components and make the system more flexible and maintainable.

Dependency Injection
// Tight Coupling
public class OrderService {
    private OrderRepository repository = 
        new JdbcOrderRepository(); // Concrete implementation
}

// Loose Coupling with DI
public class OrderService {
    private OrderRepository repository; // Interface
    
    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository; // Injected implementation
    }
}

Components depend on abstractions (interfaces) rather than concrete implementations.

Interface-based Programming
public interface OrderRepository {
    void save(Order order);
}

@Component
public class JdbcOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
    public void save(Order order) { /* JDBC implementation */ }
}

@Component  
public class JpaOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
    public void save(Order order) { /* JPA implementation */ }
}

// Can switch implementations without changing client code

Programming to interfaces allows easy implementation swapping.

Aspect-Oriented Programming

Separates cross-cutting concerns from business logic.

Template Pattern

Eliminates boilerplate code in data access operations.

Event-driven Architecture

Decouples components through event publication/listening.

Result: Spring's loose coupling enables easier testing, maintenance, and evolution of applications. Components can be developed, tested, and modified independently, and implementations can be swapped without affecting dependent components.

Spring ApplicationContext Types: Complete Guide

Spring ApplicationContext Fundamentals

The ApplicationContext is Spring's advanced container interface that provides configuration capabilities to an application. It extends the BeanFactory interface and adds easier integration with Spring's AOP features, message resource handling, event publication, and application-layer specific contexts.

Core Responsibility: ApplicationContext is responsible for instantiating, configuring, and assembling the beans in your Spring application. Different implementations provide various ways to load configuration metadata based on your application's needs.

ClassPathXmlApplicationContext

Primary Use: Loads XML configuration files from the classpath. This is the most common implementation for standalone applications using XML configuration.

Key Characteristics

  • Configuration Source: Classpath resources
  • File Location: src/main/resources/
  • Prefix: classpath:
  • Use Case: Standalone applications, traditional Spring apps
  • Portability: High - works in JAR files and different environments

Implementation Examples


// Basic usage with single configuration file
ApplicationContext context = 
    new ClassPathXmlApplicationContext("applicationContext.xml");

// Multiple configuration files
ApplicationContext context = 
    new ClassPathXmlApplicationContext(
        "services.xml", 
        "daos.xml",
        "security.xml"
    );

// Using wildcards for multiple files
ApplicationContext context = 
    new ClassPathXmlApplicationContext("classpath*:app-*.xml");

// With explicit class loader
ApplicationContext context = 
    new ClassPathXmlApplicationContext(
        new String[] {"applicationContext.xml"},
        true,  // refresh context
        getClass().getClassLoader()
    );

// Project structure example:
// src/main/resources/
//   ├── applicationContext.xml
//   ├── services.xml
//   └── daos.xml

XML Configuration Example


<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<beans xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans"
       xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
       xmlns:context="http://www.springframework.org/schema/context"
       xsi:schemaLocation="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans
        http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans/spring-beans.xsd
        http://www.springframework.org/schema/context
        http://www.springframework.org/schema/context/spring-context.xsd">

    <!-- Enable component scanning -->
    <context:component-scan base-package="com.example.service"/>
    
    <!-- Bean definitions -->
    <bean id="userService" class="com.example.service.UserServiceImpl">
        <property name="userRepository" ref="userRepository"/>
    </bean>
    
    <bean id="userRepository" class="com.example.repository.JdbcUserRepository">
        <property name="dataSource" ref="dataSource"/>
    </bean>
    
    <bean id="dataSource" class="org.apache.commons.dbcp.BasicDataSource">
        <property name="driverClassName" value="com.mysql.jdbc.Driver"/>
        <property name="url" value="jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/mydb"/>
        <property name="username" value="root"/>
        <property name="password" value="password"/>
    </bean>

</beans>

Best Practice: Use classpath*: prefix when you want to load multiple configuration files with the same name from different JAR files in the classpath. The asterisk ensures all matching files are loaded.

FileSystemXmlApplicationContext

Primary Use: Loads XML configuration files from the file system or absolute paths. Useful for external configuration files outside the application package.

Key Characteristics

  • Configuration Source: File system paths
  • File Location: Any accessible file system location
  • Prefix: file: (optional)
  • Use Case: External configuration, development flexibility
  • Portability: Low - depends on specific file system paths

Implementation Examples


// Relative path from current working directory
ApplicationContext context = 
    new FileSystemXmlApplicationContext("config/applicationContext.xml");

// Absolute path
ApplicationContext context = 
    new FileSystemXmlApplicationContext("/etc/myapp/applicationContext.xml");

// Using file: prefix
ApplicationContext context = 
    new FileSystemXmlApplicationContext("file:config/services.xml");

// Multiple configuration files
ApplicationContext context = 
    new FileSystemXmlApplicationContext(
        "file:config/services.xml",
        "file:config/daos.xml"
    );

// Windows absolute path
ApplicationContext context = 
    new FileSystemXmlApplicationContext("C:/app/config/applicationContext.xml");

// With refresh option
ApplicationContext context = 
    new FileSystemXmlApplicationContext(
        new String[] {"file:config/app.xml"},
        true  // refresh automatically
    );

Use Cases and Considerations

Advantages
  • Easy configuration changes without rebuilding
  • External configuration management
  • Development-time flexibility
  • Integration with configuration management tools
  • Support for hot-reloading configuration
Disadvantages
  • Path dependencies reduce portability
  • Security concerns with file system access
  • Deployment complexity
  • Not suitable for cloud environments
  • Environment-specific configurations
Real-World Scenario

A financial application that needs different database configurations for development, testing, and production environments. Using FileSystemXmlApplicationContext, the operations team can place environment-specific configuration files in /etc/finance-app/ without modifying the application code or rebuilding the application.

AnnotationConfigApplicationContext

Primary Use: Standalone application context that accepts component classes (@Configuration classes) as input. This is the modern, annotation-driven approach for Java-based configuration.

Key Characteristics

  • Configuration Source: Java @Configuration classes
  • Programming Model: Annotation-driven, type-safe
  • Use Case: Modern Spring applications, Java config
  • Features: Component scanning, conditional beans
  • Integration: Perfect with Spring Boot

Implementation Examples


// Basic usage with @Configuration class
ApplicationContext context = 
    new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class);

// Multiple configuration classes
ApplicationContext context = 
    new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(
        DataSourceConfig.class,
        ServiceConfig.class,
        SecurityConfig.class
    );

// Using package scanning
AnnotationConfigApplicationContext context = 
    new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext();
context.scan("com.example.config", "com.example.service");
context.refresh();

// Mixed approach - configuration classes with component scanning
ApplicationContext context = 
    new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext();
((AnnotationConfigApplicationContext) context)
    .register(AppConfig.class, WebConfig.class);
((AnnotationConfigApplicationContext) context)
    .scan("com.example.components");
context.refresh();

// With environment profiles
AnnotationConfigApplicationContext context = 
    new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext();
context.getEnvironment().setActiveProfiles("development");
context.register(AppConfig.class);
context.refresh();

Java Configuration Examples

Basic Configuration Class

@Configuration
@ComponentScan("com.example.service")
@PropertySource("classpath:application.properties")
public class AppConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public UserService userService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        return new UserServiceImpl(userRepository);
    }
    
    @Bean
    public UserRepository userRepository(DataSource dataSource) {
        return new JdbcUserRepository(dataSource);
    }
    
    @Bean
    @Profile("development")
    public DataSource developmentDataSource() {
        return new EmbeddedDatabaseBuilder()
            .setType(EmbeddedDatabaseType.H2)
            .addScript("classpath:schema.sql")
            .build();
    }
    
    @Bean
    @Profile("production")
    public DataSource productionDataSource() {
        BasicDataSource dataSource = new BasicDataSource();
        dataSource.setDriverClassName("com.mysql.jdbc.Driver");
        dataSource.setUrl(env.getProperty("db.url"));
        dataSource.setUsername(env.getProperty("db.username"));
        dataSource.setPassword(env.getProperty("db.password"));
        return dataSource;
    }
    
    @Autowired
    private Environment env;
}
Advanced Configuration Features

@Configuration
@EnableAspectJAutoProxy
@EnableTransactionManagement
@EnableCaching
@EnableScheduling
public class AdvancedConfig {
    
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnClass(name = "com.redis.RedisClient")
    public CacheManager redisCacheManager() {
        return new RedisCacheManager(redisTemplate());
    }
    
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean(CacheManager.class)
    public CacheManager simpleCacheManager() {
        return new ConcurrentMapCacheManager();
    }
    
    @Bean
    @Lazy
    public ExpensiveService expensiveService() {
        return new ExpensiveService();
    }
    
    @Bean
    @Primary
    public MessageService emailMessageService() {
        return new EmailMessageService();
    }
    
    @Bean
    public MessageService smsMessageService() {
        return new SmsMessageService();
    }
    
    @Bean
    public static PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer propertyConfig() {
        return new PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer();
    }
}

Modern Spring Development: AnnotationConfigApplicationContext is the recommended approach for modern Spring applications. It provides type-safe configuration, better IDE support, and seamless integration with Spring Boot's auto-configuration.

WebApplicationContext

Primary Use: Web-aware application context that provides configuration for web applications. It extends ApplicationContext with web-specific features and is typically used in Servlet containers.

Key Characteristics

  • Environment: Servlet container (Tomcat, Jetty, etc.)
  • Scope: Web application scope
  • Features: Servlet context, request/session scope
  • Use Case: Spring MVC applications
  • Implementation: XmlWebApplicationContext, AnnotationConfigWebApplicationContext

Web-Specific Features

  • Servlet Context: Access to ServletContext
  • Scope Support: Request, session, application scopes
  • Theme Resolution: Web theme management
  • Multipart Support: File upload capabilities
  • URL Resources: Access to web application resources

Configuration and Setup

web.xml Configuration

<!-- web.xml -->
<web-app>
    <!-- ContextLoaderListener for root WebApplicationContext -->
    <listener>
        <listener-class>
            org.springframework.web.context.ContextLoaderListener
        </listener-class>
    </listener>
    
    <!-- Root application context configuration -->
    <context-param>
        <param-name>contextConfigLocation</param-name>
        <param-value>
            classpath:applicationContext.xml
            classpath:security-context.xml
        </param-value>
    </context-param>
    
    <!-- DispatcherServlet for MVC -->
    <servlet>
        <servlet-name>dispatcher</servlet-name>
        <servlet-class>
            org.springframework.web.servlet.DispatcherServlet
        </servlet-class>
        <init-param>
            <param-name>contextConfigLocation</param-name>
            <param-value>classpath:spring-mvc.xml</param-value>
        </init-param>
        <load-on-startup>1</load-on-startup>
    </servlet>
    
    <servlet-mapping>
        <servlet-name>dispatcher</servlet-name>
        <url-pattern>/</url-pattern>
    </servlet-mapping>
</web-app>
Java Config (Servlet 3.0+)

// Java-based web configuration
public class WebAppInitializer 
    extends AbstractAnnotationConfigDispatcherServletInitializer {
    
    @Override
    protected Class<?>[] getRootConfigClasses() {
        // Root application context (services, repositories)
        return new Class[] { RootConfig.class };
    }
    
    @Override
    protected Class<?>[] getServletConfigClasses() {
        // Servlet application context (controllers, web)
        return new Class[] { WebMvcConfig.class };
    }
    
    @Override
    protected String[] getServletMappings() {
        return new String[] { "/" };
    }
    
    @Override
    protected Filter[] getServletFilters() {
        return new Filter[] { 
            new CharacterEncodingFilter(), 
            new HiddenHttpMethodFilter() 
        };
    }
}

// Root configuration
@Configuration
@ComponentScan(
    basePackages = "com.example.service",
    excludeFilters = @ComponentScan.Filter(Controller.class)
)
public class RootConfig {
    // Service layer beans, data sources, etc.
}

// Web MVC configuration
@Configuration
@EnableWebMvc
@ComponentScan("com.example.controller")
public class WebMvcConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
    
    @Override
    public void configureViewResolvers(ViewResolverRegistry registry) {
        registry.jsp("/WEB-INF/views/", ".jsp");
    }
    
    @Bean
    public MultipartResolver multipartResolver() {
        return new StandardServletMultipartResolver();
    }
}

Web Scopes and Context Hierarchy


// Web-specific bean scopes
@Component
@Scope(value = WebApplicationContext.SCOPE_REQUEST, proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)
public class RequestScopedBean {
    // New instance created for each HTTP request
}

@Component
@Scope(value = WebApplicationContext.SCOPE_SESSION, proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)
public class UserPreferences {
    // Same instance for user's entire session
    private String theme = "light";
    private String language = "en";
    
    // getters and setters
}

@Component
@Scope(value = WebApplicationContext.SCOPE_APPLICATION)
public class ApplicationScopedBean {
    // Singleton for entire web application
}

// Accessing web context in beans
@Component
public class WebAwareService {
    
    @Autowired
    private ServletContext servletContext;
    
    @Autowired
    private HttpServletRequest request;
    
    @Autowired  
    private HttpServletResponse response;
    
    public void doSomething() {
        String contextPath = servletContext.getContextPath();
        String clientIP = request.getRemoteAddr();
        // Use web-specific features
    }
}

// Context hierarchy in web applications
// Root WebApplicationContext (shared across servlets)
//   ├── Services
//   ├── Repositories  
//   └── Data sources
//
// Servlet WebApplicationContext (per servlet)
//   ├── Controllers
//   ├── View resolvers
//   └── Web-specific beans

GenericApplicationContext

Primary Use: Generic implementation of ApplicationContext that can be configured with various configuration readers. It's highly flexible and serves as the base class for many other ApplicationContext implementations.

Key Characteristics

  • Flexibility: Can be configured with different bean definition readers
  • Base Class: Serves as base for many context implementations
  • Manual Control: Full control over refresh lifecycle
  • Use Case: Custom context implementations, testing
  • Extensibility: Easy to extend for custom requirements

Bean Definition Readers

  • XmlBeanDefinitionReader: Reads XML configuration
  • AnnotatedBeanDefinitionReader: Reads annotation configuration
  • ClassPathBeanDefinitionScanner: Scans for components
  • PropertiesBeanDefinitionReader: Reads properties files
  • GroovyBeanDefinitionReader: Reads Groovy configuration

Implementation Examples

XML Configuration Reader

// Using GenericApplicationContext with XML configuration
GenericApplicationContext context = new GenericApplicationContext();

// Create XML bean definition reader
XmlBeanDefinitionReader xmlReader = new XmlBeanDefinitionReader(context);
xmlReader.loadBeanDefinitions(
    new ClassPathResource("applicationContext.xml"),
    new FileSystemResource("config/services.xml")
);

// Refresh the context to initialize beans
context.refresh();

// Use the context
UserService userService = context.getBean(UserService.class);
Annotation Configuration Reader

// Using GenericApplicationContext with annotation configuration
GenericApplicationContext context = new GenericApplicationContext();

// Create annotated bean definition reader
AnnotatedBeanDefinitionReader annotatedReader = 
    new AnnotatedBeanDefinitionReader(context);

// Register configuration classes
annotatedReader.register(AppConfig.class, ServiceConfig.class);

// Create classpath scanner for component scanning
ClassPathBeanDefinitionScanner scanner = 
    new ClassPathBeanDefinitionScanner(context);
scanner.scan("com.example.components");

// Refresh the context
context.refresh();

// Use the context
MessageService messageService = context.getBean(MessageService.class);

Advanced Usage and Customization


// Custom GenericApplicationContext with programmatic bean registration
public class CustomApplicationContext extends GenericApplicationContext {
    
    public void initialize() {
        // Programmatically register beans
        registerBean("userService", UserService.class, 
            () -> new UserServiceImpl(getBean(UserRepository.class)));
        
        registerBean("userRepository", UserRepository.class, 
            JdbcUserRepository::new);
        
        registerBean("dataSource", DataSource.class, 
            () -> createDataSource());
        
        // Add bean factory post processors
        addBeanFactoryPostProcessor(new CustomBeanFactoryPostProcessor());
        
        // Add bean post processors  
        addBeanPostProcessor(new CustomBeanPostProcessor());
        
        // Refresh to initialize
        refresh();
    }
    
    private DataSource createDataSource() {
        BasicDataSource ds = new BasicDataSource();
        ds.setDriverClassName("org.h2.Driver");
        ds.setUrl("jdbc:h2:mem:testdb");
        return ds;
    }
}

// Using the custom context
public class Application {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CustomApplicationContext context = new CustomApplicationContext();
        context.initialize();
        
        UserService userService = context.getBean(UserService.class);
        userService.processUser();
        
        context.close();
    }
}

// Bean factory post processor example
public class CustomBeanFactoryPostProcessor implements BeanFactoryPostProcessor {
    @Override
    public void postProcessBeanFactory(ConfigurableListableBeanFactory beanFactory) {
        // Modify bean definitions before instantiation
        BeanDefinition bd = beanFactory.getBeanDefinition("userService");
        bd.setScope(BeanDefinition.SCOPE_PROTOTYPE);
        bd.getPropertyValues().add("timeout", 5000);
    }
}

Power and Flexibility: GenericApplicationContext provides the ultimate flexibility for Spring configuration. It's particularly useful for testing, framework development, and situations where you need programmatic control over the application context lifecycle.

FileSystemXmlApplicationContext XML configuration from file system XML files in file system External configuration Dev flexibility, external config
AnnotationConfigApplicationContext Java-based configuration @Configuration classes Modern Spring apps New projects, type-safe config
WebApplicationContext Web applications XML or Java config Spring MVC apps Web applications, servlet containers

Spring Bean Creation Process: Complete Lifecycle Guide

Spring Bean Creation Overview

The Spring Bean creation process is a sophisticated lifecycle that transforms simple Java classes into fully managed Spring beans. Understanding this process is crucial for effective Spring application development and troubleshooting.

Core Concept: Spring beans go through a complete lifecycle from instantiation to destruction, with multiple extension points for customization. The process involves dependency injection, post-processing, and proxy creation for AOP.

Bean Creation Process Flow

Spring Bean Lifecycle Complete Flow

1. Bean Definition
Configuration parsing & registration
▼
2. Instantiation
Constructor/factory method invocation
▼
3. Dependency Injection
Property setting & autowiring
▼
4. Aware Interfaces
BeanNameAware, BeanFactoryAware, etc.
▼
5. Bean Post Processors
Pre/Post initialization processing
▼
6. Initialization
@PostConstruct, InitializingBean
▼
7. Ready for Use
Fully initialized bean
▼
8. Destruction
@PreDestroy, DisposableBean

1. Bean Definition Phase

Bean Definition Sources & Registration

Before any beans can be created, Spring must first parse configuration sources and register bean definitions in the BeanFactory. 


// Different ways to define beans
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    
    // 1. @Bean method
    @Bean
    public MyService myService() {
        return new MyServiceImpl();
    }
    
    // 2. @Component scanning
    @Component
    public class MyComponent {
        // Auto-detected by component scanning
    }
}

// XML configuration alternative
<beans>
    <bean id="myService" class="com.example.MyServiceImpl"/>
    <context:component-scan base-package="com.example"/>
</beans>

// Programmatic registration
public class CustomBeanDefinitionRegistrar implements BeanDefinitionRegistrar {
    
    @Override
    public void registerBeanDefinitions(AnnotationMetadata metadata,
                                      BeanDefinitionRegistry registry) {
        
        RootBeanDefinition beanDefinition = new RootBeanDefinition(MyService.class);
        beanDefinition.setScope(BeanDefinition.SCOPE_SINGLETON);
        beanDefinition.setLazyInit(false);
        
        registry.registerBeanDefinition("myService", beanDefinition);
    }
}

// Bean definition attributes
public class BeanDefinitionDetails {
    /*
    Key BeanDefinition Properties:
    - beanClass: The class to instantiate
    - scope: singleton, prototype, request, session
    - lazyInit: whether to initialize lazily
    - dependsOn: explicit dependency ordering
    - autowireMode: how to autowire dependencies
    - initMethodName: custom initialization method
    - destroyMethodName: custom destruction method
    - constructorArgumentValues: constructor args
    - propertyValues: property values to set
    */
}
Configuration Sources
  • @Configuration classes with @Bean methods
  • @Component and stereotype annotations
  • XML configuration files
  • Java Config classes
  • Programmatic BeanDefinitionRegistry
Bean Definition Registry
  • DefaultListableBeanFactory - main registry
  • Bean definitions stored as BeanDefinition objects
  • Supports bean definition inheritance
  • Handles bean definition merging

Bean Definition Post Processing

BeanFactoryPostProcessors can modify bean definitions before any beans are instantiated. This is where configuration properties are resolved and bean definitions are customized. 


// Custom BeanFactoryPostProcessor
@Component
public class CustomBeanFactoryPostProcessor implements BeanFactoryPostProcessor {
    
    @Override
    public void postProcessBeanFactory(ConfigurableListableBeanFactory beanFactory) 
        throws BeansException {
        
        BeanDefinition bd = beanFactory.getBeanDefinition("myService");
        
        // Modify bean definition before instantiation
        bd.setLazyInit(true);
        bd.setScope(BeanDefinition.SCOPE_PROTOTYPE);
        
        // Add property values
        MutablePropertyValues pvs = bd.getPropertyValues();
        pvs.add("timeout", 5000);
        pvs.add("retryCount", 3);
    }
}

// PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer - resolves ${} placeholders
@Configuration
public class PropertyConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public static PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer propertyConfig() {
        PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer configurer = 
            new PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer();
        configurer.setLocation(new ClassPathResource("application.properties"));
        return configurer;
    }
}

// ConfigurationClassPostProcessor - processes @Configuration classes
// This is the most important BeanFactoryPostProcessor in Spring
// It parses @Configuration classes and registers @Bean methods

// Built-in BeanFactoryPostProcessors:
// - ConfigurationClassPostProcessor: Processes @Configuration classes
// - AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor: Processes @Autowired
// - CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor: Processes @PostConstruct, @PreDestroy
// - PersistenceAnnotationBeanPostProcessor: Processes @PersistenceContext

2. Bean Instantiation Phase

Bean Instantiation Strategies

Spring uses various strategies to instantiate beans, including constructor invocation, static factory methods, and instance factory methods. 


// Different instantiation approaches
@Component
public class InstantiationExamples {
    
    // 1. Constructor Instantiation (most common)
    @Component
    public class ConstructorBean {
        public ConstructorBean() {
            System.out.println("ConstructorBean instantiated via constructor");
        }
    }
    
    // 2. Static Factory Method
    public class StaticFactoryBean {
        private StaticFactoryBean() {}
        
        public static StaticFactoryBean createInstance() {
            return new StaticFactoryBean();
        }
    }
    
    // 3. Instance Factory Method
    public class InstanceFactory {
        public FactoryBean createFactoryBean() {
            return new FactoryBean();
        }
    }
    
    // 4. FactoryBean Interface
    @Component
    public class CustomFactoryBean implements FactoryBean<ComplexObject> {
        
        @Override
        public ComplexObject getObject() throws Exception {
            return new ComplexObject("configured", 100);
        }
        
        @Override
        public Class<?> getObjectType() {
            return ComplexObject.class;
        }
        
        @Override
        public boolean isSingleton() {
            return true;
        }
    }
}

// Configuration for factory methods
@Configuration
public class FactoryConfig {
    
    // Static factory method
    @Bean
    public StaticFactoryBean staticFactoryBean() {
        return StaticFactoryBean.createInstance();
    }
    
    // Instance factory method
    @Bean
    public FactoryBean factoryBean(InstanceFactory instanceFactory) {
        return instanceFactory.createFactoryBean();
    }
}

// Instantiation using BeanDefinition
public class CustomInstantiationStrategy implements InstantiationStrategy {
    
    @Override
    public Object instantiate(RootBeanDefinition bd, String beanName, BeanFactory owner) 
        throws BeansException {
        
        // Custom instantiation logic
        if (bd.getBeanClass() == ComplexBean.class) {
            return ComplexBean.createSpecialInstance();
        }
        
        // Fall back to default strategy
        return BeanUtils.instantiateClass(bd.getBeanClass());
    }
}
Instantiation Sequence
  1. Check if bean is a FactoryBean
  2. Resolve constructor arguments
  3. Choose constructor (if multiple)
  4. Instantiate using appropriate strategy
  5. Apply merged bean definition
Constructor Resolution
  • @Autowired constructor (if present)
  • Default constructor (if only one)
  • Constructor with most matching arguments
  • @Lookup methods for prototype dependencies

Constructor Resolution & Circular Dependencies


// Constructor resolution examples
@Component
public class ConstructorResolution {
    
    // Case 1: Single constructor - always used
    @Component
    public class SingleConstructorBean {
        private final Dependency dependency;
        
        // This constructor will be used
        public SingleConstructorBean(Dependency dependency) {
            this.dependency = dependency;
        }
    }
    
    // Case 2: Multiple constructors, one with @Autowired
    @Component
    public class MultipleConstructorsBean {
        private final Dependency1 dep1;
        private final Dependency2 dep2;
        
        public MultipleConstructorsBean() {
            this.dep1 = null;
            this.dep2 = null;
        }
        
        @Autowired  // This one will be used because of @Autowired
        public MultipleConstructorsBean(Dependency1 dep1, Dependency2 dep2) {
            this.dep1 = dep1;
            this.dep2 = dep2;
        }
    }
    
    // Case 3: No @Autowired, multiple constructors
    @Component
    public class AmbiguousConstructorsBean {
        private final String name;
        private final int count;
        
        public AmbiguousConstructorsBean(String name) {
            this.name = name;
            this.count = 0;
        }
        
        public AmbiguousConstructorsBean(int count) {
            this.name = "default";
            this.count = count;
        }
        
        // Spring will throw NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
        // Need @Autowired to specify which constructor to use
    }
}

// Circular dependency scenario
@Component
public class CircularDependencyA {
    private final CircularDependencyB dependencyB;
    
    @Autowired
    public CircularDependencyA(CircularDependencyB dependencyB) {
        this.dependencyB = dependencyB;
    }
}

@Component
public class CircularDependencyB {
    private final CircularDependencyA dependencyA;
    
    @Autowired
    public CircularDependencyB(CircularDependencyA dependencyA) {
        this.dependencyA = dependencyA;
    }
}

// Solution for circular dependencies - use setter injection
@Component
public class CircularDependencyASolution {
    private CircularDependencyB dependencyB;
    
    // Setter injection instead of constructor
    @Autowired
    public void setDependencyB(CircularDependencyB dependencyB) {
        this.dependencyB = dependencyB;
    }
}

// Or use @Lazy
@Component
public class CircularDependencyALazy {
    private final CircularDependencyB dependencyB;
    
    @Autowired
    public CircularDependencyALazy(@Lazy CircularDependencyB dependencyB) {
        this.dependencyB = dependencyB;
    }
}

Circular Dependency Limitation: Spring can only resolve circular dependencies when using setter injection or field injection. Constructor injection with circular dependencies will always fail during bean creation.

3. Dependency Injection Phase

Dependency Injection Methods

After instantiation, Spring injects dependencies through various mechanisms including constructor injection, setter injection, and field injection. 


@Component
public class DependencyInjectionExamples {
    
    // 1. Constructor Injection (Recommended)
    @Component
    public class ConstructorInjectionBean {
        private final UserRepository userRepository;
        private final EmailService emailService;
        
        @Autowired  // Optional in Spring 4.3+ for single constructor
        public ConstructorInjectionBean(UserRepository userRepository, 
                                      EmailService emailService) {
            this.userRepository = userRepository;
            this.emailService = emailService;
        }
    }
    
    // 2. Setter Injection
    @Component
    public class SetterInjectionBean {
        private UserRepository userRepository;
        private EmailService emailService;
        
        @Autowired
        public void setUserRepository(UserRepository userRepository) {
            this.userRepository = userRepository;
        }
        
        @Autowired
        public void setEmailService(EmailService emailService) {
            this.emailService = emailService;
        }
    }
    
    // 3. Field Injection
    @Component
    public class FieldInjectionBean {
        @Autowired
        private UserRepository userRepository;
        
        @Autowired
        private EmailService emailService;
    }
    
    // 4. Method Injection (any method with @Autowired)
    @Component
    public class MethodInjectionBean {
        private UserRepository userRepository;
        private EmailService emailService;
        
        @Autowired
        public void injectDependencies(UserRepository userRepository, 
                                     EmailService emailService) {
            this.userRepository = userRepository;
            this.emailService = emailService;
        }
    }
}

// Qualifier for disambiguation
@Component
public class QualifierExample {
    
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("primaryDataSource")
    private DataSource primaryDataSource;
    
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("secondaryDataSource") 
    private DataSource secondaryDataSource;
}

// Optional dependencies
@Component
public class OptionalDependencies {
    
    @Autowired(required = false)
    private OptionalDependency optionalDep; // Won't fail if bean not found
    
    @Autowired
    private Optional<AnotherOptional> anotherOptional;
}

// Collection injection
@Component
public class CollectionInjection {
    
    @Autowired
    private List<Validator> validators; // All Validator beans
    
    @Autowired
    private Map<String, Processor> processors; // Bean name -> Processor
    
    @Autowired
    private Set<EventListener> eventListeners; // All EventListener beans
}
Constructor Injection
  • Immutable dependencies
  • Clear dependencies
  • Testability
  • Recommended approach
Setter Injection
  • Optional dependencies
  • Circular dependencies
  • Reconfiguration
  • Flexible but mutable
Field Injection
  • Concise code
  • Less boilerplate
  • Harder to test
  • Not immutable

Autowiring Process & Resolution


// Autowiring process details
@Component
public class AutowiringProcess {
    
    // Autowiring happens through BeanPostProcessors
    // Main processor: AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor
    
    /*
    Autowiring Steps:
    1. Find all @Autowired fields, methods, constructors
    2. For each dependency:
       a. Determine required type
       b. Look up candidate beans in BeanFactory
       c. Apply @Qualifier filtering if present
       d. If multiple candidates, determine primary/@Priority
       e. If still ambiguous, throw NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
    3. Inject dependencies using reflection
    */
}

// Custom autowiring logic
@Component
public class CustomAutowireProcessor implements BeanPostProcessor {
    
    @Override
    public Object postProcessBeforeInitialization(Object bean, String beanName) 
        throws BeansException {
        
        // Custom autowiring logic
        if (bean instanceof CustomAutowireable) {
            autowireCustomFields(bean);
        }
        return bean;
    }
    
    private void autowireCustomFields(Object bean) {
        Field[] fields = bean.getClass().getDeclaredFields();
        for (Field field : fields) {
            if (field.isAnnotationPresent(CustomInject.class)) {
                // Custom dependency resolution logic
                Object dependency = resolveDependency(field.getType());
                field.setAccessible(true);
                try {
                    field.set(bean, dependency);
                } catch (IllegalAccessException e) {
                    throw new BeanCreationException("Failed to inject field", e);
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

// Dependency resolution strategies
public class DependencyResolution {
    /*
    Resolution Order:
    1. By Type (most common)
    2. By Name (fallback)
    3. @Qualifier annotation
    4. @Primary bean
    5. @Priority value
    6. Custom Conditionals (@Conditional)
    */
}

// @Primary for default bean
@Configuration
public class PrimaryConfig {
    
    @Bean
    @Primary  // This bean will be chosen when multiple DataSource beans exist
    public DataSource primaryDataSource() {
        return new PrimaryDataSource();
    }
    
    @Bean
    public DataSource secondaryDataSource() {
        return new SecondaryDataSource();
    }
}

4. Aware Interfaces & Bean Post Processors

Aware Interfaces

Aware interfaces allow beans to be notified of and access Spring container infrastructure. These callbacks happen after dependency injection but before initialization. 


@Component
public class AwareInterfaceExamples implements 
        BeanNameAware, BeanFactoryAware, ApplicationContextAware,
        EnvironmentAware, ResourceLoaderAware, MessageSourceAware {
    
    private String beanName;
    private BeanFactory beanFactory;
    private ApplicationContext applicationContext;
    private Environment environment;
    private ResourceLoader resourceLoader;
    private MessageSource messageSource;
    
    // 1. BeanNameAware - know your own bean name
    @Override
    public void setBeanName(String name) {
        this.beanName = name;
        System.out.println("Bean name: " + name);
    }
    
    // 2. BeanFactoryAware - access BeanFactory
    @Override
    public void setBeanFactory(BeanFactory beanFactory) throws BeansException {
        this.beanFactory = beanFactory;
    }
    
    // 3. ApplicationContextAware - access ApplicationContext
    @Override
    public void setApplicationContext(ApplicationContext applicationContext) 
        throws BeansException {
        this.applicationContext = applicationContext;
    }
    
    // 4. EnvironmentAware - access Environment
    @Override
    public void setEnvironment(Environment environment) {
        this.environment = environment;
    }
    
    // 5. ResourceLoaderAware - access ResourceLoader
    @Override
    public void setResourceLoader(ResourceLoader resourceLoader) {
        this.resourceLoader = resourceLoader;
    }
    
    // 6. MessageSourceAware - access MessageSource
    @Override
    public void setMessageSource(MessageSource messageSource) {
        this.messageSource = messageSource;
    }
    
    // Other Aware interfaces:
    // - ApplicationEventPublisherAware
    // - EmbeddedValueResolverAware
    // - LoadTimeWeaverAware
    // - NotificationPublisherAware (JMX)
}

// Custom Aware interface
public interface CustomContextAware {
    void setCustomContext(CustomContext context);
}

@Component
public class CustomContextAwareProcessor implements BeanPostProcessor {
    
    @Override
    public Object postProcessBeforeInitialization(Object bean, String beanName) 
        throws BeansException {
        
        if (bean instanceof CustomContextAware) {
            ((CustomContextAware) bean).setCustomContext(new CustomContext());
        }
        return bean;
    }
}

Bean Post Processors

BeanPostProcessors are the most powerful extension point in Spring's bean lifecycle. They can modify or replace beans before and after initialization. 


// Custom BeanPostProcessor
@Component
public class CustomBeanPostProcessor implements BeanPostProcessor {
    
    // Called before initialization (@PostConstruct, InitializingBean)
    @Override
    public Object postProcessBeforeInitialization(Object bean, String beanName) 
        throws BeansException {
        
        System.out.println("Before initialization: " + beanName);
        
        // Example: Add logging to all services
        if (bean instanceof Loggable) {
            return createLoggingProxy(bean);
        }
        
        return bean;
    }
    
    // Called after initialization (@PostConstruct, InitializingBean)
    @Override
    public Object postProcessAfterInitialization(Object bean, String beanName) 
        throws BeansException {
        
        System.out.println("After initialization: " + beanName);
        
        // Example: Wrap with transaction proxy
        if (bean.getClass().isAnnotationPresent(Transactional.class)) {
            return createTransactionProxy(bean);
        }
        
        return bean;
    }
    
    private Object createLoggingProxy(Object target) {
        return Proxy.newProxyInstance(
            target.getClass().getClassLoader(),
            target.getClass().getInterfaces(),
            (proxy, method, args) -> {
                System.out.println("Before method: " + method.getName());
                Object result = method.invoke(target, args);
                System.out.println("After method: " + method.getName());
                return result;
            });
    }
}

// Important built-in BeanPostProcessors:
@Component
public class BuiltInPostProcessors {
    /*
    1. AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor - processes @Autowired
    2. CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor - processes @PostConstruct, @PreDestroy
    3. PersistenceAnnotationBeanPostProcessor - processes @PersistenceContext
    4. ApplicationContextAwareProcessor - processes Aware interfaces
    5. AbstractAutoProxyCreator - creates AOP proxies
    */
}

// BeanPostProcessor ordering
@Component
@Order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE) // Execute first
public class HighPriorityPostProcessor implements BeanPostProcessor {
    // This will execute before other BeanPostProcessors
}

@Component  
@Order(Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE) // Execute last
public class LowPriorityPostProcessor implements BeanPostProcessor {
    // This will execute after other BeanPostProcessors
}

Important: BeanPostProcessors are themselves beans and go through the same lifecycle. However, they are instantiated early in the process so they can process other beans. BeanPostProcessors cannot process other BeanPostProcessors.

5. Initialization Phase

Initialization Methods

After dependency injection and post-processing, beans are initialized through various callback mechanisms including @PostConstruct, InitializingBean, and custom init methods. 


@Component
public class InitializationExamples implements InitializingBean {
    
    private List<String> data;
    private boolean initialized = false;
    
    // 1. @PostConstruct (JSR-250) - Recommended approach
    @PostConstruct
    public void postConstruct() {
        System.out.println("@PostConstruct called");
        this.data = loadInitialData();
        validateConfiguration();
    }
    
    // 2. InitializingBean interface
    @Override
    public void afterPropertiesSet() throws Exception {
        System.out.println("InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet called");
        this.initialized = true;
        
        // @PostConstruct runs before InitializingBean
    }
    
    // 3. Custom init method (XML or @Bean(initMethod))
    public void customInit() {
        System.out.println("Custom init method called");
        // Runs after @PostConstruct and InitializingBean
    }
    
    // Initialization order for this bean:
    // 1. @PostConstruct postConstruct()
    // 2. InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()  
    // 3. customInit() (if configured)
    
    private List<String> loadInitialData() {
        return Arrays.asList("data1", "data2", "data3");
    }
    
    private void validateConfiguration() {
        if (data == null || data.isEmpty()) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Data not loaded properly");
        }
    }
}

// Configuration with custom init method
@Configuration
public class InitMethodConfig {
    
    @Bean(initMethod = "customInit", destroyMethod = "cleanup")
    public InitializationExamples initializationExamples() {
        return new InitializationExamples();
    }
}

// XML configuration equivalent
<bean id="initializationExamples" 
      class="com.example.InitializationExamples"
      init-method="customInit"
      destroy-method="cleanup"/>

// @PostConstruct with dependencies
@Component
public class DatabaseInitializer {
    
    private final DataSource dataSource;
    private final JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate;
    
    @Autowired
    public DatabaseInitializer(DataSource dataSource) {
        this.dataSource = dataSource;
        this.jdbcTemplate = new JdbcTemplate(dataSource);
    }
    
    @PostConstruct
    public void initializeDatabase() {
        // All dependencies are injected at this point
        jdbcTemplate.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (...)");
        System.out.println("Database initialized");
    }
}
@PostConstruct
  • JSR-250 standard
  • Runs first in initialization
  • Recommended approach
  • Works with any method name
InitializingBean
  • Spring-specific interface
  • Runs after @PostConstruct
  • Tightly coupled to Spring
  • Fixed method name
Custom Init
  • Configurable method name
  • Runs last in initialization
  • No interface dependency
  • XML or Java config

6. Bean Scopes & Special Beans

Bean Scopes

Spring supports different bean scopes that control the lifecycle and instance creation strategy. 


@Component
@Scope("singleton") // Default scope
public class SingletonBean {
    // One instance per Spring container
    // Created at startup (unless lazy)
}

@Component
@Scope("prototype")
public class PrototypeBean {
    // New instance every time bean is requested
    // Created when getBean() is called
}

@Component
@Scope(value = "request", proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)
public class RequestScopedBean {
    // One instance per HTTP request
    // Web application context only
}

@Component
@Scope(value = "session", proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS) 
public class SessionScopedBean {
    // One instance per HTTP session
    // Web application context only
}

@Component
@Scope(value = "application")
public class ApplicationScopedBean {
    // One instance per ServletContext
    // Web application context only
}

// Custom scope
@Component
public class CustomScopeConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public CustomScope customScope() {
        return new CustomScope();
    }
    
    @Bean
    public static CustomScopeRegistry scopeRegistry() {
        return new CustomScopeRegistry();
    }
}

// Lazy initialization
@Component
@Lazy
public class LazyBean {
    // Created only when first requested
    // Useful for expensive-to-create beans
    
    public LazyBean() {
        System.out.println("LazyBean created on first access");
    }
}
Scope Description When Created Use Case
singleton Single instance per container At startup (or first use if lazy) Services, repositories, utilities
prototype New instance each time Every getBean() call Stateful objects, user sessions
request Per HTTP request Each HTTP request Request-specific data
session Per HTTP session Each HTTP session User-specific data
application Per ServletContext Web app startup Application-wide data

Special Bean Types


// FactoryBean - creates objects of a different type
@Component
public class CustomFactoryBean implements FactoryBean<ComplexObject> {
    
    @Override
    public ComplexObject getObject() throws Exception {
        return new ComplexObject("configured", 42);
    }
    
    @Override
    public Class<?> getObjectType() {
        return ComplexObject.class;
    }
    
    @Override
    public boolean isSingleton() {
        return true;
    }
}

// Usage: Getting the FactoryBean itself vs its product
@Service
public class FactoryBeanUsage {
    
    @Autowired
    private ComplexObject complexObject; // The product
    
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("&customFactoryBean") 
    private CustomFactoryBean factoryBean; // The factory itself
}

// BeanFactoryPostProcessor - modifies bean definitions
@Component
public class CustomBeanFactoryPostProcessor implements BeanFactoryPostProcessor {
    
    @Override
    public void postProcessBeanFactory(ConfigurableListableBeanFactory beanFactory) 
        throws BeansException {
        
        // Modify bean definitions before instantiation
        BeanDefinition bd = beanFactory.getBeanDefinition("someBean");
        bd.setLazyInit(true);
    }
}

// ImportSelector - conditionally import configurations
public class CustomImportSelector implements ImportSelector {
    
    @Override
    public String[] selectImports(AnnotationMetadata importingClassMetadata) {
        // Conditionally return configuration classes to import
        if (isProduction()) {
            return new String[]{"com.example.ProductionConfig"};
        } else {
            return new String[]{"com.example.DevelopmentConfig"};
        }
    }
}

// BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor - register new bean definitions
@Component
public class CustomRegistryPostProcessor implements BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor {
    
    @Override
    public void postProcessBeanDefinitionRegistry(BeanDefinitionRegistry registry) 
        throws BeansException {
        
        // Register new bean definitions programmatically
        GenericBeanDefinition bd = new GenericBeanDefinition();
        bd.setBeanClass(DynamicService.class);
        registry.registerBeanDefinition("dynamicService", bd);
    }
    
    @Override
    public void postProcessBeanFactory(ConfigurableListableBeanFactory beanFactory) 
        throws BeansException {
        // Modify bean factory if needed
    }
}

Bean Creation Quick Reference

Lifecycle Phases

  1. Bean Definition
  2. Instantiation
  3. Dependency Injection
  4. Aware Interfaces
  5. Post Processors
  6. Initialization
  7. Ready
  8. Destruction

Initialization Order

  1. @PostConstruct
  2. InitializingBean
  3. Custom init method

Bean Scopes

  • singleton (default)
  • prototype
  • request
  • session
  • application

Special Beans

  • FactoryBean
  • BeanPostProcessor
  • BeanFactoryPostProcessor
  • ImportSelector

Critical Bean Creation Rules

  • BeanPostProcessors are instantiated early and can process other beans
  • FactoryBeans create objects of a different type than themselves
  • Circular dependencies require setter/field injection, not constructor
  • @PostConstruct runs before InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()
  • Prototype beans are not destroyed by the container
  • BeanFactoryPostProcessors run before any beans are instantiated

Spring Dependency Injection: Complete Guide with Examples

Dependency Injection Overview

Dependency Injection (DI) is a fundamental design pattern and core feature of the Spring Framework that enables loose coupling between components, making applications more maintainable, testable, and scalable.

Core Concept: Dependency Injection is the process where objects define their dependencies (other objects they work with) and an external container (Spring IoC) injects those dependencies rather than the objects creating them directly.

What is Dependency Injection (DI) in Spring?

Dependency Injection Definition

Dependency Injection is a design pattern that implements Inversion of Control (IoC) for resolving dependencies. Instead of objects creating their own dependencies, dependencies are provided (injected) by an external entity.

Without DI (Traditional Approach)
public class OrderService {
    private PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor;
    private EmailService emailService;
    
    public OrderService() {
        // Tight coupling - creating dependencies internally
        this.paymentProcessor = new PaymentProcessor();
        this.emailService = new EmailService();
        // Hard to test, hard to change implementations
    }
}

Tight coupling, hard to test

With DI (Spring Approach)
@Service
public class OrderService {
    private PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor;
    private EmailService emailService;
    
    // Dependencies injected by Spring
    public OrderService(PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor, 
                       EmailService emailService) {
        this.paymentProcessor = paymentProcessor;
        this.emailService = emailService;
        // Loose coupling, easy to test and maintain
    }
}

Loose coupling, easy to test

Key Point: In Spring, the ApplicationContext (IoC Container) is responsible for creating and managing beans, and injecting dependencies where needed.

Advantages of Using Dependency Injection

Loose Coupling

Components don't depend on concrete implementations, only interfaces

Testability

Easy to mock dependencies for unit testing

Maintainability

Easy to change implementations without modifying dependent classes

Reusability

Components can be easily reused in different contexts

Configurability

Dependencies can be configured externally (XML, Java Config, Annotations)

Readability

Dependencies are explicitly declared, making code easier to understand


// EXAMPLE: Testing with DI (Easy mocking)
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class OrderServiceTest {
    
    @Mock
    private PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor;
    
    @Mock
    private EmailService emailService;
    
    @InjectMocks
    private OrderService orderService;
    
    @Test
    void shouldProcessOrderSuccessfully() {
        // Given
        Order order = new Order();
        when(paymentProcessor.process(any())).thenReturn(true);
        
        // When
        boolean result = orderService.processOrder(order);
        
        // Then
        assertTrue(result);
        verify(emailService).sendConfirmation(order);
    }
}

// Without DI, testing would be much harder - 
// would need to use PowerMock or other complex tools

Dependency Injection vs Dependency Lookup

Dependency Injection vs Dependency Lookup

While both approaches manage dependencies, they differ in how dependencies are obtained and who controls the process.

Aspect Dependency Injection Dependency Lookup
Control Flow Container injects dependencies (Hollywood Principle) Component looks up dependencies actively
Coupling Loose coupling to container Tight coupling to lookup mechanism
Testability Easy - dependencies can be mocked Harder - requires mock lookup context
Complexity Container manages complexity Component manages complexity
Dependency Lookup (EJB Style)
public class OrderService {
    private PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor;
    
    public OrderService() {
        // Actively looking up dependency
        Context context = new InitialContext();
        this.paymentProcessor = (PaymentProcessor) 
            context.lookup("java:comp/env/PaymentProcessor");
        // Tight coupling to JNDI, hard to test
    }
}

Component actively fetches dependencies

Dependency Injection (Spring Style)
@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor;
    
    // Dependencies provided by container
    public OrderService(PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor) {
        this.paymentProcessor = paymentProcessor;
        // No container coupling in business logic
    }
}

Container provides dependencies passively

Inversion of Control (IoC) vs Dependency Injection (DI)

IoC vs DI Relationship

Inversion of Control (IoC) is a broader design principle, while Dependency Injection is a specific pattern that implements IoC for dependency management.

Inversion of Control (IoC)

Principle: Inverting the control flow - framework calls application code rather than application calling framework.

  • Generic principle about control flow
  • "Don't call us, we'll call you"
  • Framework controls program execution
  • Includes DI, events, templates, etc.
Dependency Injection (DI)

Pattern: Specific implementation of IoC for dependency management.

  • Specific pattern for dependencies
  • External entity provides dependencies
  • Eliminates direct dependency creation
  • One way to achieve IoC

// IoC EXAMPLE: Template pattern (another IoC implementation)
@Repository
public class UserRepository {
    
    private final JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate;
    
    public UserRepository(JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate) {
        this.jdbcTemplate = jdbcTemplate;
    }
    
    // Framework controls the transaction, connection management
    // Application just provides the business logic (callback)
    public List<User> findAll() {
        return jdbcTemplate.query(
            "SELECT * FROM users", 
            (rs, rowNum) -> new User(
                rs.getLong("id"),
                rs.getString("name"),
                rs.getString("email")
            )
        );
    }
}

// DI is the mechanism Spring uses to provide JdbcTemplate to UserRepository

Analogy: IoC is like a Hollywood agent (manages your career calls), while DI is specifically how the agent gets you roles (injects opportunities).

How Spring Implements Dependency Injection

Spring DI Implementation Mechanism

Spring implements DI through its IoC Container (ApplicationContext) which manages the complete lifecycle of beans and their dependencies. 


// 1. COMPONENT SCANNING
@Component
public class PaymentProcessor {
    public boolean process(Payment payment) {
        // payment processing logic
        return true;
    }
}

@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor;
    
    // 2. CONSTRUCTOR INJECTION (Recommended)
    public OrderService(PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor) {
        this.paymentProcessor = paymentProcessor;
    }
    
    public boolean placeOrder(Order order) {
        return paymentProcessor.process(order.getPayment());
    }
}

// 3. SPRING BOOT AUTOCONFIGURATION
@SpringBootApplication
public class Application {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 4. APPLICATION CONTEXT INITIALIZATION
        ApplicationContext context = 
            SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args);
        
        // 5. DEPENDENCY RESOLUTION
        OrderService orderService = context.getBean(OrderService.class);
        orderService.placeOrder(new Order());
    }
}

// SPRING'S INTERNAL PROCESS:
// 1. Component Scan → finds @Component, @Service, @Repository classes
// 2. Bean Definition → creates BeanDefinition for each component
// 3. Dependency Analysis → analyzes constructor/method parameters
// 4. Bean Creation → instantiates beans in correct order
// 5. Dependency Injection → injects dependencies through constructor/setter
// 6. Post-processing → applies @PostConstruct, proxies, etc.
Component Scanning
Finds classes with Spring annotations
Bean Creation
Instantiates beans in correct order
Dependency Injection
Injects dependencies via constructor/setter

Types of Dependency Injection in Spring

Constructor-based Dependency Injection

Dependencies are provided through a class constructor. This is the recommended approach as it ensures that required dependencies are available when the object is created. 


@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    private final PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor;
    private final EmailService emailService;
    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;
    
    // Constructor Injection (Spring automatically detects and injects)
    public OrderService(PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor,
                       EmailService emailService,
                       OrderRepository orderRepository) {
        this.paymentProcessor = paymentProcessor;
        this.emailService = emailService;
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
    }
    
    // Explicit @Autowired (optional for single constructor)
    @Autowired
    public OrderService(PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor,
                       EmailService emailService,
                       OrderRepository orderRepository) {
        this.paymentProcessor = paymentProcessor;
        this.emailService = emailService;
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
    }
    
    // With @Qualifier for multiple beans of same type
    @Autowired
    public OrderService(@Qualifier("creditCardProcessor") PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor,
                       EmailService emailService,
                       OrderRepository orderRepository) {
        this.paymentProcessor = paymentProcessor;
        this.emailService = emailService;
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
    }
    
    public Order processOrder(OrderRequest request) {
        Order order = createOrder(request);
        orderRepository.save(order);
        
        boolean paymentSuccess = paymentProcessor.process(order);
        if (paymentSuccess) {
            emailService.sendConfirmation(order);
            order.confirm();
        }
        
        return order;
    }
}

// Configuration for multiple PaymentProcessor implementations
@Configuration
public class PaymentConfig {
    
    @Bean
    @Qualifier("creditCardProcessor")
    public PaymentProcessor creditCardProcessor() {
        return new CreditCardProcessor();
    }
    
    @Bean
    @Qualifier("paypalProcessor") 
    public PaymentProcessor paypalProcessor() {
        return new PayPalProcessor();
    }
}
Advantages
  • Immutability - fields can be final
  • Thread-safe object creation
  • Clear required dependencies
  • Easy testing with mocks
  • No circular dependency issues
Considerations
  • Many dependencies can make constructor large
  • All dependencies must be available at creation
  • Can be verbose for simple cases

Setter-based Dependency Injection

Dependencies are injected through setter methods. This allows for optional dependencies and reconfiguration of dependencies after object creation. 


@Service
public class NotificationService {
    
    private EmailService emailService;
    private SmsService smsService;
    private PushNotificationService pushService;
    
    // No-argument constructor
    public NotificationService() {
        // Dependencies will be set via setters
    }
    
    // Setter injection with @Autowired
    @Autowired
    public void setEmailService(EmailService emailService) {
        this.emailService = emailService;
    }
    
    @Autowired
    public void setSmsService(SmsService smsService) {
        this.smsService = smsService;
    }
    
    // Optional dependency (required = false)
    @Autowired(required = false)
    public void setPushService(PushNotificationService pushService) {
        this.pushService = pushService;
    }
    
    // Multiple setters for same type with @Qualifier
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("primaryEmailService")
    public void setPrimaryEmailService(EmailService emailService) {
        this.emailService = emailService;
    }
    
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("secondaryEmailService") 
    public void setSecondaryEmailService(EmailService emailService) {
        // For backup or different purpose
    }
    
    public void sendNotifications(User user, String message) {
        emailService.send(user.getEmail(), message);
        
        if (user.hasPhone()) {
            smsService.send(user.getPhone(), message);
        }
        
        // Optional dependency check
        if (pushService != null && user.hasPushEnabled()) {
            pushService.send(user.getDeviceId(), message);
        }
    }
}

// XML configuration equivalent (legacy)
<bean id="notificationService" class="com.example.NotificationService">
    <property name="emailService" ref="emailService"/>
    <property name="smsService" ref="smsService"/>
    <property name="pushService" ref="pushService"/>
</bean>
Advantages
  • Optional dependencies supported
  • Can reconfigure dependencies later
  • More flexible for complex scenarios
  • Compatible with JavaBeans standard
Considerations
  • Object can be in incomplete state
  • Not immutable - state can change
  • Circular dependency possible
  • Harder to ensure required dependencies

Field-based Dependency Injection

Dependencies are injected directly into fields using reflection. While convenient, this approach has several drawbacks and is generally not recommended. 


@Service
public class ProductService {
    
    // FIELD INJECTION (Not recommended)
    @Autowired
    private ProductRepository productRepository;
    
    @Autowired
    private CategoryRepository categoryRepository;
    
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("cacheService")
    private CacheService cacheService;
    
    // Optional dependency
    @Autowired(required = false)
    private AuditService auditService;
    
    // With @Resource (JSR-250) - by name
    @Resource(name = "inventoryService")
    private InventoryService inventoryService;
    
    // With @Inject (JSR-330) - similar to @Autowired
    @Inject
    private PriceCalculator priceCalculator;
    
    public Product getProductById(Long id) {
        // Problem: Can be called without dependencies being injected
        // if someone uses new ProductService() directly
        return productRepository.findById(id).orElse(null);
    }
}

// PROBLEMATIC USAGE:
public class ProductController {
    
    @Autowired
    private ProductService productService; // Field injection
    
    // Constructor is needed for testing but might be missing
    // If someone adds: public ProductController() { }
    // Then productService will be null!
    
    public Product getProduct(Long id) {
        return productService.getProductById(id); // NPE risk
    }
}
Advantages
  • Very concise - less boilerplate
  • Quick to write and read
  • Popular in legacy code
Disadvantages
  • Cannot make fields final (not immutable)
  • Hard to test - requires reflection or Spring context
  • Hides dependencies - not explicit in API
  • Circular dependency issues
  • Violates encapsulation principles

Recommended Dependency Injection Approach

Which DI Method is Recommended and Why?

Constructor-based injection is generally recommended by the Spring team and modern Java development practices for most scenarios.

Criteria Constructor Setter Field
Immutability ✅ Excellent ❌ Poor ❌ Poor
Testability ✅ Excellent ⚠️ Moderate ❌ Poor
Readability ✅ Excellent ✅ Good ⚠️ Hidden
Circular Dependencies ✅ Prevented ❌ Possible ❌ Possible
Spring Team Recommendation ✅ Recommended ⚠️ Optional deps ❌ Not recommended
Use Constructor Injection When:
  • Dependencies are mandatory
  • You want immutable objects
  • Testing is important
  • You want to avoid circular dependencies
  • Most business service classes
Use Setter Injection When:
  • Dependencies are optional
  • You need to reconfigure dependencies
  • Working with legacy code that requires no-arg constructor
  • Using JavaBeans compatible frameworks

// RECOMMENDED APPROACH: Constructor Injection
@Service
public class RecommendedOrderService {
    
    private final PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor;
    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;
    private final EmailService emailService;
    
    // Single constructor - no @Autowired needed (Spring 4.3+)
    public RecommendedOrderService(PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor,
                                  OrderRepository orderRepository,
                                  EmailService emailService) {
        this.paymentProcessor = paymentProcessor;
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
        this.emailService = emailService;
    }
    
    // Clean testing - no Spring context needed
    @Test
    void shouldProcessOrder() {
        // Arrange
        PaymentProcessor mockProcessor = mock(PaymentProcessor.class);
        OrderRepository mockRepo = mock(OrderRepository.class);
        EmailService mockEmail = mock(EmailService.class);
        
        RecommendedOrderService service = 
            new RecommendedOrderService(mockProcessor, mockRepo, mockEmail);
        
        // Act & Assert
        // ... clean test code
    }
}

// With Lombok (even cleaner)
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class LombokOrderService {
    
    private final PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor;
    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;
    private final EmailService emailService;
    
    // Lombok generates constructor automatically
    // Clean, immutable, testable
}

Spring Official Stance: Since Spring 4.3, if a class has only one constructor, @Autowired is not required. The Spring team recommends using constructor injection for mandatory dependencies and setter injection for optional dependencies. Field injection is discouraged.

Dependency Injection Quick Reference

DI Types

  • Constructor Injection
  • Setter Injection
  • Field Injection
  • Method Injection

Annotations

  • @Autowired
  • @Qualifier
  • @Resource
  • @Inject

Concepts

  • Inversion of Control
  • Dependency Lookup
  • Loose Coupling
  • Bean Lifecycle

Best Practices

  • Prefer constructor injection
  • Use final fields when possible
  • Avoid field injection
  • Test without Spring context

Critical DI Rules

  • Always use constructor injection for mandatory dependencies
  • Use setter injection only for optional dependencies
  • Avoid field injection in new code
  • Make dependencies final with constructor injection
  • Test classes without Spring container when possible
  • Use @Qualifier for multiple beans of same type

Spring Dependency Injection: Complete Injection Methods Guide

Constructor Injection

When to Use Constructor Injection

Constructor injection is the preferred and recommended approach for dependency injection in Spring. It ensures that required dependencies are provided when the object is created, making the class immutable and thread-safe. 


// RECOMMENDED: Constructor injection for mandatory dependencies
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;
    private final PaymentService paymentService;
    private final NotificationService notificationService;
    
    // Constructor with all mandatory dependencies
    @Autowired
    public OrderService(OrderRepository orderRepository,
                       PaymentService paymentService,
                       NotificationService notificationService) {
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
