        this.notificationService = notificationService;
    }
    
    // Business methods can assume all dependencies are available
    public Order processOrder(Order order) {
        Order savedOrder = orderRepository.save(order);
        paymentService.processPayment(order);
        notificationService.sendConfirmation(order);
        return savedOrder;
    }
}

// Even better: Omit @Autowired in Spring 4.3+ for single constructor
@Service
public class UserService {
    
    private final UserRepository userRepository;
    private final PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder;
    
    // Spring automatically uses this constructor for injection
    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository, 
                      PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
        this.passwordEncoder = passwordEncoder;
    }
}
Use Constructor Injection When:
  • Dependencies are mandatory for the class to function
  • You want immutable and thread-safe components
  • Testing requires explicit dependency passing
  • You want to avoid circular dependencies
  • Class state should be fully initialized after construction
Benefits:
  • Immutability: Fields can be final
  • Thread Safety: No setter methods
  • Clear Contracts: Explicit dependencies
  • Testability: Easy to mock in tests
  • Null Safety: Dependencies guaranteed

Spring Recommendation: Since Spring 4.3, if a class has only one constructor, @Autowired is not required. For multiple constructors, you still need to annotate the one you want Spring to use.

Setter Injection

When to Use Setter Injection

Setter injection is useful for optional dependencies or when you need to change dependencies at runtime. It provides more flexibility but sacrifices immutability. 


@Service
public class ReportService {
    
    private ReportGenerator reportGenerator;
    private EmailService emailService; // Optional dependency
    private FormatService formatService; // Optional dependency
    
    // Mandatory dependency via constructor
    public ReportService(ReportGenerator reportGenerator) {
        this.reportGenerator = reportGenerator;
    }
    
    // Optional dependencies via setter injection
    @Autowired
    public void setEmailService(EmailService emailService) {
        this.emailService = emailService;
    }
    
    @Autowired(required = false) // Truly optional dependency
    public void setFormatService(FormatService formatService) {
        this.formatService = formatService;
    }
    
    // Setter with custom logic
    @Autowired
    public void setNotificationService(NotificationService notificationService) {
        // Custom initialization logic
        notificationService.configure("REPORT_SERVICE");
        this.notificationService = notificationService;
    }
    
    public void generateReport(ReportRequest request) {
        Report report = reportGenerator.generate(request);
        
        // Use optional dependency if available
        if (formatService != null) {
            report = formatService.format(report);
        }
        
        if (emailService != null) {
            emailService.sendReport(report);
        }
    }
}

// Setter injection in configuration classes
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    
    private DataSource dataSource;
    
    @Autowired
    public void setDataSource(DataSource dataSource) {
        this.dataSource = dataSource;
    }
    
    @Bean
    public JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate() {
        return new JdbcTemplate(dataSource);
    }
}
Use Setter Injection When:
  • Dependencies are optional
  • You need to change dependencies at runtime
  • Class has reasonable defaults
  • You need custom initialization logic
  • Working with legacy code that uses JavaBeans pattern
Benefits:
  • Flexibility: Dependencies can be changed
  • Optional Dependencies: Can be null
  • Custom Logic: Validation in setters
  • JavaBeans Compatible: Standard pattern
  • Circular Dependencies: Can help resolve

Combined Constructor and Setter Injection

Can We Use Both Constructor and Setter Injection Together?

Yes, you can use both constructor and setter injection together in the same class. This hybrid approach allows you to define mandatory dependencies via constructor and optional dependencies via setters, providing both safety and flexibility. 


@Service
public class OrderProcessingService {
    
    // Mandatory dependencies - final via constructor
    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;
    private final PaymentGateway paymentGateway;
    
    // Optional dependencies - via setter injection
    private AuditService auditService;
    private NotificationService notificationService;
    private AnalyticsService analyticsService;
    
    // Constructor for mandatory dependencies
    public OrderProcessingService(OrderRepository orderRepository,
                                PaymentGateway paymentGateway) {
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
        this.paymentGateway = paymentGateway;
    }
    
    // Setter for optional dependency with default
    @Autowired(required = false)
    public void setAuditService(AuditService auditService) {
        this.auditService = auditService;
    }
    
    // Setter for optional dependency with validation
    @Autowired
    public void setNotificationService(NotificationService notificationService) {
        if (notificationService != null) {
            notificationService.configureTemplate("ORDER_PROCESSING");
        }
        this.notificationService = notificationService;
    }
    
    // Setter with custom qualifier for multiple implementations
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("advancedAnalytics")
    public void setAnalyticsService(AnalyticsService analyticsService) {
        this.analyticsService = analyticsService;
    }
    
    public Order processOrder(Order order) {
        // Mandatory operations - always available
        Order savedOrder = orderRepository.save(order);
        paymentGateway.charge(order);
        
        // Optional operations - check if available
        if (auditService != null) {
            auditService.logOrderCreation(order);
        }
        
        if (notificationService != null) {
            notificationService.sendOrderConfirmation(order);
        }
        
        if (analyticsService != null) {
            analyticsService.trackOrderEvent(order);
        }
        
        return savedOrder;
    }
}

// Configuration with mixed injection
@Configuration
public class SecurityConfig {
    
    // Mandatory from constructor
    private final UserDetailsService userDetailsService;
    
    // Optional from setters
    private PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder;
    private RememberMeServices rememberMeServices;
    
    public SecurityConfig(UserDetailsService userDetailsService) {
        this.userDetailsService = userDetailsService;
    }
    
    @Autowired(required = false)
    public void setPasswordEncoder(PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder) {
        this.passwordEncoder = passwordEncoder;
    }
    
    @Autowired(required = false)
    public void setRememberMeServices(RememberMeServices rememberMeServices) {
        this.rememberMeServices = rememberMeServices;
    }
    
    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http.userDetailsService(userDetailsService);
        
        if (passwordEncoder != null) {
            http.passwordEncoder(passwordEncoder);
        }
        
        if (rememberMeServices != null) {
            http.rememberMe().rememberMeServices(rememberMeServices);
        }
        
        return http.build();
    }
}
Best Practices for Mixed Injection:
  • Use constructor for mandatory dependencies
  • Use setters for optional dependencies
  • Mark optional setters with @Autowired(required = false)
  • Keep constructors simple and focused
  • Use final fields for constructor-injected dependencies
Execution Order:
  • Constructor injection happens first
  • Setter injection happens after construction
  • Field injection happens after setter injection
  • @PostConstruct methods run after all injection

Spring Team Recommendation: Use constructor injection for mandatory dependencies and setter injection for optional dependencies. This approach gives you the benefits of immutability for required dependencies while maintaining flexibility for optional ones.

Field Injection

How Does Field Injection Work Internally?

Field injection uses Java Reflection to directly set field values after object instantiation. Spring creates the object using the default constructor, then injects dependencies by directly accessing and modifying the private fields. 


// Field injection example
@Service
public class UserService {
    
    @Autowired
    private UserRepository userRepository;
    
    @Autowired
    private PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder;
    
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("emailNotification")
    private NotificationService notificationService;
    
    // Default constructor required
    public UserService() {
        // Object created with empty dependencies
    }
    
    public User createUser(User user) {
        user.setPassword(passwordEncoder.encode(user.getPassword()));
        User savedUser = userRepository.save(user);
        notificationService.sendWelcomeEmail(savedUser);
        return savedUser;
    }
}

// WHAT SPRING DOES INTERNALLY (simplified):
public class SpringContainer {
    
    public Object createBean(Class beanClass) {
        // 1. Create instance using default constructor
        Object bean = beanClass.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();
        
        // 2. Find all @Autowired fields
        Field[] fields = beanClass.getDeclaredFields();
        for (Field field : fields) {
            if (field.isAnnotationPresent(Autowired.class)) {
                
                // 3. Make field accessible (bypass private modifier)
                field.setAccessible(true);
                
                // 4. Get dependency from container
                Object dependency = getDependency(field.getType(), field.getAnnotations());
                
                // 5. Set field value using reflection
                field.set(bean, dependency);
            }
        }
        
        return bean;
    }
}

// Field injection with different annotations
@Repository
public class ProductRepository {
    
    @Autowired // Standard Spring
    private DataSource dataSource;
    
    @Inject // JSR-330 equivalent
    private EntityManager entityManager;
    
    @Resource // JNDI-style injection
    private JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate;
    
    @Value("${app.page.size:20}") // Property injection
    private int pageSize;
}
Internal Process:
  1. Instantiate bean using default constructor
  2. Scan class for @Autowired fields
  3. Use reflection to make fields accessible
  4. Resolve dependencies from application context
  5. Set field values directly via reflection
  6. Call @PostConstruct methods if any
Reflection Overhead:
  • Field access bypasses access modifiers
  • Reflection is slower than direct method calls
  • Performance impact is minimal in modern JVMs
  • Most overhead occurs during startup, not runtime

Why is Field Injection Generally Not Recommended?

While field injection is convenient and requires less code, it has several significant drawbacks that make it unsuitable for production code in most cases. 


// PROBLEMATIC: Field injection hides dependencies
@Service
public class ProblematicOrderService {
    
    @Autowired
    private OrderRepository orderRepository; // Hidden dependency
    
    @Autowired
    private PaymentService paymentService; // Hidden dependency
    
    @Autowired
    private NotificationService notificationService; // Hidden dependency
    
    // No constructor - dependencies are invisible from outside
    public ProblematicOrderService() {}
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        // All dependencies magically appear - not clear what's needed
        orderRepository.save(order);
        paymentService.processPayment(order);
        notificationService.sendConfirmation(order);
    }
}

// TESTING PROBLEMS with field injection
class ProblematicOrderServiceTest {
    
    @Test
    void testProcessOrder() {
        ProblematicOrderService service = new ProblematicOrderService();
        // How to set dependencies? They're private fields!
        // service.orderRepository = mock(OrderRepository.class); // Can't do this!
        
        // Must use reflection or Spring container for testing
        // This makes unit testing much harder
    }
}

// IMMUTABILITY PROBLEM
@Service
public class ShoppingCartService {
    
    @Autowired
    private ProductRepository productRepository; // Can be changed via reflection
    
    @Autowired
    private PricingService pricingService; // Not final, not immutable
    
    // Someone could change these dependencies at runtime
    // No guarantee of consistency
}

// CIRCULAR DEPENDENCY PROBLEMS
@Service
public class ServiceA {
    @Autowired
    private ServiceB serviceB; // Circular dependency hidden
}

@Service
public class ServiceB {
    @Autowired
    private ServiceA serviceA; // Circular dependency hidden
}
// With field injection, this compiles but fails at runtime
Major Drawbacks of Field Injection
  • Hidden Dependencies: Dependencies are not visible in API. You can't tell what a class needs by looking at its constructor.
  • Poor Testability: Difficult to unit test without Spring container. You must use reflection or Spring-specific test runners.
  • No Immutability: Fields cannot be final, making classes mutable and potentially thread-unsafe.
  • Circular Dependencies: Hides circular dependencies that would be caught at compile time with constructor injection.
  • Violates SOLID Principles: Breaks dependency inversion by hiding what dependencies a class actually needs.
Constructor Injection Advantages
  • Explicit Dependencies: Clear contract showing what's required. Easy to see dependencies at a glance.
  • Easy Testing: Simple to create instances with mocks in tests. No Spring container needed for unit tests.
  • Immutability: Fields can be final, ensuring thread safety and preventing accidental modification.
  • Early Problem Detection: Circular dependencies are caught early. Compile-time safety for dependency requirements.
  • Clean Code: Follows clean code principles and makes dependencies explicit and manageable.

Official Spring Recommendation: The Spring team recommends using constructor injection for mandatory dependencies and setter injection for optional dependencies. Field injection should be avoided in most production code due to its numerous drawbacks.

When Field Injection Might Be Acceptable:
  • Configuration classes with @Configuration
  • Test classes with @SpringBootTest
  • Simple prototype beans with no business logic
  • Quick prototypes and proof-of-concepts
  • When migrating legacy code gradually
When to Avoid Field Injection:
  • Production business logic classes
  • Classes with complex dependencies
  • When writing pure unit tests
  • When immutability is important
  • In large, long-lived codebases

Dependency Injection Quick Reference

Constructor Injection

  • Use for: Mandatory dependencies
  • Benefits: Immutability, testability
  • Fields: Should be final
  • Spring 4.3+: @Autowired optional

Setter Injection

  • Use for: Optional dependencies
  • Benefits: Flexibility, runtime changes
  • Fields: Cannot be final
  • Annotation: @Autowired required

Field Injection

  • Use for: Avoid in production
  • Drawbacks: Hidden dependencies
  • Testing: Difficult without container
  • Recommendation: Don't use

Critical Injection Rules

  • Always prefer constructor injection for mandatory dependencies
  • Use setter injection only for optional dependencies
  • Avoid field injection in production business logic
  • Make constructor-injected dependencies final for immutability
  • Test classes should work without Spring container
  • Use @Autowired(required=false) for truly optional setters
Modern Spring Best Practice
@Service
public class GoodService {
    
    private final MandatoryService mandatory;
    private OptionalService optional;
    
    // Single constructor - no @Autowired needed
    public GoodService(MandatoryService mandatory) {
        this.mandatory = mandatory;
    }
    
    // Optional dependency
    @Autowired(required = false)
    public void setOptionalService(OptionalService optional) {
        this.optional = optional;
    }
}
Anti-Pattern to Avoid
@Service
public class BadService {
    
    @Autowired
    private Dependency1 dep1;
    
    @Autowired  
    private Dependency2 dep2;
    
    @Autowired
    private Dependency3 dep3;
    
    // Hidden dependencies, hard to test
}

Spring @Autowired Annotation: Complete Guide

What is @Autowired Annotation?

The @Autowired annotation is Spring's core dependency injection mechanism that automatically wires beans together by injecting dependencies into your Spring-managed components. It eliminates the need for manual dependency configuration through XML or Java configuration.

Core Concept: @Autowired enables Spring to automatically resolve and inject collaborating beans into your bean, following the Dependency Injection (DI) and Inversion of Control (IoC) principles.

Basic @Autowired Usage

Before @Autowired


// Manual dependency injection
@Service
public class UserService {
    
    private UserRepository userRepository;
    private EmailService emailService;
    
    public UserService() {
        // Manual instantiation - tight coupling
        this.userRepository = new UserRepositoryImpl();
        this.emailService = new EmailServiceImpl();
    }
    
    // OR via constructor
    public UserService(UserRepository repo, EmailService email) {
        this.userRepository = repo;
        this.emailService = email;
    }
}

// XML configuration required
<bean id="userService" class="com.example.UserService">
    <constructor-arg ref="userRepository"/>
    <constructor-arg ref="emailService"/>
</bean>

With @Autowired


// Automatic dependency injection
@Service
public class UserService {
    
    @Autowired
    private UserRepository userRepository;
    
    @Autowired
    private EmailService emailService;
    
    // No manual instantiation needed
    // Spring automatically injects dependencies
}

// No XML configuration needed
// Spring automatically detects and wires beans

How @Autowired Works Internally

Spring Autowiring Process

Spring's autowiring process involves several steps to resolve and inject dependencies automatically.

@Autowired Internal Process Flow

1. Bean Discovery
Spring scans and registers beans
▼
2. Dependency Analysis
Finds @Autowired fields/methods
▼
3. Bean Resolution
Matches dependencies with beans
▼
4. Dependency Injection
Injects resolved beans

// INTERNAL SPRING PROCESS (Simplified)
public class AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor implements BeanPostProcessor {
    
    @Override
    public Object postProcessProperties(
        PropertyValues pvs, Object bean, String beanName) {
        
        // 1. Find all @Autowired fields and methods
        ReflectionUtils.doWithLocalFields(bean.getClass(), field -> {
            Autowired autowired = field.getAnnotation(Autowired.class);
            if (autowired != null) {
                // 2. Resolve dependency type
                Class fieldType = field.getType();
                
                // 3. Find matching bean from application context
                Object dependency = beanFactory.getBean(fieldType);
                
                // 4. Make field accessible and inject dependency
                field.setAccessible(true);
                field.set(bean, dependency);
            }
        });
        
        return bean;
    }
}

// Spring uses this processor to handle @Autowired
// It runs after bean instantiation but before initialization

Integration with Bean Lifecycle

@Autowired processing happens during Spring's bean lifecycle, specifically in the bean post-processing phase.

Bean Lifecycle with @Autowired

1. Instantiate Bean
Constructor called
▼
2. Populate Properties
@Autowired fields injected here
▼
3. BeanNameAware callbacks
▼
4. InitializingBean callbacks
▼
5. Custom init methods
▼
6. Bean Ready for Use

Where @Autowired Can Be Used

Constructor Injection

Recommended approach for mandatory dependencies. Ensures immutability and testability. 

@Service
public class UserService {
    
    private final UserRepository userRepository;
    private final EmailService emailService;
    
    @Autowired
    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository, 
                      EmailService emailService) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
        this.emailService = emailService;
    }
}

// Since Spring 4.3, @Autowired is optional 
// for single constructors
public UserService(UserRepository userRepository) {
    this.userRepository = userRepository;
}

Benefits: Immutable, safe for testing, clearly defines dependencies

Field Injection

Convenient but less testable. Use for optional dependencies or in legacy code. 

@Service
public class UserService {
    
    @Autowired
    private UserRepository userRepository;
    
    @Autowired
    private EmailService emailService;
    
    // No constructor or setter needed
    // Dependencies injected directly into fields
}

Note: Harder to test, breaks encapsulation

Setter Injection

Useful for optional dependencies or when you need to change dependencies at runtime. 

@Service
public class UserService {
    
    private UserRepository userRepository;
    private EmailService emailService;
    
    @Autowired
    public void setUserRepository(UserRepository userRepository) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
    }
    
    @Autowired
    public void setEmailService(EmailService emailService) {
        this.emailService = emailService;
    }
}

Use Case: Optional dependencies, configuration changes

Arbitrary Method Injection

@Autowired can be used on any method, not just setters. All method parameters are autowired. 

@Service
public class DataProcessor {
    
    private DataSource dataSource;
    private Validator validator;
    
    @Autowired
    public void prepareDependencies(DataSource dataSource, 
                                   Validator validator) {
        this.dataSource = dataSource;
        this.validator = validator;
    }
    
    @Autowired
    public void configure(Environment env, 
                         @Value("${batch.size}") int batchSize) {
        // Mixed dependency injection
    }
}

Collection/Array Injection

Inject all beans of a specific type as a collection or array. 

@Service
public class NotificationService {
    
    @Autowired
    private List<NotificationHandler> handlers;
    // Injects all NotificationHandler implementations
    
    @Autowired
    private Set<Validator> validators;
    // Injects all Validator implementations
    
    @Autowired
    private Map<String, Processor> processors;
    // Bean name as key, bean instance as value
}

@Component("emailHandler")
public class EmailHandler implements NotificationHandler { }

@Component("smsHandler")  
public class SmsHandler implements NotificationHandler { }
// Both injected into 'handlers' list

Different Modes of @Autowired

Required vs Optional Dependencies

Required Dependencies (Default)
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    @Autowired  // required=true by default
    private PaymentService paymentService;
    
    // Throws NoSuchBeanDefinitionException 
    // if PaymentService bean not found
}

Fails fast if dependency missing

Optional Dependencies
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    @Autowired(required = false)
    private AnalyticsService analyticsService;
    // Injected if available, null otherwise
    
    // With Java 8 Optional
    @Autowired
    private Optional<CacheService> cacheService;
    // Optional.empty() if bean not found
    
    // With @Nullable
    @Autowired
    public void setLogger(@Nullable Logger logger) {
        // logger may be null
    }
}

Graceful handling of missing dependencies

Default Autowiring Mode

The default behavior of @Autowired is by-type autowiring with required=true. 


// DEFAULT BEHAVIOR EXPLAINED
@Service
public class DefaultBehaviorExample {
    
    // Default: by-type, required=true
    @Autowired
    private UserRepository userRepository;
    // Spring looks for bean of type UserRepository
    // Throws exception if no bean found
    // Throws exception if multiple beans found (ambiguity)
    
    // This is equivalent to:
    @Autowired(required = true)
    private UserRepository userRepository;
}

// KEY DEFAULTS:
// 1. Autowiring by type (not by name)
// 2. Required dependency (fails if bean not found)  
// 3. Throws exception on ambiguity
// 4. Processes during bean post-processing phase

Important: The default behavior changed in Spring 4.3 - for classes with a single constructor, @Autowired became optional. However, the autowiring rules for fields and methods remain the same.

Multiple Beans of Same Type - Resolution Strategies

The Multiple Bean Problem

When multiple beans of the same type exist in the Spring context, @Autowired faces ambiguity and cannot determine which bean to inject. 


// MULTIPLE BEANS OF SAME TYPE
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public DataSource mysqlDataSource() {
        return new MysqlDataSource();
    }
    
    @Bean
    public DataSource postgresDataSource() {
        return new PostgresDataSource();
    }
    
    @Bean  
    public DataSource h2DataSource() {
        return new H2DataSource();
    }
}

@Service
public class DataService {
    
    @Autowired
    private DataSource dataSource; 
    // WHICH ONE? Throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
    
    // Error: No qualifying bean of type 'DataSource' available: 
    // expected single matching bean but found 3: 
    // mysqlDataSource, postgresDataSource, h2DataSource
}

Exception: Spring throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException when multiple beans of the same type exist and @Autowired cannot resolve the ambiguity.

Ambiguity Resolution Strategies

1. @Primary Annotation
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    
    @Bean
    @Primary  // This bean gets preference
    public DataSource mysqlDataSource() {
        return new MysqlDataSource();
    }
    
    @Bean
    public DataSource postgresDataSource() {
        return new PostgresDataSource();
    }
}

@Service
public class DataService {
    
    @Autowired
    private DataSource dataSource; 
    // Injects mysqlDataSource (because it's @Primary)
}

Marks a bean as the default choice

2. @Qualifier Annotation
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    
    @Bean
    @Qualifier("mysql")
    public DataSource mysqlDataSource() {
        return new MysqlDataSource();
    }
    
    @Bean
    @Qualifier("postgres")  
    public DataSource postgresDataSource() {
        return new PostgresDataSource();
    }
}

@Service
public class DataService {
    
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("mysql")  // Explicitly choose bean
    private DataSource dataSource;
    // Injects mysqlDataSource
}

Explicitly specifies which bean to use

3. Field Name Matching
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public DataSource mysqlDataSource() {
        return new MysqlDataSource();
    }
    
    @Bean
    public DataSource postgresDataSource() {
        return new PostgresDataSource();
    }
}

@Service
public class DataService {
    
    @Autowired
    private DataSource mysqlDataSource;
    // Field name 'mysqlDataSource' matches bean name
    // Injects mysqlDataSource bean
}

Field name must match bean name

4. Custom Qualifiers
// Custom qualifier annotation
@Target({ElementType.FIELD, ElementType.PARAMETER, ElementType.METHOD})
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Qualifier
public @interface Database {
    String value();
}

@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    
    @Bean
    @Database("mysql")
    public DataSource mysqlDataSource() {
        return new MysqlDataSource();
    }
    
    @Bean
    @Database("postgres")
    public DataSource postgresDataSource() {
        return new PostgresDataSource();
    }
}

@Service
public class DataService {
    
    @Autowired
    @Database("mysql")
    private DataSource dataSource;
}

Type-safe qualifier annotations

Advanced Resolution Techniques

Programmatic Resolution
@Service
public class DataService {
    
    @Autowired
    private ApplicationContext context;
    
    private DataSource dataSource;
    
    @PostConstruct
    public void init() {
        // Programmatically choose bean
        if (isProduction()) {
            this.dataSource = context.getBean("mysqlDataSource", DataSource.class);
        } else {
            this.dataSource = context.getBean("h2DataSource", DataSource.class);
        }
    }
    
    // Or using ObjectProvider
    @Autowired
    private ObjectProvider<DataSource> dataSourceProvider;
    
    public void process() {
        DataSource ds = dataSourceProvider.getIfUnique();
        // Or get with qualifier
        DataSource mysql = dataSourceProvider.getObject("mysqlDataSource");
    }
}
Conditional Injection
@Service
public class NotificationService {
    
    // Inject all implementations
    @Autowired
    private List<NotificationHandler> allHandlers;
    
    // Or use @ConditionalOnProperty
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "notification.email.enabled", havingValue = "true")
    public EmailHandler emailHandler() {
        return new EmailHandler();
    }
    
    // Profile-based beans
    @Bean
    @Profile("dev")
    public DataSource devDataSource() {
        return new EmbeddedDataSource();
    }
    
    @Bean
    @Profile("prod")
    public DataSource prodDataSource() {
        return new ProductionDataSource();
    }
}

Best Practices & Common Issues

@Autowired Best Practices

  • Prefer constructor injection for mandatory dependencies
  • Use final fields with constructor injection for immutability
  • Make dependencies optional when appropriate with required=false
  • Use @Qualifier for explicit bean selection in multi-bean scenarios
  • Consider using @Primary for default implementations
  • Avoid field injection in new code for better testability
  • Use custom qualifiers for type-safe dependency resolution

Common Issues & Solutions

  • NoSuchBeanDefinitionException: Check if bean is properly annotated and scanned
  • NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException: Use @Primary or @Qualifier to resolve ambiguity
  • Circular dependencies: Use setter injection or @Lazy to break cycles
  • Null dependencies: Ensure required=false or use Optional for optional dependencies
  • Test failures: Use @MockBean in tests instead of relying on Spring context

Performance Considerations

Reflection Overhead

@Autowired uses reflection which has minor performance impact. However, this only occurs during application startup and doesn't affect runtime performance.

Startup Time

Complex dependency graphs can increase startup time. Use component scanning carefully and consider lazy initialization for rarely used beans.

@Autowired Quick Reference

Usage Locations

  • Constructors
  • Fields
  • Setters
  • Arbitrary methods

Default Behavior

  • By-type autowiring
  • Required=true
  • Throws on ambiguity
  • Processed at startup

Resolution Strategies

  • @Primary
  • @Qualifier
  • Field name matching
  • Custom qualifiers

Common Exceptions

  • NoSuchBeanDefinition
  • NoUniqueBeanDefinition
  • BeanCreationException
  • UnsatisfiedDependency

Critical @Autowired Rules

  • Always prefer constructor injection for mandatory dependencies
  • Use @Qualifier when multiple beans of the same type exist
  • Make dependencies optional with required=false when appropriate
  • Avoid circular dependencies by using setter injection or @Lazy
  • Test your configuration to ensure all dependencies are properly wired

Spring @Autowired Annotation: Complete Dependency Injection Guide

Spring @Autowired Overview

The @Autowired annotation is Spring's mechanism for dependency injection through autowiring. It allows Spring to resolve and inject collaborating beans into your bean automatically, reducing the need for explicit configuration in XML or Java Config.

Core Concept: @Autowired can be used on fields, setters, constructors, and configuration methods. By default, it requires the dependency to be available, but this behavior can be configured.

What happens when no bean is found for autowiring?

Default Behavior: NoSuchBeanDefinitionException

By default, when Spring cannot find a matching bean for @Autowired injection, it throws a NoSuchBeanDefinitionException during application context initialization. 


@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    // PROBLEM: No bean of type EmailService found in context
    @Autowired
    private EmailService emailService;  // Throws NoSuchBeanDefinitionException
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        // This method will never be called due to initialization failure
        emailService.sendConfirmation(order);
    }
}

// Missing bean - no @Service annotation or bean definition
public class EmailService {
    public void sendConfirmation(Order order) {
        // implementation
    }
}

// APPLICATION STARTUP FAILURE:
/*
Caused by: org.springframework.beans.factory.NoSuchBeanDefinitionException: 
No qualifying bean of type 'com.example.EmailService' available: 
expected at least 1 bean which qualifies as autowire candidate. 
Dependency annotations: {@org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired(required=true)}
*/
Common Causes
  • Missing @Component, @Service, @Repository annotation
  • Bean not scanned (wrong package, missing @ComponentScan)
  • Wrong type or interface used
  • Profile-specific beans not active
  • Conditional beans not meeting conditions
Solutions
  • Add appropriate stereotype annotation
  • Configure component scanning properly
  • Use @Autowired(required=false)
  • Provide @Bean method in configuration
  • Check active profiles and conditions

Important: The exception occurs during application context initialization, preventing the application from starting. This ensures that all required dependencies are available before the application begins processing requests.

Multiple Beans Scenario: NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException

When multiple beans of the same type exist, Spring cannot determine which one to inject and throws a NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. 


// Multiple implementations of same interface
public interface NotificationService {
    void sendNotification(String message);
}

@Service
public class EmailNotificationService implements NotificationService {
    @Override
    public void sendNotification(String message) {
        // email implementation
    }
}

@Service  
public class SmsNotificationService implements NotificationService {
    @Override
    public void sendNotification(String message) {
        // SMS implementation
    }
}

@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    // PROBLEM: Which NotificationService to inject?
    @Autowired
    private NotificationService notificationService;
    
    /*
    Throws:
    NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException: No qualifying bean of type 'NotificationService' available: 
    expected single matching bean but found 2: emailNotificationService,smsNotificationService
    */
}

// SOLUTIONS:

// 1. Use @Primary
@Service
@Primary
public class EmailNotificationService implements NotificationService {
    // This bean will be injected by default
}

// 2. Use @Qualifier
@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("smsNotificationService")  // Bean name
    private NotificationService notificationService;
}

// 3. Use field name matching
@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Autowired
    private NotificationService emailNotificationService;  // Matches bean name
}

// 4. Use custom qualifier
@Qualifier
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface EmailService {}

@Service
@EmailService
public class EmailNotificationService implements NotificationService {}

@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Autowired
    @EmailService
    private NotificationService notificationService;
}

What is @Autowired(required=false)?

Optional Dependencies with required=false

When @Autowired(required = false) is used, Spring will not throw an exception if the bean is not found. Instead, the dependency will be left as null (for fields) or the method will not be called (for methods). 


@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    // Optional dependency - won't fail if EmailService bean not found
    @Autowired(required = false)
    private EmailService emailService;  // Could be null
    
    @Autowired(required = false)
    private SmsService smsService;      // Could be null
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        // Check for null before using optional dependencies
        if (emailService != null) {
            emailService.sendConfirmation(order);
        }
        
        if (smsService != null) {
            smsService.sendSmsNotification(order);
        }
        
        // Required business logic continues regardless
        orderRepository.save(order);
    }
}

// Alternative: Use Java 8 Optional
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    @Autowired(required = false)
    private Optional<EmailService> emailService;
    
    @Autowired(required = false)
    private Optional<SmsService> smsService;
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        emailService.ifPresent(service -> service.sendConfirmation(order));
        smsService.ifPresent(service -> service.sendSmsNotification(order));
        
        orderRepository.save(order);
    }
}

// Using with setter methods
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    private EmailService emailService;
    private SmsService smsService;
    
    @Autowired(required = false)
    public void setEmailService(EmailService emailService) {
        this.emailService = emailService;
    }
    
    @Autowired(required = false)
    public void setSmsService(SmsService smsService) {
        this.smsService = smsService;
    }
}

// BE CAREFUL: Null checks are required!
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    @Autowired(required = false)
    private EmailService emailService;
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        // DANGER: Could throw NullPointerException
        emailService.sendConfirmation(order);  // If emailService is null
        
        // SAFE: Always check for null
        if (emailService != null) {
            emailService.sendConfirmation(order);
        }
    }
}
Use Cases for required=false
  • Optional features or plugins
  • Fallback mechanisms
  • Feature toggles
  • Backward compatibility
  • Testing scenarios
Risks & Considerations
  • Null checks are required
  • Runtime NPE instead of startup failure
  • Harder to debug missing dependencies
  • Can mask configuration problems

Better Alternative: Consider using @Autowired with Optional<T> or implement the Null Object pattern instead of using required=false with null checks.

Can we use @Autowired on constructors?

Constructor Injection with @Autowired

Yes, @Autowired can be used on constructors. In fact, constructor injection is generally recommended as it makes dependencies explicit and ensures the object is always in a valid state. 


@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;
    private final PaymentService paymentService;
    private final NotificationService notificationService;
    
    // Constructor injection - recommended approach
    @Autowired
    public OrderService(OrderRepository orderRepository,
                       PaymentService paymentService,
                       NotificationService notificationService) {
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
        this.notificationService = notificationService;
    }
    
    // In Spring 4.3+, @Autowired is optional for single constructor
    public OrderService(OrderRepository orderRepository,
                       PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
        this.notificationService = null;  // Optional dependency
    }
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        // All dependencies are guaranteed to be available
        paymentService.processPayment(order);
        orderRepository.save(order);
        notificationService.sendConfirmation(order);
    }
}

// With optional dependencies in constructor
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;
    private final PaymentService paymentService;
    private final NotificationService notificationService;
    
    // Use @Autowired(required=false) for optional constructor dependencies
    @Autowired(required = false)
    public OrderService(OrderRepository orderRepository,
                       PaymentService paymentService,
                       NotificationService notificationService) {
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
        this.notificationService = notificationService;
    }
    
    // Overloaded constructor for when NotificationService is not available
    @Autowired
    public OrderService(OrderRepository orderRepository,
                       PaymentService paymentService) {
        this(orderRepository, paymentService, null);
    }
}

// Constructor injection with @Qualifier
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    private final NotificationService notificationService;
    
    @Autowired
    public OrderService(@Qualifier("emailNotificationService") 
                       NotificationService notificationService) {
        this.notificationService = notificationService;
    }
}

// BENEFITS OF CONSTRUCTOR INJECTION:

// 1. Immutable dependencies
@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;  // final - immutable
    
    @Autowired
    public OrderService(OrderRepository orderRepository) {
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;  // Set once, never changed
    }
}

// 2. Clear dependencies - no hidden dependencies
// 3. Easier testing - no need for reflection
class OrderServiceTest {
    @Test
    void testProcessOrder() {
        OrderRepository mockRepo = mock(OrderRepository.class);
        OrderService service = new OrderService(mockRepo);  // Easy to test
        // ...
    }
}

// 3. Avoids circular dependencies
// Constructor injection fails fast for circular dependencies
@Service
public class ServiceA {
    private final ServiceB serviceB;
    
    @Autowired
    public ServiceA(ServiceB serviceB) {  // Circular dependency detected at startup
        this.serviceB = serviceB;
    }
}

@Service
public class ServiceB {
    private final ServiceA serviceA;
    
    @Autowired
    public ServiceB(ServiceA serviceA) {  // Circular dependency!
        this.serviceA = serviceA;
    }
}
Benefits
  • Dependencies are explicit and clear
  • Immutable dependencies (with final)
  • Easier unit testing
  • Prevents circular dependencies
  • Object always in valid state
Spring 4.3+ Enhancement
  • @Autowired optional for single constructor
  • Cleaner code with less annotations
  • Still works with multiple constructors
  • Explicit @Autowired for specific constructor

Can we use @Autowired on static fields?

Static Field Injection: Generally Not Recommended

While technically possible through some workarounds, @Autowired on static fields is generally not recommended and doesn't work out of the box. Spring doesn't support direct static field injection because it goes against the dependency injection principles. 


// THIS DOES NOT WORK - static field won't be autowired
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    @Autowired
    private static OrderRepository orderRepository;  // WILL BE NULL!
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        orderRepository.save(order);  // NullPointerException!
    }
}

// WORKAROUND 1: Use @PostConstruct with static field
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    private static OrderRepository staticOrderRepository;
    
    @Autowired
    private OrderRepository orderRepository;  // Instance field
    
    @PostConstruct
    private void initStatic() {
        staticOrderRepository = this.orderRepository;  // Copy to static
    }
    
    public static void staticMethod() {
        staticOrderRepository.findAll();  // Now works
    }
}

// WORKAROUND 2: Use setter method for static field
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    private static OrderRepository orderRepository;
    
    @Autowired
    public void setOrderRepository(OrderRepository orderRepository) {
        OrderService.orderRepository = orderRepository;  // Set static field
    }
}

// WORKAROUND 3: Use ApplicationContext in static method
@Component
public class StaticContextHolder {
    
    private static ApplicationContext applicationContext;
    
    @Autowired
    public StaticContextHolder(ApplicationContext applicationContext) {
        StaticContextHolder.applicationContext = applicationContext;
    }
    
    public static <T> T getBean(Class<T> beanClass) {
        return applicationContext.getBean(beanClass);
    }
}

// Usage in static method
public class OrderUtils {
    
    public static void validateOrder(Order order) {
        OrderRepository repo = StaticContextHolder.getBean(OrderRepository.class);
        // use repo...
    }
}

// BETTER APPROACH: Avoid static dependencies
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;
    
    @Autowired
    public OrderService(OrderRepository orderRepository) {
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
    }
    
    // Non-static method using injected dependency
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        orderRepository.save(order);
    }
}

// WHY STATIC INJECTION IS PROBLEMATIC:

// 1. Breaks dependency injection principles
// 2. Hard to test - dependencies are global state
// 3. Lifecycle issues - when is the static field set?
// 4. Not thread-safe in some scenarios
// 5. Makes code harder to reason about

Recommendation: Avoid static field injection. Instead, design your classes to use instance dependencies. If you need static access to beans, consider using the ApplicationContext directly or refactoring your design to avoid static dependencies.

Can we use @Autowired on method parameters?

Method Parameter Injection with @Autowired

While @Autowired is typically used on fields, constructors, and methods, it can also be used on method parameters in specific scenarios, particularly in @Bean methods in configuration classes. 


@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    
    // @Autowired on @Bean method parameters
    @Bean
    public OrderService orderService(@Autowired OrderRepository orderRepository,
                                    @Autowired PaymentService paymentService) {
        return new OrderService(orderRepository, paymentService);
    }
    
    // @Autowired is optional in @Bean methods
    @Bean
    public UserService userService(UserRepository userRepository,  // Autowired automatically
                                  RoleService roleService) {       // Autowired automatically  
        return new UserService(userRepository, roleService);
    }
    
    // Using @Qualifier with parameter injection
    @Bean
    public NotificationService notificationService(
            @Autowired @Qualifier("emailTemplate") Template emailTemplate,
            @Autowired @Qualifier("smsTemplate") Template smsTemplate) {
        return new NotificationService(emailTemplate, smsTemplate);
    }
}

// In regular component methods - NOT SUPPORTED
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    // This WON'T WORK - @Autowired not supported on regular method parameters
    public void processOrder(@Autowired PaymentService paymentService,  // IGNORED
                            Order order) {
        paymentService.processPayment(order);  // paymentService is null!
    }
}

// Alternative: Use setter injection instead
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    private PaymentService paymentService;
    
    // Setter injection with @Autowired
    @Autowired
    public void setPaymentService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        paymentService.processPayment(order);  // Now works
    }
}

// Using in @EventListener methods
@Service
public class OrderEventListener {
    
    @EventListener
    public void handleOrderCreated(OrderCreatedEvent event,
                                  @Autowired EmailService emailService) {
        // emailService is injected automatically
        emailService.sendConfirmation(event.getOrder());
    }
}

// Using in @Scheduled methods (with caution)
@Service
public class ScheduledTasks {
    
    @Scheduled(fixedRate = 5000)
    public void cleanupOldOrders(@Autowired OrderRepository orderRepository) {
        // orderRepository is available
        orderRepository.deleteOldOrders();
    }
}

// LIMITATIONS:

// 1. Only works in specific Spring-managed scenarios:
//    - @Bean methods in @Configuration classes
//    - @EventListener methods  
//    - Some specific handler methods

// 2. Does NOT work in regular service method parameters
@Service
public class InvalidExample {
    
    public void someMethod(@Autowired SomeService service) {  // WON'T WORK
        service.doSomething();
    }
}

// 3. Can make testing more difficult
class OrderServiceTest {
    @Test
    void testProcessOrder() {
        OrderService service = new OrderService();
        // How to provide the @Autowired parameter? Can't easily test
        service.processOrder(order);  // The PaymentService parameter is problematic
    }
}
Supported Scenarios
  • @Bean method parameters in @Configuration
  • @EventListener method parameters
  • Custom handler methods in Spring MVC
  • Some specific framework callbacks
Unsupported Scenarios
  • Regular service method parameters
  • Repository method parameters
  • Controller method parameters
  • Any arbitrary method parameters

What is the execution order of @Autowired methods?

@Autowired Method Execution Order

When multiple methods in a class are annotated with @Autowired, Spring follows a specific order for their execution during bean initialization. 


@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    private OrderRepository orderRepository;
    private PaymentService paymentService;
    private NotificationService notificationService;
    private AuditService auditService;
    
    // 1. CONSTRUCTOR injection happens first (if present)
    @Autowired
    public OrderService(OrderRepository orderRepository) {
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
        System.out.println("1. Constructor executed");
    }
    
    // 2. @Autowired FIELDS are injected next
    @Autowired
    private PaymentService paymentServiceField;  // Injected after constructor
    
    // 3. @Autowired METHODS execute in undefined order by default
    @Autowired
    public void setPaymentService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
        System.out.println("3. setPaymentService executed");
    }
    
    @Autowired
    public void setNotificationService(NotificationService notificationService) {
        this.notificationService = notificationService;
        System.out.println("3. setNotificationService executed");
    }
    
    @Autowired
    public void configureAuditService(AuditService auditService) {
        this.auditService = auditService;
        System.out.println("3. configureAuditService executed");
    }
    
    // 4. @PostConstruct methods execute after all dependency injection
    @PostConstruct
    public void init() {
        System.out.println("4. @PostConstruct init() executed");
        // All dependencies are available here
    }
    
    // 5. Regular methods can be called in any order
    public void someMethod() {
        System.out.println("5. Regular method - called when invoked");
    }
}

// EXECUTION ORDER OBSERVED:
// 1. Constructor executed
// 2. Field injection (paymentServiceField)
// 3. setPaymentService executed (order may vary)
// 3. setNotificationService executed (order may vary)  
// 3. configureAuditService executed (order may vary)
// 4. @PostConstruct init() executed

// IMPORTANT: @Autowired method execution order is NOT guaranteed!
// Don't rely on the order of @Autowired method execution

// PROBLEMATIC EXAMPLE - relying on execution order
@Service
public class ProblematicService {
    
    private PaymentService paymentService;
    private OrderService orderService;
    
    @Autowired
    public void setOrderService(OrderService orderService) {
        this.orderService = orderService;
        // Assumes paymentService is already set - DANGEROUS!
        orderService.configurePayment(paymentService);  // paymentService might be null!
    }
    
    @Autowired
    public void setPaymentService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }
}

// BETTER APPROACH: Use @PostConstruct for order-dependent initialization
@Service
public class BetterService {
    
    private PaymentService paymentService;
    private OrderService orderService;
    
    @Autowired
    public void setOrderService(OrderService orderService) {
        this.orderService = orderService;
    }
    
    @Autowired
    public void setPaymentService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }
    
    @PostConstruct
    public void initialize() {
        // All dependencies are guaranteed to be set
        orderService.configurePayment(paymentService);
    }
}

// USING @DependsOn for explicit ordering between beans
@Service
@DependsOn({"paymentService", "notificationService"})  // Ensure these beans created first
public class OrderService {
    // This bean will be created after paymentService and notificationService
}

// ORDER SUMMARY:
// 1. Constructor injection
// 2. Field injection  
// 3. @Autowired method injection (arbitrary order)
// 4. @PostConstruct methods
// 5. Bean is ready for use
Guaranteed Order
  • Constructor injection first
  • Field injection after constructor
  • @PostConstruct after all injection
  • @DependsOn for bean creation order
Non-Guaranteed Order
  • Multiple @Autowired methods
  • Multiple field injections
  • Setter method execution order
  • Configuration method order

Best Practice: Never rely on the execution order of multiple @Autowired methods. Use @PostConstruct for any initialization that requires all dependencies to be set, or use constructor injection which guarantees that all dependencies are available when the constructor runs.

@Autowired Quick Reference

Supported Locations

  • Fields (instance variables)
  • Constructors (recommended)
  • Setter methods
  • Configuration method parameters
  • Arbitrary methods

Execution Order

  • Constructor first
  • Fields after constructor
  • Methods in arbitrary order
  • @PostConstruct last

Not Supported

  • Static fields (directly)
  • Regular method parameters
  • Static methods
  • Final fields (with field injection)

Critical @Autowired Rules

  • Always use constructor injection for mandatory dependencies
  • Never rely on @Autowired method execution order
  • Avoid static field injection - use workarounds sparingly
  • Use @Autowired(required=false) only for truly optional dependencies
  • Check for null when using required=false dependencies
  • Prefer @PostConstruct for initialization over @Autowired methods

Spring @Autowired: Complete Under-the-Hood Mechanism

@Autowired Fundamentals

The @Autowired annotation is Spring's core dependency injection mechanism that automatically wires beans together by type. Under the hood, it uses sophisticated resolution strategies and lifecycle hooks to fulfill dependencies between Spring-managed components.

Core Concept: @Autowired enables Spring's Inversion of Control (IoC) by automatically resolving and injecting dependencies without manual bean lookup or instantiation.

@Autowired Under the Hood Process

Injection Process: Spring performs autowiring during bean creation through a multi-phase process involving bean post-processors, dependency resolution, and lifecycle callbacks.

Bean Creation and Autowiring Flow


// Underlying Spring Autowiring Process
1. Bean Instantiation
   ↓
2. Population of Properties (setter injection)
   ↓
3. BeanNameAware.setBeanName()
   ↓
4. BeanClassLoaderAware.setBeanClassLoader()
   ↓
5. BeanFactoryAware.setBeanFactory()
   ↓
6. **@Autowired Processing (AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor)**
   ↓
7. InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()
   ↓
8. Custom init-method
   ↓
9. Bean is ready for use

// Key Component: AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor
public class AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor 
    implements InstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor, BeanFactoryAware {
    
    public PropertyValues postProcessProperties(
        PropertyValues pvs, Object bean, String beanName) {
        
        // Find all @Autowired fields and methods
        InjectionMetadata metadata = findAutowiringMetadata(beanName, bean.getClass());
        
        // Perform actual injection
        metadata.inject(bean, beanName, pvs);
        return pvs;
    }
}

AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor Deep Dive

Metadata Discovery

// How Spring discovers @Autowired members
private InjectionMetadata findAutowiringMetadata(String beanName, Class clazz) {
    // Check cache first
    InjectionMetadata metadata = this.injectionMetadataCache.get(clazz);
    if (metadata == null) {
        // Reflectively scan class hierarchy
        metadata = buildAutowiringMetadata(clazz);
        this.injectionMetadataCache.put(clazz, metadata);
    }
    return metadata;
}

private InjectionMetadata buildAutowiringMetadata(Class clazz) {
    List elements = new ArrayList<>();
    Class targetClass = clazz;
    
    // Traverse class hierarchy (including superclasses)
    do {
        List currElements = new ArrayList<>();
        
        // Process fields
        ReflectionUtils.doWithLocalFields(targetClass, field -> {
            AnnotationAttributes ann = findAutowiredAnnotation(field);
            if (ann != null) {
                if (Modifier.isStatic(field.getModifiers())) {
                    return; // Skip static fields
                }
                currElements.add(new AutowiredFieldElement(field, ann));
            }
        });
        
        // Process methods
        ReflectionUtils.doWithLocalMethods(targetClass, method -> {
            // Similar processing for @Autowired methods
        });
        
        elements.addAll(0, currElements);
        targetClass = targetClass.getSuperclass();
    }
    while (targetClass != null && targetClass != Object.class);
    
    return new InjectionMetadata(clazz, elements);
}
Dependency Resolution

// Actual dependency injection
public class AutowiredFieldElement extends InjectionMetadata.InjectedElement {
    
    protected void inject(Object bean, String beanName, PropertyValues pvs) throws Throwable {
        Field field = (Field) this.member;
        Object value;
        
        if (this.cached) {
            value = resolvedCachedArgument(beanName, this.cachedFieldValue);
        } else {
            // Resolve dependency from BeanFactory
            DependencyDescriptor desc = new DependencyDescriptor(field, this.required);
            desc.setContainingClass(bean.getClass());
            Set autowiredBeanNames = new LinkedHashSet<>(1);
            
            value = beanFactory.resolveDependency(desc, beanName, 
                     autowiredBeanNames, this.typeConverter);
            
            // Cache for performance
            if (value != null) {
                this.cachedFieldValue = desc;
            }
        }
        
        if (value != null) {
            // Make field accessible and set value
            ReflectionUtils.makeAccessible(field);
            field.set(bean, value);
        }
    }
}

// DefaultListableBeanFactory resolution
public Object resolveDependency(DependencyDescriptor descriptor, String beanName,
    Set autowiredBeanNames, TypeConverter typeConverter) throws BeansException {
    
    // Use autowire candidate resolver to find matching beans
    return doResolveDependency(descriptor, beanName, autowiredBeanNames, typeConverter);
}

@Autowired Resolution Strategies

Primary Resolution Strategy: By Type


// 1. BY_TYPE (Default Strategy)
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    @Autowired
    private PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor;
    // Spring looks for bean of type PaymentProcessor
}

@Component
public class CreditCardProcessor implements PaymentProcessor {
    // This bean will be autowired
}

// Resolution Process:
// 1. Find all beans of type PaymentProcessor
// 2. If exactly one → inject it
// 3. If multiple → check @Primary, @Qualifier
// 4. If none and required=true → throw exception

Multiple Bean Resolution


// 2. Handling Multiple Candidates
public interface PaymentProcessor {
    void process(Payment payment);
}

@Component
public class CreditCardProcessor implements PaymentProcessor { }

@Component  
public class PayPalProcessor implements PaymentProcessor { }

@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Autowired
    private PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor; 
    // ❌ NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException!
    
    // Solutions:
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("creditCardProcessor")
    private PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor;
    
    @Autowired
    private List allProcessors; // Inject all
    
    @Autowired
    private Map processorsMap; // Map by bean name
}

Advanced Resolution Strategies

@Primary

@Component
@Primary  // Preferred when multiple candidates
public class CreditCardProcessor 
    implements PaymentProcessor {
}

@Component
public class PayPalProcessor 
    implements PaymentProcessor {
}

@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Autowired
    private PaymentProcessor processor; 
    // Gets CreditCardProcessor (because @Primary)
}
@Qualifier

@Component
@Qualifier("creditCard")
public class CreditCardProcessor 
    implements PaymentProcessor {
}

@Component
@Qualifier("paypal")  
public class PayPalProcessor 
    implements PaymentProcessor {
}

@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("paypal")  // Explicit selection
    private PaymentProcessor processor;
}
Custom Qualifiers

@Target({ElementType.FIELD, ElementType.PARAMETER})
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Qualifier
public @interface PaymentType {
    String value();
}

@Component
@PaymentType("creditCard")
public class CreditCardProcessor { }

@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Autowired
    @PaymentType("creditCard")
    private PaymentProcessor processor;
}

@Autowired Injection Types

Field Injection


@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    @Autowired
    private PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor;
    
    @Autowired
    private InventoryService inventoryService;
    
    // Pros: Concise, less boilerplate
    // Cons: Hard to test, violates immutability
}

// Under the hood - uses reflection:
Field field = OrderService.class.getDeclaredField("paymentProcessor");
field.setAccessible(true);
field.set(orderServiceInstance, paymentProcessorBean);

Constructor Injection


@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    private final PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor;
    private final InventoryService inventoryService;
    
    @Autowired // Optional in Spring 4.3+
    public OrderService(PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor,
                       InventoryService inventoryService) {
        this.paymentProcessor = paymentProcessor;
        this.inventoryService = inventoryService;
    }
    
    // Pros: Immutable, testable, clear dependencies
    // Cons: More verbose
}

// Resolution: Spring analyzes constructor parameters
// and resolves each dependency by type

Setter Injection


@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    private PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor;
    private InventoryService inventoryService;
    
    @Autowired
    public void setPaymentProcessor(PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor) {
        this.paymentProcessor = paymentProcessor;
    }
    
    @Autowired
    public void setInventoryService(InventoryService inventoryService) {
        this.inventoryService = inventoryService;
    }
    
    // Pros: Optional dependencies, mutable
    // Cons: Objects can be in partially initialized state
}

// Spring calls setter methods after constructor
// but before @PostConstruct

Method Injection (Any Method)


@Component
public class DataInitializer {
    
    private UserRepository userRepository;
    private ProductRepository productRepository;
    
    @Autowired
    public void initializeRepositories(UserRepository userRepo,
                                      ProductRepository productRepo) {
        this.userRepository = userRepo;
        this.productRepository = productRepo;
        // Can contain initialization logic
    }
    
    @Autowired
    public void configure(Environment environment) {
        // Can be used for configuration
    }
}

// Spring calls @Autowired methods after dependency injection
// but before @PostConstruct

Dependency Resolution Algorithm

Resolution Flow: Spring follows a specific algorithm to resolve @Autowired dependencies, checking various sources and conditions in a defined order.

Complete Resolution Process


// DefaultListableBeanFactory.doResolveDependency()
public Object doResolveDependency(DependencyDescriptor descriptor, String beanName,
        Set autowiredBeanNames, TypeConverter typeConverter) throws BeansException {
    
    // Step 1: Check for @Value annotation
    Object value = getAutowireCandidateResolver().getSuggestedValue(descriptor);
    if (value != null) {
        return evaluateBeanDefinitionString((String) value, beanFactory);
    }
    
    // Step 2: Handle multiple beans (collections, maps, arrays)
    if (descriptor.getDependencyType().isArray() || 
        Collection.class.isAssignableFrom(descriptor.getDependencyType()) ||
        Map.class.isAssignableFrom(descriptor.getDependencyType())) {
        return resolveMultipleBeans(descriptor, beanName, autowiredBeanNames, typeConverter);
    }
    
    // Step 3: Find candidate beans by type
    Map matchingBeans = findAutowireCandidates(beanName, 
        descriptor.getDependencyType(), descriptor);
    
    // Step 4: Handle no candidates
    if (matchingBeans.isEmpty()) {
        if (descriptor.isRequired()) {
            raiseNoMatchingBeanFound(descriptor.getDependencyType(), descriptor);
        }
        return null;
    }
    
    // Step 5: Handle single candidate
    if (matchingBeans.size() == 1) {
        return matchingBeans.values().iterator().next();
    }
    
    // Step 6: Handle multiple candidates
    String autowiredBeanName = determineAutowireCandidate(matchingBeans, descriptor);
    if (autowiredBeanName == null) {
        if (descriptor.isRequired() || !indicatesMultipleBeans(descriptor.getDependencyType())) {
            return descriptor.resolveNotUnique(descriptor.getDependencyType(), matchingBeans);
        }
        return null;
    }
    
    return matchingBeans.get(autowiredBeanName);
}

// Key helper method: determineAutowireCandidate()
protected String determineAutowireCandidate(Map candidates, 
        DependencyDescriptor descriptor) {
    
    Class requiredType = descriptor.getDependencyType();
    
    // Step 1: Check @Primary
    String primaryCandidate = determinePrimaryCandidate(candidates, requiredType);
    if (primaryCandidate != null) {
        return primaryCandidate;
    }
    
    // Step 2: Check @Priority
    String priorityCandidate = determineHighestPriorityCandidate(candidates, requiredType);
    if (priorityCandidate != null) {
        return priorityCandidate;
    }
    
    // Step 3: Check @Qualifier by name
    for (Map.Entry entry : candidates.entrySet()) {
        String candidateName = entry.getKey();
        Object beanInstance = entry.getValue();
        if (isQualifierMatch(requiredType, candidateName, beanInstance, descriptor)) {
            return candidateName;
        }
    }
    
    // Step 4: Fallback to bean name matching
    return fallbackToBeanNameMatching(candidates, descriptor);
}

Resolution Priority Order

  1. @Qualifier with explicit value
    @Autowired @Qualifier("specificBean")
  2. @Primary annotation
    @Component @Primary
  3. @Priority annotation (JSR-330)
    @Component @Priority(1)
  4. Bean name matching (field name = bean name)
    @Autowired DataSource dataSource → looks for "dataSource" bean
  5. Fallback to first bean found
    Only if none of the above resolve ambiguity

Optional and Required Dependencies

Required Dependencies (Default)


@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    @Autowired  // required = true by default
    private PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor;
    
    // If no PaymentProcessor bean exists:
    // ❌ BeanCreationException: Could not autowire field
}

// Under the hood check:
if (descriptor.isRequired() && matchingBeans.isEmpty()) {
    raiseNoMatchingBeanFound(descriptor.getDependencyType(), descriptor);
}

Optional Dependencies


@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    @Autowired(required = false)
    private AnalyticsService analyticsService; // Optional
    
    // If no AnalyticsService bean exists:
    // ✅ Field remains null, no exception
    
    @PostConstruct
    public void init() {
        if (analyticsService != null) {
            analyticsService.track("Service started");
        }
    }
}

// Java 8+ Optional style
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    @Autowired
    private Optional analyticsService;
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        analyticsService.ifPresent(analytics -> 
            analytics.trackOrder(order));
    }
}

@Nullable Annotation Support


// JSR-305 @Nullable annotation
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    @Autowired
    @Nullable  // Explicitly indicates optional dependency
    private AnalyticsService analyticsService;
    
    // Equivalent to required = false
    // But more explicit in intent
}

// Spring's internal handling:
private boolean determineRequiredStatus(DependencyDescriptor descriptor) {
    // Check @Autowired required attribute
    if (descriptor.getDependencyAnnotation(Autowired.class) != null) {
        return descriptor.getAnnotationAttributes(Autowired.class)
               .getBoolean("required");
    }
    
    // Check @Nullable annotation
    if (descriptor.getDependencyAnnotation(Nullable.class) != null) {
        return false;
    }
    
    return true; // Default to required
}

Performance Optimizations and Caching

Caching Strategy: Spring extensively caches reflection metadata and resolution results to optimize @Autowired processing, especially important in large applications.

Caching Mechanisms


// AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor caching
public class AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor {
    
    // Cache for injection metadata (fields/methods with @Autowired)
    private final ConcurrentMap, InjectionMetadata> injectionMetadataCache = 
        new ConcurrentHashMap<>(256);
    
    // Cache for resolved dependencies
    private final Map resolvedDependenciesCache = 
        new ConcurrentHashMap<>(256);
    
    private InjectionMetadata findAutowiringMetadata(String beanName, Class clazz) {
        // Double-check locking pattern for thread safety
        InjectionMetadata metadata = this.injectionMetadataCache.get(clazz);
        if (metadata == null) {
            synchronized (this.injectionMetadataCache) {
                metadata = this.injectionMetadataCache.get(clazz);
                if (metadata == null) {
                    metadata = buildAutowiringMetadata(clazz);
                    this.injectionMetadataCache.put(clazz, metadata);
                }
            }
        }
        return metadata;
    }
}

// Benefits:
// - Reflection metadata computed only once per class
// - Dependency resolution cached per bean definition
// - Significant performance improvement in large applications

Resolution Caching Example


// How dependency resolution is cached
public class AutowiredFieldElement extends InjectionMetadata.InjectedElement {
    
    private volatile Object cachedFieldValue;
    
    protected void inject(Object bean, String beanName, PropertyValues pvs) throws Throwable {
        Field field = (Field) this.member;
        Object value;
        
        if (this.cached) {
            // Use cached resolution result
            value = resolvedCachedArgument(beanName, this.cachedFieldValue);
        } else {
            // Perform fresh resolution
            DependencyDescriptor desc = new DependencyDescriptor(field, this.required);
            value = beanFactory.resolveDependency(desc, beanName, autowiredBeanNames, typeConverter);
            
            // Cache for future use
            if (value != null) {
                this.cachedFieldValue = desc;
                registerDependentBeans(beanName, autowiredBeanNames);
            }
        }
        
        if (value != null) {
            ReflectionUtils.makeAccessible(field);
            field.set(bean, value);
        }
    }
}

// Cache invalidation happens when:
// - Bean factory configuration changes
// - Refresh of application context
// - Specific bean definitions change

Common Pitfalls and Best Practices

Common Pitfalls

  • Circular dependencies with constructor injection
  • Forgetting @Component on dependency classes
  • Multiple beans without @Primary or @Qualifier
  • Using field injection in @Configuration classes
  • Mixing JSR-330 @Inject with @Autowired
  • Not understanding resolution order
  • Using @Autowired on static fields

Best Practices

  • Prefer constructor injection for required dependencies
  • Use @Qualifier for explicit bean selection
  • Mark optional dependencies with required=false or Optional
  • Use @Primary for common/default implementations
  • Avoid circular dependencies through design
  • Use custom qualifiers for semantic bean selection
  • Test autowiring configurations thoroughly

Service Discovery: Complete Guide with Step-by-Step Processes

Service Discovery Fundamentals

Service discovery is a key pattern in microservices architecture that enables services to dynamically find and communicate with each other in a distributed environment. It solves the problem of service location in environments where services have dynamic IP addresses and ports due to scaling, failures, and deployments.

Core Problem: In cloud-native environments, services don't have static IP addresses. Service discovery provides a way for services to find each other without hard-coded configuration.

Client-Side Discovery: Step-by-Step Process

Client-Side Approach: The service client is responsible for determining the network locations of available service instances and load balancing requests across them. The client queries a service registry to get current instances.

Step-by-Step Client-Side Discovery Process

1
Service Registration

When a service instance starts up, it registers itself with the service registry, providing:

  • Service name (logical identifier)
  • IP address and port (physical location)
  • Health check endpoint
  • Metadata (version, region, etc.)
POST /registry/services/order-service
{
  "name": "order-service",
  "address": "192.168.1.100",
  "port": 8080,
  "healthCheck": "/health"
}
2
Health Checking

The service registry continuously monitors registered instances through health checks:

  • Periodic HTTP health checks (every 10-30 seconds)
  • Heartbeat mechanisms
  • Automatic deregistration of unhealthy instances
# Service Registry → Service Instance
GET http://192.168.1.100:8080/health
Response: 200 OK - {"status": "UP"}

# If unhealthy, instance is removed from registry
3
Client Query

When a client service needs to call another service, it queries the service registry:

  • Client asks registry for available instances of target service
  • Registry returns list of healthy instances with network locations
  • Client caches this information for performance
# Payment Service → Service Registry
GET /registry/services/order-service

# Response
{
  "instances": [
    {
      "address": "192.168.1.100",
      "port": 8080,
      "status": "UP"
    },
    {
      "address": "192.168.1.101", 
      "port": 8080,
      "status": "UP"
    }
  ]
}
4
Load Balancing & Request

The client selects an instance using client-side load balancing and makes the request:

  • Client uses load balancing algorithm (round-robin, random, least connections)
  • Direct HTTP/RPC call to selected instance
  • No intermediate proxy - direct service-to-service communication
# Payment Service → Selected Order Service Instance
POST http://192.168.1.100:8080/orders
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "paymentId": "pay_123",
  "amount": 99.99
}

# Direct service-to-service call
5
Cache Refresh & Failure Handling

The client maintains and periodically updates its service instance cache:

  • Periodic cache refresh from service registry
  • On request failure, retry with different instance
  • Remove failed instances from local cache
  • Circuit breaker pattern for fault tolerance
// Client-side logic
if (currentInstanceFails) {
    removeFromCache(currentInstance);
    selectNewInstanceFromCache();
    retryRequest(newInstance);
}

// Periodic cache refresh
scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(() -> {
    refreshServiceInstancesFromRegistry();
}, 30, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
Client-Side Discovery Architecture
[Payment Service] ←→ [Service Registry] (Query for instances)
     ↓
[Payment Service] ←→ [Order Service Instance 1] (Direct call)
[Payment Service] ←→ [Order Service Instance 2] (Direct call)

Key Characteristics:
• Client contains discovery logic
• Direct service-to-service communication  
• Client handles load balancing
• Examples: Netflix Eureka with Ribbon

Server-Side Discovery: Step-by-Step Process

Server-Side Approach: The client makes requests to a load balancer (or API gateway) that queries the service registry and forwards requests to available instances. The client doesn't know about the service registry.

Step-by-Step Server-Side Discovery Process

1
Service Registration

Service instances register with the service registry (same as client-side discovery):

  • Instance provides service name, IP, port, health endpoint
  • Registry maintains current list of healthy instances
  • Automatic deregistration on failure
# Same registration process as client-side
POST /registry/services/inventory-service
{
  "name": "inventory-service", 
  "address": "10.0.1.50",
  "port": 8080,
  "healthCheck": "/actuator/health"
}
2
Client Request to Load Balancer

The client sends requests to a known load balancer address using the service's logical name:

  • Client uses DNS name or fixed IP of load balancer
  • Request contains logical service name in URL or header
  • Client has no knowledge of service registry
# Client → Load Balancer
GET http://api-gateway.company.com/inventory-service/products/123
# OR
GET http://load-balancer:80/services/inventory-service/products/123

# Client only knows load balancer address
# Logical service name in URL path
3
