Load Balancer Query

The load balancer queries the service registry to find healthy instances:

  • Load balancer extracts service name from request
  • Queries service registry for available instances
  • Receives current list of healthy instances
# Load Balancer → Service Registry
GET /registry/services/inventory-service

# Response
{
  "instances": [
    {"address": "10.0.1.50", "port": 8080},
    {"address": "10.0.1.51", "port": 8080},
    {"address": "10.0.1.52", "port": 8080}
  ]
}
4
Request Routing

The load balancer selects an instance and forwards the request:

  • Load balancing algorithm selects target instance
  • Request is proxied to the selected instance
  • Load balancer may modify headers or path
# Load Balancer → Selected Inventory Service
Forward: GET http://10.0.1.51:8080/products/123
Headers: 
  X-Forwarded-For: client-ip
  X-Service-Instance: lb-selected

# Load balancer acts as reverse proxy
5
Response Return

The response flows back through the load balancer to the client:

  • Service instance processes request and returns response
  • Load balancer forwards response to original client
  • Client is unaware of the actual service instance location
# Response Flow
[Inventory Service] → [Load Balancer] → [Client]

Client sees response as if it came directly from:
http://api-gateway.company.com/inventory-service/products/123

Actual service instance (10.0.1.51:8080) is hidden
Server-Side Discovery Architecture
[Client] ←→ [Load Balancer/API Gateway] ←→ [Service Registry] (LB queries registry)
                         ↓
[Load Balancer] ←→ [Service Instance 1] (Proxied call)
[Load Balancer] ←→ [Service Instance 2] (Proxied call)  
[Load Balancer] ←→ [Service Instance 3] (Proxied call)

Key Characteristics:
• Client has simple configuration (just LB address)
• Load balancer contains discovery logic
• Indirect service communication through proxy
• Examples: AWS ELB, Kubernetes Service, Istio

Logical Name vs Physical Network Address

Logical Service Name

  • Purpose: Stable identifier for service functionality
  • Format: Human-readable name (e.g., "order-service", "payment-api")
  • Stability: Never changes during service lifetime
  • Location: Used in application configuration and code
  • Example: order-service.production.company.com
Usage in Code
// Using logical name
String orderServiceUrl = "http://order-service/api/orders";

// Not physical address!
// NOT: http://192.168.1.100:8080/api/orders

Physical Network Address

  • Purpose: Actual network location where service is running
  • Format: IP address + port (e.g., "192.168.1.100:8080")
  • Stability: Changes frequently (scaling, failures, deployments)
  • Location: Managed by service discovery system
  • Example: 10.0.12.45:8080
Managed by Discovery
// Service Registry Entry
{
  "name": "order-service",           // Logical
  "address": "10.0.12.45",          // Physical  
  "port": 8080,                     // Physical
  "instanceId": "order-service-1"
}

Key Differences and Importance


// ❌ PROBLEMATIC: Hard-coded physical addresses
@Configuration
public class ServiceConfig {
    // These will break when services move!
    public String orderServiceUrl = "http://192.168.1.100:8080";
    public String paymentServiceUrl = "http://192.168.1.101:8080";
}

// ✅ CORRECT: Using logical names
@Configuration  
public class ServiceConfig {
    // Stable logical names
    public String orderServiceUrl = "http://order-service";
    public String paymentServiceUrl = "http://payment-service";
}

// Service discovery resolves:
// "order-service" → ["192.168.1.100:8080", "192.168.1.102:8080"]
// "payment-service" → ["192.168.1.101:8080"]

// Benefits of logical names:
// 1. No configuration changes when services scale
// 2. Automatic failover to healthy instances  
// 3. Load balancing across multiple instances
// 4. Environment independence (dev/staging/prod use same names)

Architecture Principle: Applications should only know about logical service names. The service discovery system is responsible for mapping these logical names to current physical network addresses. This decoupling enables dynamic scaling, failure recovery, and environment portability.

Service Discovery Client Integration

Integration Approach: Service discovery clients integrate with microservice applications through libraries, frameworks, or sidecars that handle service registration, health checking, and instance discovery.

Integration Methods

1. Application Library Integration

// Spring Cloud with Eureka Example
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableEurekaClient  // Enable discovery client
public class OrderServiceApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(OrderServiceApplication.class, args);
    }
}

// application.yml
eureka:
  client:
    service-url:
      defaultZone: http://eureka-server:8761/eureka/
  instance:
    prefer-ip-address: true
    instance-id: ${spring.application.name}:${vcap.application.instance_id:${spring.application.instance_id:${random.value}}}

// Service registration happens automatically
// Health checks are automatic
// Client queries via DiscoveryClient

@RestController
public class OrderController {
    
    private final DiscoveryClient discoveryClient;
    private final RestTemplate restTemplate;
    
    // Service discovery aware RestTemplate
    @LoadBalanced
    @Bean
    public RestTemplate restTemplate() {
        return new RestTemplate();
    }
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        // Using logical service name
        String paymentUrl = "http://payment-service/payments";
        
        // RestTemplate with @LoadBalanced resolves service name
        PaymentResponse response = restTemplate.postForObject(
            paymentUrl, order, PaymentResponse.class);
    }
}
2. Sidecar Pattern (Service Mesh)

# Kubernetes with Istio Service Mesh
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: order-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: order-service
      annotations:
        sidecar.istio.io/inject: "true"  # Inject Istio sidecar
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: order-service
        image: company/order-service:1.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        env:
        - name: SPRING_APPLICATION_NAME
          value: "order-service"
        # No discovery configuration needed!
        # Sidecar handles service discovery

---
# Service definition (logical name)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: order-service  # Logical name
spec:
  selector:
    app: order-service
  ports:
  - port: 80           # Service port
    targetPort: 8080   # Pod port

# Application uses logical names:
# http://payment-service/ (not http://10.0.12.34:8080/)

3. Programmatic Integration


// Manual integration with Consul
public class ConsulServiceDiscovery {
    
    private final ConsulClient consulClient;
    private final Map<String, List<ServiceInstance>> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    
    public ConsulServiceDiscovery(String consulHost, int consulPort) {
        this.consulClient = new ConsulClient(consulHost, consulPort);
    }
    
    // Service registration
    public void registerService(String serviceName, String address, int port) {
        NewService newService = new NewService();
        newService.setId(serviceName + "-" + address + ":" + port);
        newService.setName(serviceName);
        newService.setAddress(address);
        newService.setPort(port);
        
        // Health check
        NewService.Check check = new NewService.Check();
        check.setHttp("http://" + address + ":" + port + "/health");
        check.setInterval("10s");
        newService.setCheck(check);
        
        consulClient.agentServiceRegister(newService);
    }
    
    // Service discovery
    public List<ServiceInstance> getHealthyInstances(String serviceName) {
        // Check cache first
        if (cache.containsKey(serviceName)) {
            return cache.get(serviceName);
        }
        
        // Query Consul
        Response<List<HealthService>> healthyServices = 
            consulClient.getHealthServices(serviceName, true, QueryParams.DEFAULT);
        
        List<ServiceInstance> instances = healthyServices.getValue().stream()
            .map(healthService -> {
                Service service = healthService.getService();
                return new ServiceInstance(service.getAddress(), service.getPort());
            })
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
        
        // Update cache
        cache.put(serviceName, instances);
        return instances;
    }
    
    // Make request using discovered instance
    public <T> T callService(String serviceName, String path, Class<T> responseType) {
        List<ServiceInstance> instances = getHealthyInstances(serviceName);
        
        if (instances.isEmpty()) {
            throw new ServiceUnavailableException(serviceName + " has no healthy instances");
        }
        
        // Simple round-robin load balancing
        ServiceInstance instance = instances.get(nextIndex++ % instances.size());
        
        String url = "http://" + instance.getAddress() + ":" + instance.getPort() + path;
        return restTemplate.getForObject(url, responseType);
    }
}

4. Framework Auto-Configuration

Spring Cloud Configuration

# Maven Dependencies
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
    <groupId>spring-cloud-starter-netflix-eureka-client</groupId>
</dependency>

# application.yml
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service  # Logical name for registration
    
eureka:
  client:
    enabled: true
    fetch-registry: true    # Discover other services
    register-with-eureka: true  # Register itself
    service-url:
      defaultZone: http://eureka1:8761/eureka/,http://eureka2:8761/eureka/
  
  instance:
    hostname: ${spring.application.name}
    prefer-ip-address: true
    lease-renewal-interval-in-seconds: 30

# Auto-configuration provides:
# - Automatic service registration on startup
# - Periodic health checks
# - Automatic deregistration on shutdown
# - DiscoveryClient bean for querying services
# - @LoadBalanced RestTemplate for service calls
Usage in Business Logic

@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    // Option 1: Using @LoadBalanced RestTemplate
    private final RestTemplate restTemplate;
    
    public OrderService(@LoadBalanced RestTemplate restTemplate) {
        this.restTemplate = restTemplate;
    }
    
    public PaymentResponse processPayment(Order order) {
        // Logical service name in URL
        return restTemplate.postForObject(
            "http://payment-service/payments", 
            order, 
            PaymentResponse.class
        );
    }
    
    // Option 2: Using DiscoveryClient directly
    private final DiscoveryClient discoveryClient;
    
    public List<ServiceInstance> getPaymentServiceInstances() {
        return discoveryClient.getInstances("payment-service");
    }
    
    // Option 3: Using Feign Client (declarative)
    @FeignClient(name = "payment-service")
    public interface PaymentClient {
        @PostMapping("/payments")
        PaymentResponse processPayment(@RequestBody Order order);
    }
}

// Feign auto-resolves "payment-service" to actual instances
// Includes load balancing and retry mechanisms

Discovery Pattern Comparison Summary

Aspect Client-Side Discovery Server-Side Discovery
Complexity Client is more complex Client is simpler
Load Balancing Client-side logic Server/Infrastructure side
Network Hops Direct service-to-service Through intermediary
Failure Handling Client handles retries Infrastructure handles
Examples Netflix Eureka + Ribbon AWS ELB, Kubernetes
Language Support Requires client libraries Language agnostic

Integration Best Practices

  • Always use logical service names in application code
  • Implement proper health checks for accurate service discovery
  • Use framework integration when possible (Spring Cloud, Istio)
  • Implement retry logic with circuit breakers for resilience
  • Cache service instance lists with appropriate TTL
  • Monitor service discovery metrics and logs

Spring Circular Dependencies: Complete Guide to Understanding & Resolution

What is Circular Dependency?

A circular dependency occurs when two or more Spring beans depend on each other directly or indirectly, creating a cycle that prevents Spring from properly instantiating and wiring the beans.

Core Concept: Circular dependencies create a "chicken and egg" problem where Bean A needs Bean B to be created, but Bean B also needs Bean A to be created, resulting in a dependency cycle that Spring cannot resolve during the normal bean initialization process.

Circular Dependency Visualization

How Circular Dependencies Form

Direct Circular Dependency
Service A
depends on
↔
Service B
depends on
Indirect Circular Dependency
Service A
→
Service B
→
Service C
→
back to Service A

How Circular Dependency Occurs in Spring

Spring Bean Creation Process

Understanding how Spring creates beans helps explain why circular dependencies occur. The bean creation process involves several distinct phases. 


// Spring Bean Creation Steps:
// 1. Instantiation: Create raw object using constructor
// 2. Population: Inject dependencies using setters/fields
// 3. Initialization: Call @PostConstruct and InitializingBean methods
// 4. Ready: Bean is fully initialized and available

@Component
public class ServiceA {
    private ServiceB serviceB;
    
    // Constructor injection - creates immediate dependency
    public ServiceA(ServiceB serviceB) {
        this.serviceB = serviceB; // ServiceB must exist already!
    }
}

@Component  
public class ServiceB {
    private ServiceA serviceA;
    
    public ServiceB(ServiceA serviceA) {
        this.serviceA = serviceA; // ServiceA must exist already!
    }
}

// PROBLEM: Which one gets created first?
// ServiceA needs ServiceB, but ServiceB needs ServiceA
// Circular dependency detected!
Step 1
Instantiate Bean A
Needs Bean B
Step 2
Instantiate Bean B
Needs Bean A
Step 3
Deadlock!
Cannot resolve

Real-world Circular Dependency Examples


// EXAMPLE 1: UserService and RoleService dependency
@Service
public class UserService {
    private final RoleService roleService;
    
    @Autowired
    public UserService(RoleService roleService) {
        this.roleService = roleService;
    }
    
    public void assignDefaultRole(User user) {
        Role defaultRole = roleService.getDefaultRole();
        // Uses roleService
    }
}

@Service
public class RoleService {
    private final UserService userService;
    
    @Autowired
    public RoleService(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }
    
    public void updateRoleUsers(Role role) {
        List<User> users = userService.getUsersWithRole(role.getId());
        // Uses userService - CIRCULAR DEPENDENCY!
    }
}

// EXAMPLE 2: Three-way circular dependency
@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final PaymentService paymentService;
    
    public OrderService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }
}

@Service
public class PaymentService {
    private final NotificationService notificationService;
    
    public PaymentService(NotificationService notificationService) {
        this.notificationService = notificationService;
    }
}

@Service
public class NotificationService {
    private final OrderService orderService;
    
    public NotificationService(OrderService orderService) {
        this.orderService = orderService;
    }
    
    public void sendOrderNotification(Long orderId) {
        Order order = orderService.getOrder(orderId); // Completes the circle!
    }
}

// EXAMPLE 3: Self-dependency (rare but possible)
@Service
public class CacheService {
    @Autowired
    private CacheService self; // Self-injection
    
    @Async
    public void refreshCacheAsync() {
        // Method that calls itself through proxy
    }
}

Types of Circular Dependencies

Direct Circular Dependency

Two beans directly depend on each other through constructor injection. 

@Service
public class ServiceA {
    private ServiceB serviceB;
    public ServiceA(ServiceB serviceB) {
        this.serviceB = serviceB;
    }
}

@Service
public class ServiceB {
    private ServiceA serviceA;
    public ServiceB(ServiceA serviceA) {
        this.serviceA = serviceA;
    }
}
Characteristics:
  • Most common type
  • Easiest to detect
  • Cannot be resolved with constructor injection
  • Spring throws BeanCurrentlyInCreationException

Indirect Circular Dependency

Three or more beans form a dependency cycle through multiple hops. 

@Service
public class ServiceA {
    public ServiceA(ServiceB serviceB) { }
}

@Service
public class ServiceB {
    public ServiceB(ServiceC serviceC) { }
}

@Service
public class ServiceC {
    public ServiceC(ServiceA serviceA) { }
}
Characteristics:
  • Harder to detect
  • Involves multiple beans
  • Can span across different packages
  • Often discovered at runtime

Field/Setter Circular Dependency

Beans depend on each other through field or setter injection. 

@Service
public class ServiceA {
    @Autowired
    private ServiceB serviceB;
}

@Service
public class ServiceB {
    @Autowired
    private ServiceA serviceA;
}
Characteristics:
  • Spring can usually resolve automatically
  • Uses three-level cache mechanism
  • Less problematic than constructor injection
  • Can still cause issues in complex scenarios

Configuration Circular Dependency

Circular dependencies involving @Configuration classes and @Bean methods. 

@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    @Bean
    public ServiceA serviceA(ServiceB serviceB) {
        return new ServiceA(serviceB);
    }
    
    @Bean
    public ServiceB serviceB(ServiceA serviceA) {
        return new ServiceB(serviceA);
    }
}
Characteristics:
  • Occurs in configuration classes
  • @Bean methods depend on each other
  • Can be resolved with @Lazy
  • Often indicates design issues

How Spring Handles Circular Dependencies

Spring's Three-Level Cache Mechanism

Spring uses a sophisticated three-level cache system to handle circular dependencies for field and setter injection scenarios. 


// Spring's Dependency Resolution Process:

// Level 1: Singleton Objects Cache
// - Fully initialized beans
// - Ready for use
Map singletonObjects;

// Level 2: Early Singleton References  
// - Objects exposed early for circular dependencies
// - May not be fully initialized
Map earlySingletonObjects;

// Level 3: Singleton Factories
// - ObjectFactory for creating early references
// - Used to break circular dependencies
Map> singletonFactories;

// HOW IT WORKS:
// 1. When creating BeanA, it's added to singletonFactories
// 2. BeanA needs BeanB, so Spring starts creating BeanB
// 3. BeanB needs BeanA, so Spring gets early reference from singletonFactories
// 4. BeanB completes initialization
// 5. BeanA gets the fully initialized BeanB and completes
Level 1
singletonObjects
Complete beans
Level 2
earlySingletonObjects
Early references
Level 3
singletonFactories
Object factories

Constructor Injection Limitation

Spring cannot automatically resolve circular dependencies when using constructor injection because the dependencies are required during object construction. 


// THIS WILL FAIL: Constructor injection circular dependency
@Service
public class ServiceA {
    private final ServiceB serviceB;
    
    // ServiceB must be available during construction
    public ServiceA(ServiceB serviceB) {
        this.serviceB = serviceB;
    }
}

@Service
public class ServiceB {
    private final ServiceA serviceA;
    
    // ServiceA must be available during construction  
    public ServiceB(ServiceA serviceA) {
        this.serviceA = serviceA;
    }
}

// ERROR MESSAGE:
// The dependencies of some of the beans in the application context form a cycle:
// ┌─────┐
// |  serviceA defined in file [ServiceA.class]
// ↑     ↓
// |  serviceB defined in file [ServiceB.class]
// └─────┘

// WHY IT FAILS:
// 1. Spring tries to create ServiceA first
// 2. ServiceA constructor needs ServiceB
// 3. Spring tries to create ServiceB  
// 4. ServiceB constructor needs ServiceA
// 5. ServiceA is still being created → CIRCULAR DEPENDENCY!
// 6. Spring throws BeanCurrentlyInCreationException

Key Point: Constructor injection requires all dependencies to be fully resolved before object creation, making circular dependencies impossible to resolve automatically. Field/setter injection allows Spring to create objects first and wire dependencies later.

How to Resolve Circular Dependencies

Using @Lazy Annotation

The @Lazy annotation defers bean creation until first use, breaking the circular dependency by creating a proxy instead of the actual bean during initialization. 


// SOLUTION 1: @Lazy on constructor parameter
@Service
public class ServiceA {
    private final ServiceB serviceB;
    
    // ServiceB will be created lazily when first used
    public ServiceA(@Lazy ServiceB serviceB) {
        this.serviceB = serviceB;
    }
    
    public void doWork() {
        serviceB.process(); // ServiceB created here
    }
}

@Service
public class ServiceB {
    private final ServiceA serviceA;
    
    public ServiceB(ServiceA serviceA) {
        this.serviceA = serviceA; // ServiceA is already available
    }
}

// SOLUTION 2: @Lazy on field injection
@Service
public class ServiceA {
    @Lazy
    @Autowired
    private ServiceB serviceB;
}

@Service  
public class ServiceB {
    @Autowired
    private ServiceA serviceA;
}

// SOLUTION 3: @Lazy on class level
@Lazy
@Service
public class ServiceA {
    @Autowired
    private ServiceB serviceB;
}

@Service
public class ServiceB {
    @Autowired
    private ServiceA serviceA; // Gets lazy proxy
}

// HOW @Lazy WORKS:
// 1. Spring creates a proxy for the lazy bean
// 2. The proxy is injected instead of the actual bean
// 3. Actual bean is created when first method is called
// 4. Circular dependency is broken
@Lazy Advantages
  • Simple to implement
  • Works with constructor injection
  • Can improve startup performance
  • Minimal code changes required
@Lazy Disadvantages
  • Moves runtime errors to first usage
  • Can hide design problems
  • Proxy overhead
  • May delay discovery of configuration issues

Using Setter/Field Injection

Setter or field injection allows Spring to create beans first and inject dependencies later, enabling automatic resolution of circular dependencies. 


// SOLUTION: Use setter injection instead of constructor
@Service
public class ServiceA {
    private ServiceB serviceB;
    
    // No-args constructor allows object creation
    public ServiceA() {
        // Bean created without dependencies
    }
    
    // Dependencies injected after construction
    @Autowired
    public void setServiceB(ServiceB serviceB) {
        this.serviceB = serviceB;
    }
}

@Service
public class ServiceB {
    private ServiceA serviceA;
    
    public ServiceB() {
        // Bean created without dependencies  
    }
    
    @Autowired
    public void setServiceA(ServiceA serviceA) {
        this.serviceA = serviceA;
    }
}

// FIELD INJECTION (also works):
@Service
public class ServiceA {
    @Autowired
    private ServiceB serviceB;
}

@Service
public class ServiceB {
    @Autowired
    private ServiceA serviceA;
}

// HOW IT WORKS:
// 1. Spring creates ServiceA instance (no constructor args)
// 2. Spring creates ServiceB instance (no constructor args)  
// 3. Spring injects ServiceB into ServiceA
// 4. Spring injects ServiceA into ServiceB
// 5. Both beans are fully initialized

Note: While setter/field injection can resolve circular dependencies, constructor injection is generally preferred for mandatory dependencies as it ensures objects are always in a valid state. Consider if the circular dependency indicates a design problem that should be addressed.

Using ApplicationContextAware

Implement ApplicationContextAware to manually retrieve dependencies from the context, breaking the automatic dependency injection cycle. 


@Service
public class ServiceA implements ApplicationContextAware {
    private ServiceB serviceB;
    private ApplicationContext applicationContext;
    
    @PostConstruct
    public void init() {
        // Manually get ServiceB after construction
        this.serviceB = applicationContext.getBean(ServiceB.class);
    }
    
    @Override
    public void setApplicationContext(ApplicationContext applicationContext) {
        this.applicationContext = applicationContext;
    }
}

@Service
public class ServiceB {
    private final ServiceA serviceA;
    
    // ServiceA can be injected normally
    public ServiceB(ServiceA serviceA) {
        this.serviceA = serviceA;
    }
}

// ALTERNATIVE: Use @PostConstruct for manual wiring
@Service
public class ServiceA {
    @Autowired
    private ApplicationContext applicationContext;
    private ServiceB serviceB;
    
    @PostConstruct
    public void init() {
        this.serviceB = applicationContext.getBean(ServiceB.class);
    }
}

// ADVANTAGES:
// - Full control over dependency resolution
// - Works with complex scenarios
// - Can implement custom initialization logic

// DISADVANTAGES:
// - More verbose
// - Bypasses Spring's dependency management
// - Can lead to harder-to-maintain code

Architectural Refactoring Solutions

The best long-term solution is often to refactor the code to eliminate the circular dependency through better design patterns.

Extract Common Interface
// BEFORE: Circular dependency
@Service
class UserService {
    private RoleService roleService;
}

@Service  
class RoleService {
    private UserService userService;
}

// AFTER: Extract interface
interface RoleOperations {
    void assignDefaultRole(User user);
}

@Service
class UserService implements RoleOperations {
    // No direct dependency on RoleService
}

@Service
class RoleService {
    private RoleOperations roleOperations;
    // Depends on interface, not concrete class
}
Introduce Service Layer
// BEFORE: Circular dependency
@Service
class OrderService {
    private PaymentService paymentService;
}

@Service
class PaymentService {
    private OrderService orderService;
}

// AFTER: Introduce coordinating service
@Service
class OrderProcessingService {
    private OrderService orderService;
    private PaymentService paymentService;
    // Coordinates between services
}

@Service
class OrderService {
    // No dependency on PaymentService
}

@Service
class PaymentService {
    // No dependency on OrderService
}
Use Event-Driven Architecture
// Replace direct calls with events
@Service
class OrderService {
    @EventListener
    public void handlePaymentEvent(PaymentEvent event) {
        // React to payment events
    }
}

@Service
class PaymentService {
    @EventListener  
    public void handleOrderEvent(OrderEvent event) {
        // React to order events
    }
}

// ApplicationEventPublisher used to decouple
class OrderProcessingService {
    @Autowired
    private ApplicationEventPublisher eventPublisher;
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        eventPublisher.publishEvent(new OrderEvent(order));
    }
}
Dependency Inversion
// Apply Dependency Inversion Principle
interface NotificationSender {
    void sendNotification(String message);
}

@Service
class EmailService implements NotificationSender {
    public void sendNotification(String message) {
        // Email implementation
    }
}

@Service
class OrderService {
    private NotificationSender notificationSender;
    
    public OrderService(NotificationSender notificationSender) {
        this.notificationSender = notificationSender;
    }
    // Depends on abstraction, not concrete implementation
}

When Circular Dependency Cannot Be Resolved

Error Scenarios and Symptoms

When Spring cannot resolve a circular dependency, it throws specific exceptions and provides detailed information about the dependency cycle. 


// TYPICAL ERROR MESSAGE:
/*
***************************
APPLICATION FAILED TO START
***************************

Description:

The dependencies of some of the beans in the application context form a cycle:

┌─────┐
|  serviceA defined in file [com/example/ServiceA.class]
↑     ↓
|  serviceB defined in file [com/example/ServiceB.class]
↑     ↓  
|  serviceC defined in file [com/example/ServiceC.class]
└─────┘

Action:

Relying upon circular references is discouraged and they are prohibited by default. 
Update your application to remove the dependency cycle between beans. 
As a last resort, it may be possible to break the cycle automatically by setting 
spring.main.allow-circular-references to true.
*/

// SPECIFIC EXCEPTIONS:
// - BeanCurrentlyInCreationException
// - BeanCreationException
// - UnsatisfiedDependencyException

// COMMON SYMPTOMS:
// 1. Application fails to start
// 2. StackOverflowError during bean creation
// 3. Beans not being initialized properly
// 4. @PostConstruct methods not being called
// 5. Intermittent issues depending on bean creation order
Immediate Failures
  • BeanCurrentlyInCreationException
  • Application startup failure
  • Clear dependency cycle in logs
  • Easy to identify and fix
Subtle Issues
  • Beans partially initialized
  • Methods not being called
  • Inconsistent behavior
  • Harder to debug

Spring Boot Circular Reference Configuration

Spring Boot 2.6+ disabled circular references by default, but you can re-enable them as a temporary solution (not recommended for production). 


# application.properties - Enable circular references (NOT RECOMMENDED)
spring.main.allow-circular-references=true

# application.yml equivalent
spring:
  main:
    allow-circular-references: true

# WARNING: This is a temporary workaround!
# It doesn't fix the underlying design issue.
# Use only for development or while refactoring.

# Better approach: Use specific resolution techniques
# - @Lazy annotation
# - Setter/field injection  
# - Refactoring to remove circular dependency

Production Warning: Enabling circular references with spring.main.allow-circular-references=true is not recommended for production applications. It can lead to unpredictable behavior, hidden bugs, and makes the codebase harder to maintain. Always prefer proper architectural solutions.

Best Practices to Avoid Circular Dependencies

Prevention Strategies

  • Use Constructor Injection: Makes dependencies explicit and helps identify cycles early
  • Follow Single Responsibility Principle: Each class should have one reason to change
  • Apply Dependency Inversion: Depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations
  • Use Interface Segregation: Create focused interfaces instead of large ones
  • Implement Layered Architecture: Clear separation between presentation, business, and data layers
  • Avoid Bidirectional Relationships: Prefer unidirectional dependencies when possible

Design Principles

  • Command-Query Separation: Separate read and write operations
  • Event-Driven Architecture: Use events for cross-service communication
  • Facade Pattern: Introduce facades to coordinate between services
  • Strategy Pattern: Extract varying behaviors into strategies
  • Observer Pattern: Use observers for reactive dependencies
  • Mediator Pattern: Introduce mediators for complex interactions

Code Review Checklist

  • Does the class have a single responsibility?
  • Are dependencies flowing in one direction?
  • Are we using interfaces for dependencies?
  • Can the dependency be removed or replaced?
  • Is there a clear architectural layer separation?
  • Can events be used instead of direct calls?
  • Would a facade help decouple services?
  • Are we following dependency injection best practices?

When Circular Dependencies Are Acceptable

While generally discouraged, there are rare scenarios where circular dependencies might be acceptable:

  • Infrastructure components that are tightly coupled by design
  • Framework extensions that require bidirectional communication
  • Legacy code where refactoring is not immediately feasible
  • Performance-critical code where indirection would be too costly

Even in these cases, document the reasoning and consider long-term maintenance implications.

Circular Dependencies Quick Reference

Problem Types

  • Direct circular dependency
  • Indirect circular dependency
  • Field/setter circular dependency
  • Configuration circular dependency

Resolution Methods

  • @Lazy annotation
  • Setter/field injection
  • ApplicationContextAware
  • Architectural refactoring

Spring Mechanism

  • Three-level cache
  • Early singleton references
  • Object factories
  • Proxy creation

Prevention

  • Constructor injection
  • Dependency inversion
  • Layered architecture
  • Interface segregation

Critical Best Practices

  • Prefer constructor injection to make dependencies explicit
  • Use @Lazy as a temporary solution, not a permanent fix
  • Refactor to eliminate circular dependencies rather than working around them
  • Follow SOLID principles in your class design
  • Use architectural patterns to decouple components
  • Monitor and test for circular dependencies during development

Spring Dependency Resolution: Complete Injection Mechanism Guide

Spring Dependency Injection Overview

Spring Framework's dependency injection mechanism is a sophisticated system that resolves, instantiates, and wires dependencies between beans. Understanding how Spring resolves dependencies is crucial for building robust and maintainable applications.

Core Concept: Spring uses a multi-phase dependency resolution process that involves bean definition parsing, dependency descriptor analysis, candidate resolution, and type matching to wire dependencies automatically.

Dependency Resolution Algorithm

Spring Dependency Resolution Process

Spring follows a well-defined algorithm to resolve dependencies, ensuring that beans are created in the correct order with all their dependencies satisfied.

Dependency Resolution Flow

1. Bean Definition Parsing
Parse configuration and create BeanDefinition
▼
2. Dependency Analysis
Analyze constructor, field, and method dependencies
▼
3. Candidate Resolution
Find matching bean candidates
▼
4. Type Matching & Qualification
Resolve type conflicts with @Qualifier
▼
5. Dependency Injection
Inject resolved dependencies

// Example demonstrating the resolution process
@Component
public class OrderService {
    
    private final UserService userService;
    private final ProductService productService;
    private final PaymentService paymentService;
    
    // Constructor dependency resolution
    @Autowired
    public OrderService(UserService userService, 
                       ProductService productService,
                       @Qualifier("primaryPaymentService") PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.userService = userService;
        this.productService = productService;
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }
    
    // Field dependency resolution
    @Autowired
    private NotificationService notificationService;
    
    // Method dependency resolution  
    @Autowired
    public void setAuditService(AuditService auditService) {
        this.auditService = auditService;
    }
}

// Spring's internal resolution process (simplified)
public class DefaultListableBeanFactory {
    
    public Object resolveDependency(DependencyDescriptor descriptor, 
                                   String beanName,
                                   Set autowiredBeanNames,
                                   TypeConverter typeConverter) throws BeansException {
        
        // 1. Get the dependency type
        Class type = descriptor.getDependencyType();
        
        // 2. Look for @Qualifier annotation
        String qualifier = findQualifier(descriptor);
        
        // 3. Find candidate beans
        Map candidates = findAutowireCandidates(beanName, type, descriptor);
        
        // 4. If multiple candidates, resolve using @Primary, @Qualifier, or bean name
        if (candidates.size() > 1) {
            String determinedBeanName = determineAutowireCandidate(candidates, descriptor);
            if (determinedBeanName == null) {
                throw new NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException(type, candidates.keySet());
            }
            return candidates.get(determinedBeanName);
        }
        
        // 5. Return single candidate or throw exception
        if (candidates.size() == 1) {
            return candidates.values().iterator().next();
        }
        
        throw new NoSuchBeanDefinitionException(type);
    }
}

Detailed Resolution Steps

Type-Based Resolution
  • Exact Type Match: Find beans of exact type
  • Supertype Match: Find beans implementing interface/extending class
  • Generic Type Resolution: Handle generic types with TypeFactory
  • Collection Resolution: Inject all beans of type for List/Set
// Collection dependency - gets all UserService implementations
@Autowired
private List<UserService> userServices;

// Map dependency - bean name as key
@Autowired
private Map<String, UserService> userServiceMap;
Qualifier Resolution
  • @Qualifier Annotation: Explicit bean qualification
  • @Primary Annotation: Default bean when multiple exist
  • Bean Name Matching: Field name matches bean name
  • Custom Qualifiers: Custom annotation with @Qualifier
@Autowired
@Qualifier("emailService")
private NotificationService notificationService;

@Component
@Primary
public class PrimaryUserService implements UserService { }

@Component("specialUserService")  
public class SpecialUserService implements UserService { }

BeanPostProcessor in Dependency Injection

BeanPostProcessor Mechanism

BeanPostProcessor is a fundamental extension point in Spring that allows custom modification of new bean instances. It plays a crucial role in dependency injection, AOP proxying, and other bean lifecycle events. 


// BeanPostProcessor interface
public interface BeanPostProcessor {
    
    // Called before initialization callbacks
    default Object postProcessBeforeInitialization(Object bean, String beanName) {
        return bean;
    }
    
    // Called after initialization callbacks  
    default Object postProcessAfterInitialization(Object bean, String beanName) {
        return bean;
    }
}

// Custom BeanPostProcessor example
@Component
public class CustomBeanPostProcessor implements BeanPostProcessor {
    
    @Override
    public Object postProcessBeforeInitialization(Object bean, String beanName) {
        // Called after dependency injection but before init methods
        System.out.println("Before initialization: " + beanName);
        return bean; // Can return wrapped/proxied instance
    }
    
    @Override
    public Object postProcessAfterInitialization(Object bean, String beanName) {
        // Called after init methods (afterPropertiesSet, @PostConstruct)
        System.out.println("After initialization: " + beanName);
        return bean; // Can return wrapped/proxied instance
    }
}

// Spring's built-in BeanPostProcessors for dependency injection:
// 1. AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor - handles @Autowired
// 2. CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor - handles @Resource, @PostConstruct
// 3. PersistenceAnnotationBeanPostProcessor - handles @PersistenceContext
// 4. RequiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor - handles @Required
Before Initialization
  • Dependency injection has completed
  • Bean properties are set
  • @PostConstruct not called yet
  • InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet() not called
  • Custom init method not called
After Initialization
  • All initialization methods completed
  • Bean is fully configured
  • AOP proxies are typically created here
  • Bean is ready for use

BeanPostProcessor Execution Order

BeanPostProcessors are executed in a specific order, which is crucial for proper bean initialization and dependency resolution.

BeanPostProcessor Execution Flow

Bean Instantiation
Constructor called
▼
Dependency Injection
@Autowired, @Value, @Resource
▼
BeanPostProcessor.beforeInitialization
In ordered sequence
▼
Initialization Methods
@PostConstruct, afterPropertiesSet, init-method
▼
BeanPostProcessor.afterInitialization
In ordered sequence

AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor

AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor Deep Dive

AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor is the core component responsible for processing @Autowired and @Value annotations. It implements the SmartInstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor interface to handle dependency injection. 


// Simplified view of AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor
public class AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor implements 
    SmartInstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor, BeanFactoryAware {
    
    private final Set> autowiredAnnotationTypes = 
        new HashSet<>(Arrays.asList(Autowired.class, Value.class));
    
    @Override
    public PropertyValues postProcessProperties(
            PropertyValues pvs, Object bean, String beanName) {
        
        // Find all injection points (fields, methods)
        InjectionMetadata metadata = findAutowiringMetadata(beanName, bean.getClass(), pvs);
        
        try {
            // Perform actual injection
            metadata.inject(bean, beanName, pvs);
        } catch (Throwable ex) {
            throw new BeanCreationException(beanName, "Injection of autowired dependencies failed", ex);
        }
        return pvs;
    }
    
    private InjectionMetadata findAutowiringMetadata(String beanName, Class clazz, PropertyValues pvs) {
        // Build metadata for all @Autowired fields and methods
        List elements = new ArrayList<>();
        
        // Process fields
        ReflectionUtils.doWithFields(clazz, field -> {
            AnnotationAttributes ann = findAutowiredAnnotation(field);
            if (ann != null) {
                if (Modifier.isStatic(field.getModifiers())) {
                    logger.info("@Autowired annotation is not supported on static fields: " + field);
                    return;
                }
                boolean required = determineRequiredStatus(ann);
                elements.add(new AutowiredFieldElement(field, required));
            }
        });
        
        // Process methods
        ReflectionUtils.doWithMethods(clazz, method -> {
            Method bridgedMethod = BridgeMethodResolver.findBridgedMethod(method);
            AnnotationAttributes ann = findAutowiredAnnotation(bridgedMethod);
            if (ann != null && method.equals(ClassUtils.getMostSpecificMethod(method, clazz))) {
                if (Modifier.isStatic(method.getModifiers())) {
                    logger.info("@Autowired annotation is not supported on static methods: " + method);
                    return;
                }
                boolean required = determineRequiredStatus(ann);
                elements.add(new AutowiredMethodElement(method, required));
            }
        });
        
        return new InjectionMetadata(clazz, elements);
    }
}

// How injection works internally
private class AutowiredFieldElement extends InjectionMetadata.InjectedElement {
    
    private final boolean required;
    
    public AutowiredFieldElement(Field field, boolean required) {
        super(field, null);
        this.required = required;
    }
    
    @Override
    protected void inject(Object bean, String beanName, PropertyValues pvs) throws Throwable {
        Field field = (Field) this.member;
        Object value;
        
        try {
            // Resolve the dependency value
            value = beanFactory.resolveDependency(
                new DependencyDescriptor(field, this.required), beanName);
        } catch (BeansException ex) {
            throw new UnsatisfiedDependencyException(null, beanName, new InjectionPoint(field), ex);
        }
        
        if (value != null) {
            ReflectionUtils.makeAccessible(field);
            field.set(bean, value); // Actual field injection
        }
    }
}
Key Responsibilities
  • Scan classes for @Autowired and @Value annotations
  • Build injection metadata cache for performance
  • Resolve dependencies using BeanFactory
  • Perform actual field/method injection
  • Handle required vs optional dependencies
Injection Points
  • Field Injection: Direct field assignment
  • Method Injection: Setter/arbitrary method calls
  • Constructor Injection: Handled separately in constructor resolution
  • Array/Collection Injection: All matching beans

Dependency Injection Order & Lifecycle

Order of Dependency Injection

Spring follows a specific order when injecting dependencies, which ensures that circular dependencies are detected and resolved properly. 


@Component
public class ExampleBean {
    
    // Injection order:
    // 1. Constructor parameters (mandatory)
    @Autowired
    public ExampleBean(UserService userService, ProductService productService) {
        this.userService = userService;
        this.productService = productService;
    }
    
    // 2. Field injection (optional dependencies)
    @Autowired
    private NotificationService notificationService;
    
    // 3. Setter methods (optional dependencies)  
    @Autowired
    public void setAuditService(AuditService auditService) {
        this.auditService = auditService;
    }
    
    // 4. Arbitrary methods (optional dependencies)
    @Autowired
    public void configure(ConfigurationService configService,
                         @Value("${app.timeout}") Long timeout) {
        this.configService = configService;
        this.timeout = timeout;
    }
}

// Spring's injection order algorithm:
public class DefaultListableBeanFactory {
    
    protected void autowireConstructor(String beanName, RootBeanDefinition mbd,
                                      Constructor[] ctors, Object[] args) {
        // Constructor injection happens first
        // Spring chooses constructor with most parameters that can be satisfied
    }
    
    protected void populateBean(String beanName, RootBeanDefinition mbd, BeanWrapper bw) {
        // Then field and method injection happens
        for (BeanPostProcessor bp : getBeanPostProcessors()) {
            if (bp instanceof InstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor) {
                InstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor ibp = (InstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor) bp;
                // This calls AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor
                PropertyValues pvs = ibp.postProcessProperties(pvs, bw.getWrappedInstance(), beanName);
            }
        }
    }
}

Important: Constructor injection happens during bean instantiation, while field and method injection occur after instantiation but before initialization callbacks. This order is fixed and cannot be changed.

Dependency Injection in Bean Lifecycle

Complete Bean Lifecycle with Dependency Injection

1. Bean Definition Loading
Parse configuration, create BeanDefinition
▼
2. Bean Instantiation
Constructor called, Constructor DI
▼
3. Dependency Injection Phase
Field & Method DI, @Value injection
▼
4. BeanPostProcessor.beforeInitialization
Custom pre-init processing
▼
5. Initialization Callbacks
@PostConstruct, afterPropertiesSet, init-method
▼
6. BeanPostProcessor.afterInitialization
AOP proxying, custom post-init
▼
7. Bean Ready for Use
Fully configured and initialized

@Component
public class LifecycleExampleBean implements InitializingBean {
    
    private UserService userService;
    private boolean initialized = false;
    
    // Constructor DI - Step 2
    @Autowired
    public LifecycleExampleBean(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
        System.out.println("Constructor called, userService injected: " + (userService != null));
    }
    
    // Field DI - Step 3
    @Autowired
    private ProductService productService;
    
    // Method DI - Step 3  
    @Autowired
    public void setConfigService(ConfigService configService) {
        System.out.println("Method injection called");
    }
    
    // @PostConstruct - Step 5
    @PostConstruct
    public void init() {
        System.out.println("@PostConstruct called");
        this.initialized = true;
    }
    
    // InitializingBean - Step 5
    @Override
    public void afterPropertiesSet() {
        System.out.println("afterPropertiesSet called");
    }
    
    // Custom init method - Step 5
    @Bean(initMethod = "customInit")
    public void customInit() {
        System.out.println("Custom init method called");
    }
}

// Output order:
// 1. Constructor called, userService injected: true
// 2. Method injection called  
// 3. @PostConstruct called
// 4. afterPropertiesSet called
// 5. Custom init method called

Optional Dependencies & DependencyDescriptor

Handling Optional Dependencies

Spring provides several ways to handle optional dependencies, allowing beans to function even when certain dependencies are not available in the application context. 


@Component
public class OptionalDependencyExample {
    
    // Method 1: required = false (most common)
    @Autowired(required = false)
    private OptionalService optionalService;
    
    // Method 2: Java 8 Optional type
    @Autowired
    private Optional anotherService;
    
    // Method 3: @Nullable annotation
    @Autowired
    @Nullable
    private NullableService nullableService;
    
    // Method 4: ObjectProvider (Spring 4.3+)
    @Autowired
    private ObjectProvider providerService;
    
    // Constructor with optional parameters
    @Autowired
    public OptionalDependencyExample(
            @Autowired(required = false) ConstructorOptionalService optService) {
        // optService may be null
    }
    
    public void useOptionalDependencies() {
        // Using required = false
        if (optionalService != null) {
            optionalService.doSomething();
        }
        
        // Using Java 8 Optional
        anotherService.ifPresent(AnotherOptionalService::process);
        
        // Using ObjectProvider
        ProviderService service = providerService.getIfAvailable();
        if (service != null) {
            service.execute();
        }
        
        // Or get with default
        ProviderService defaultService = providerService.getIfAvailable(() -> new DefaultProviderService());
    }
}

// How Spring handles optional dependencies internally
private class AutowiredFieldElement extends InjectionMetadata.InjectedElement {
    
    protected void inject(Object bean, String beanName, PropertyValues pvs) throws Throwable {
        // ...
        try {
            value = beanFactory.resolveDependency(descriptor, beanName);
        } catch (BeansException ex) {
            if (this.required) {  // required = true by default
                throw ex;
            }
            // For required = false, just log and continue
            logger.debug("Failed to autowire field: " + ex.getMessage());
            value = null;
        }
        // ...
    }
}

// For Java 8 Optional, Spring has special handling
public class OptionalDependencyFactory {
    
    public Object resolveDependency(DependencyDescriptor descriptor, String beanName) {
        if (descriptor.getDependencyType() == Optional.class) {
            // Extract the actual type from Optional
            Class actualType = descriptor.getResolvableType().getGeneric(0).resolve();
            DependencyDescriptor actualDescriptor = new DependencyDescriptor(descriptor);
            actualDescriptor.increaseNestingLevel();
            
            try {
                Object result = beanFactory.resolveDependency(actualDescriptor, beanName);
                return Optional.ofNullable(result);
            } catch (BeansException ex) {
                return Optional.empty(); // Return empty Optional instead of throwing
            }
        }
        // ... handle other types
    }
}
Optional Dependency Strategies
  • @Autowired(required = false) - Most common
  • Optional<T> - Type-safe, Java 8+
  • @Nullable - Explicit nullability
  • ObjectProvider - Flexible dependency access
When to Use Which
  • required=false: Simple optional fields
  • Optional: Type-safe, functional style
  • ObjectProvider: Multiple instances, lazy access
  • @Nullable: Documentation and static analysis

DependencyDescriptor Role

DependencyDescriptor is a key internal class that encapsulates all information about a dependency point, including type, annotations, and contextual information needed for resolution. 


// DependencyDescriptor encapsulates dependency information
public class DependencyDescriptor extends InjectionPoint {
    
    private final Class declaringClass;
    private String methodName;
    private Class[] parameterTypes;
    private int parameterIndex;
    private String fieldName;
    private final boolean required;
    private final boolean eager;
    private volatile ResolvableType resolvableType;
    
    // Creates descriptor for constructor parameter
    public DependencyDescriptor(ConstructorParameter original) {
        // ...
    }
    
    // Creates descriptor for method parameter  
    public DependencyDescriptor(MethodParameter methodParameter, boolean required) {
        // ...
    }
    
    // Creates descriptor for field
    public DependencyDescriptor(Field field, boolean required) {
        // ...
    }
    
    // Key methods used during dependency resolution
    public Class getDependencyType() {
        return this.resolvableType.resolve();
    }
    
    public ResolvableType getResolvableType() {
        return this.resolvableType;
    }
    
    public boolean isRequired() {
        return this.required;
    }
    
    public Annotation[] getAnnotations() {
        // Returns annotations on the dependency point
    }
    
    public String getDependencyName() {
        // Used for bean name matching
    }
}

// How DependencyDescriptor is used in resolution
public class DefaultListableBeanFactory {
    
    public Object resolveDependency(DependencyDescriptor descriptor, String beanName) {
        
        // Get the type to look for
        Class type = descriptor.getDependencyType();
        
        // Check for @Qualifier
        Annotation qualifier = descriptor.getAnnotation(Qualifier.class);
        
        // Handle different dependency types
        if (descriptor.getDependencyType().isArray()) {
            return resolveArrayDependency(descriptor, beanName);
        } else if (Collection.class.isAssignableFrom(type) && type.isInterface()) {
            return resolveCollectionDependency(descriptor, beanName);
        } else if (Map.class.isAssignableFrom(type) && type.isInterface()) {
            return resolveMapDependency(descriptor, beanName);
        } else {
            // Resolve single bean dependency
            return resolveSingleDependency(descriptor, beanName);
        }
    }
    
    private Object resolveSingleDependency(DependencyDescriptor descriptor, String beanName) {
        // Find candidate beans matching the type
        Map matchingBeans = findAutowireCandidates(beanName, 
            descriptor.getDependencyType(), descriptor);
        
        if (matchingBeans.isEmpty()) {
            if (descriptor.isRequired()) {
                throw new NoSuchBeanDefinitionException(descriptor.getDependencyType());
            }
            return null;
        }
        
        if (matchingBeans.size() > 1) {
            // Determine primary candidate or throw exception
            String autowiredBeanName = determineAutowireCandidate(matchingBeans, descriptor);
            return matchingBeans.get(autowiredBeanName);
        }
        
        return matchingBeans.values().iterator().next();
    }
}

// Example of DependencyDescriptor in action
@Component
public class ExampleBean {
    
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("specialService")
    private MyService service; // Creates DependencyDescriptor with field info and @Qualifier
}
DependencyDescriptor Information
  • Type Information: Dependency type, generics
  • Annotations: @Qualifier, @Value, custom annotations
  • Context: Declaring class, method/field name
  • Requirements: Required vs optional
  • Nesting Level: For nested generics
Resolution Process
  • Type Analysis: Determine actual type to look for
  • Candidate Lookup: Find beans matching type
  • Qualifier Resolution: Apply @Qualifier filters
  • Primary/Ordering: Resolve conflicts
  • Instance Creation: Get or create bean instance

Dependency Resolution Quick Reference

Resolution Order

  • Constructor parameters first
  • Field injection second
  • Method injection third
  • @Value injection with fields

BeanPostProcessors

  • AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor
  • CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor
  • PersistenceAnnotationBeanPostProcessor
  • Custom BeanPostProcessors

Optional Dependencies

  • @Autowired(required=false)
  • Optional<T> type
  • @Nullable annotation
  • ObjectProvider

Key Classes

  • DependencyDescriptor
  • InjectionMetadata
  • ResolvableType
  • DefaultListableBeanFactory

Critical Dependency Resolution Rules

  • Constructor injection happens during instantiation and is mandatory
  • Field and method injection occur after instantiation but before @PostConstruct
  • Circular dependencies are detected during constructor injection
  • @Primary beans are preferred when multiple candidates exist
  • @Qualifier takes precedence over bean name matching
  • Optional dependencies must be explicitly marked as optional

Spring @Qualifier Annotation: Complete Guide

@Qualifier Annotation Overview

The @Qualifier annotation is a powerful Spring feature that helps resolve ambiguity when multiple beans of the same type are available in the application context. It provides fine-grained control over bean selection during dependency injection.

Core Concept: When Spring encounters multiple beans of the same type, @Qualifier allows you to specify exactly which bean should be injected by providing a qualifier value that matches the target bean's qualifier.

What is @Qualifier Annotation?

@Qualifier Definition & Purpose

@Qualifier is a Spring annotation used to resolve autowiring conflicts when multiple beans of the same type exist in the Spring container. It works alongside @Autowired to specify which exact bean should be injected. 


package org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation;

@Target({ElementType.FIELD, ElementType.METHOD, ElementType.PARAMETER, 
         ElementType.TYPE, ElementType.ANNOTATION_TYPE})
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Inherited
@Documented
public @interface Qualifier {
    String value() default "";
}
Primary Use Cases
  • Resolving multiple bean conflicts
  • Explicit bean selection
  • Working with third-party beans
  • Conditional bean injection
Applicable To
  • Fields (Field injection)
  • Methods (Setter injection)
  • Parameters (Constructor injection)
  • Types (Custom qualifiers)

Basic @Qualifier Usage Example


// Multiple beans of the same type
@Component("emailService")
public class EmailService implements MessageService {
    public void sendMessage(String message) {
        System.out.println("Email: " + message);
    }
}

@Component("smsService") 
public class SmsService implements MessageService {
    public void sendMessage(String message) {
        System.out.println("SMS: " + message);
    }
}

// Using @Qualifier to resolve ambiguity
@Service
public class NotificationService {
    
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("emailService")  // Explicitly specify which bean to inject
    private MessageService messageService;
    
    public void notifyUser(String message) {
        messageService.sendMessage(message);
    }
}

// Alternative: Using @Qualifier on parameters
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    private final MessageService messageService;
    
    @Autowired
    public OrderService(@Qualifier("smsService") MessageService messageService) {
        this.messageService = messageService;
    }
}

Key Point: Without @Qualifier, Spring would throw NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException because it cannot decide which MessageService implementation to inject.

When Should We Use @Qualifier?

Common Scenarios for @Qualifier Usage

1. Multiple Implementations
@Component("mysqlDataSource")
public class MySqlDataSource implements DataSource { }

@Component("oracleDataSource")  
public class OracleDataSource implements DataSource { }

@Service
public class ReportService {
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("mysqlDataSource")
    private DataSource dataSource;
}
2. Different Configurations
@Configuration
public class DataSourceConfig {
    
    @Bean("primaryDataSource")
    public DataSource primaryDataSource() {
        return DataSourceBuilder.create().build();
    }
    
    @Bean("backupDataSource")
    public DataSource backupDataSource() {
        return DataSourceBuilder.create().build();
    }
}

@Service
public class BackupService {
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("backupDataSource")
    private DataSource dataSource;
}
3. Third-party Beans
@Configuration
public class ExternalServiceConfig {
    
    @Bean("restTemplateV1")
    public RestTemplate restTemplateV1() {
        return new RestTemplate();
    }
    
    @Bean("restTemplateV2") 
    public RestTemplate restTemplateV2() {
        RestTemplate template = new RestTemplate();
        template.getMessageConverters()
               .add(new MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter());
        return template;
    }
}

@Service
public class ApiService {
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("restTemplateV2")
    private RestTemplate restTemplate;
}
4. Environment-specific Beans
@Profile("dev")
@Component("devPaymentService")
public class DevPaymentService implements PaymentService { }

@Profile("prod")
@Component("prodPaymentService")  
public class ProdPaymentService implements PaymentService { }

@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("devPaymentService")
    private PaymentService paymentService;
}

When NOT to Use @Qualifier

Use @Primary Instead When:
  • One bean should be default for most cases
  • Multiple beans exist but one is primary
  • You want to avoid repetitive @Qualifier usage
  • The bean selection is consistent across the application
Consider Alternatives When:
  • Only one bean of the type exists (unnecessary)
  • Using constructor injection with clear parameter names
  • Bean selection logic is complex (use factory)
  • Dynamic bean selection is needed (use ApplicationContext)

How @Qualifier Resolves Bean Conflicts

Bean Resolution Process

Spring follows a specific process to resolve bean dependencies when multiple candidates exist. Understanding this process helps in debugging and designing better bean configurations.

Spring Bean Resolution Algorithm
1
Check for @Qualifier match
Matches qualifier value with bean name or qualifier annotation
2
Check for @Primary bean
If no @Qualifier, looks for @Primary annotated bean
3
Check by bean name
Matches field name with bean name (if no @Qualifier)
4
Throw Exception
NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException if ambiguity remains

// Example demonstrating resolution process
@Component("databaseService")
public class DatabaseService implements DataService {
    // implementation
}

@Component("fileService")
@Primary  // This would be chosen if no @Qualifier specified
public class FileService implements DataService {
    // implementation  
}

@Component("cloudService")
public class CloudService implements DataService {
    // implementation
}

@Service
public class DataProcessor {
    
    // CASE 1: @Qualifier takes highest precedence
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("databaseService")  // This bean is injected
    private DataService dataService1;
    
    // CASE 2: No @Qualifier, @Primary is chosen  
    @Autowired
    private DataService dataService2;  // FileService injected (because of @Primary)
    
    // CASE 3: Field name matching (if no @Primary)
    @Autowired
    private DataService cloudService;  // Would match cloudService bean by name
    
    // CASE 4: Exception if no @Primary and multiple matches
    @Autowired
    private DataService service;  // ERROR: NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
}

Practical Resolution Examples

Using Bean Names as Qualifiers
@Component("pdfReportGenerator")
public class PdfReportGenerator implements ReportGenerator { }

@Component("excelReportGenerator")
public class ExcelReportGenerator implements ReportGenerator { }

@Service
public class ReportService {
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("pdfReportGenerator")  // Matches bean name
    private ReportGenerator generator;
}
Explicit @Qualifier on Beans
@Component
@Qualifier("secure")
public class SecureHttpClient implements HttpClient { }

@Component  
@Qualifier("standard")
public class StandardHttpClient implements HttpClient { }

@Service
public class ApiClient {
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("secure")  // Matches qualifier annotation
    private HttpClient httpClient;
}

Custom Qualifier Annotations

Creating Custom Qualifier Annotations

For more complex scenarios, you can create custom qualifier annotations that provide type-safe and meaningful bean selection mechanisms. 


// Custom qualifier for database types
@Target({ElementType.FIELD, ElementType.METHOD, ElementType.PARAMETER, ElementType.TYPE})
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Qualifier
public @interface DatabaseType {
    String value();
}

// Custom qualifier for format types  
@Target({ElementType.FIELD, ElementType.METHOD, ElementType.PARAMETER, ElementType.TYPE})
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Qualifier
public @interface Format {
    FormatType value();
}

enum FormatType {
    JSON, XML, CSV
}

// Using custom qualifiers
@Component
@DatabaseType("mysql")
public class MySqlDataSource implements DataSource {
    // implementation
}

@Component
@DatabaseType("postgres")
public class PostgresDataSource implements DataSource {
    // implementation  
}

@Component
@Format(FormatType.JSON)
public class JsonFormatter implements Formatter {
    // implementation
}

@Component
@Format(FormatType.XML)
public class XmlFormatter implements Formatter {
    // implementation
}

// Injection using custom qualifiers
@Service
public class DataService {
    
    @Autowired
    @DatabaseType("mysql")
    private DataSource dataSource;
    
    @Autowired
    @Format(FormatType.JSON)
    private Formatter formatter;
    
    public DataService(@DatabaseType("postgres") DataSource backupDataSource) {
        // constructor injection with custom qualifier
    }
}

Benefits of Custom Qualifiers: Type safety, better readability, compile-time checking, and self-documenting code. Custom qualifiers make the intention clear and reduce string-based qualifier errors.

Advanced Custom Qualifier Patterns

Multi-value Qualifiers
@Target({ElementType.FIELD, ElementType.METHOD, 
         ElementType.PARAMETER, ElementType.TYPE})
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Qualifier
public @interface ServiceConfig {
    String environment();
    String region();
    boolean secure() default false;
}

@Component
@ServiceConfig(environment = "production", 
              region = "us-east", 
              secure = true)
public class ProductionUSService implements BusinessService { }

@Component
@ServiceConfig(environment = "development", 
              region = "local")
public class DevelopmentService implements BusinessService { }
Meta-Qualifier Annotations
// Meta-annotation for specific use cases
@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Qualifier("caching")
public @interface Caching { }

@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)  
@Qualifier("nonCaching")
public @interface NonCaching { }

@Component
@Caching
public class CachingRepository implements Repository { }

@Component
@NonCaching
public class NonCachingRepository implements Repository { }

@Service
public class BusinessService {
    @Autowired
    @Caching  // Uses meta-qualifier
    private Repository repository;
}

Difference Between @Qualifier and @Primary

@Qualifier vs @Primary Comparison

Aspect @Qualifier @Primary
Purpose Explicit bean selection Default bean selection
Precedence Higher (takes priority over @Primary) Lower (used when no @Qualifier specified)
Usage Scope Per injection point Application-wide
Flexibility High (different beans at different points) Low (same bean everywhere)
Configuration Annotation on injection points Annotation on bean definition
Use Case Specific bean needed in specific places One bean should be default everywhere

Practical Examples: @Qualifier vs @Primary


// Bean definitions
@Component("emailService")
@Primary  // Default message service
public class EmailService implements MessageService {
    public void sendMessage(String message) {
        System.out.println("Email: " + message);
    }
}

@Component("smsService")
public class SmsService implements MessageService {
    public void sendMessage(String message) {
        System.out.println("SMS: " + message);
    }
}

@Component("pushService")  
public class PushService implements MessageService {
    public void sendMessage(String message) {
        System.out.println("Push: " + message);
    }
}

// Usage in different services
@Service
public class NotificationService {
    
    @Autowired
    private MessageService messageService;  // Gets EmailService (@Primary)
    
    public void sendNotification(String message) {
        messageService.sendMessage(message);
    }
}

@Service  
public class AlertService {
    
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("smsService")  // Explicitly chooses SMS service
    private MessageService messageService;
    
    public void sendAlert(String message) {
        messageService.sendMessage(message);
    }
}

@Service
public class MarketingService {
    
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("pushService")  // Explicitly chooses Push service
    private MessageService messageService;
    
    public void sendPromotion(String message) {
        messageService.sendMessage(message);
    }
}

Design Strategy: Use @Primary for the most commonly used bean implementation, and @Qualifier for specific cases where a different implementation is needed. This reduces repetitive @Qualifier annotations while maintaining flexibility.

What Happens When Both @Qualifier and @Primary Are Used?

Resolution Rules and Precedence

When both @Qualifier and @Primary are present in the application context, Spring follows specific precedence rules to determine which bean to inject. 


// Bean configurations with both @Primary and @Qualifier
@Component("mysqlDataSource")
@Primary  // Marked as primary data source
public class MySqlDataSource implements DataSource {
    // implementation
}

@Component("oracleDataSource")
public class OracleDataSource implements DataSource {
    // implementation  
}

@Component("postgresDataSource")
public class PostgresDataSource implements DataSource {
    // implementation
}

// Different injection scenarios
@Service
public class ReportService {
    
    // CASE 1: No qualifier - @Primary wins
    @Autowired
    private DataSource dataSource1;  // MySqlDataSource injected
    
    // CASE 2: @Qualifier specified - @Qualifier wins over @Primary
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("oracleDataSource")
    private DataSource dataSource2;  // OracleDataSource injected
    
    // CASE 3: @Qualifier matches @Primary bean
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("mysqlDataSource")  
    private DataSource dataSource3;  // MySqlDataSource injected (same as primary)
    
    // CASE 4: Invalid @Qualifier - Exception
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("invalidDataSource")  // ERROR: NoSuchBeanDefinitionException
    private DataSource dataSource4;
}

// PRECEDENCE SUMMARY:
// 1. @Qualifier value match (highest priority)
// 2. @Primary bean (if no @Qualifier specified)  
// 3. Bean name matching (if no @Primary)
// 4. Exception if ambiguity remains

Key Rule: @Qualifier always takes precedence over @Primary. When a @Qualifier is specified, Spring ignores the @Primary annotation and looks only for beans matching the qualifier value.

Complex Scenarios and Edge Cases

Multiple @Primary Beans
@Component
@Primary  // ERROR: Multiple primary beans
public class PrimaryServiceA implements MyService { }

@Component  
@Primary  // ERROR: Multiple primary beans
public class PrimaryServiceB implements MyService { }

// Results in: NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
// Even though both are @Primary, Spring cannot choose

Solution: Use only one @Primary per type

Conflicting Qualifiers
@Component
@Qualifier("serviceA")
public class ServiceA implements MyService { }

@Component
@Qualifier("serviceA")  // Same qualifier, different beans
public class ServiceB implements MyService { }

@Service
public class Consumer {
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("serviceA")  // ERROR: Multiple beans with same qualifier
    private MyService service;
}

Solution: Ensure unique qualifier values

Using @Qualifier with Constructor Injection

Constructor Injection with @Qualifier

Constructor injection is the preferred dependency injection method in Spring. @Qualifier can be applied to constructor parameters to resolve bean ambiguities. 


// Multiple service implementations
@Component("userService")
public class UserService implements BusinessService {
    public void process() {
        System.out.println("Processing users");
    }
}

@Component("orderService")
public class OrderService implements BusinessService {
    public void process() {
        System.out.println("Processing orders");
    }
}

@Component("paymentService")
public class PaymentService implements BusinessService {
    public void process() {
        System.out.println("Processing payments");
    }
}

// Using @Qualifier with constructor injection
@Service
public class ApplicationFacade {
    
    private final BusinessService userService;
    private final BusinessService orderService;
    private final BusinessService paymentService;
    
    // @Qualifier on constructor parameters
    @Autowired
    public ApplicationFacade(
            @Qualifier("userService") BusinessService userService,
            @Qualifier("orderService") BusinessService orderService, 
            @Qualifier("paymentService") BusinessService paymentService) {
        
        this.userService = userService;
        this.orderService = orderService;
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }
    
    public void processAll() {
        userService.process();
        orderService.process();
        paymentService.process();
    }
}

// Alternative: Using custom qualifiers with constructor injection
@Service
public class ReportGenerator {
    
    private final Formatter jsonFormatter;
    private final Formatter xmlFormatter;
    
    @Autowired
    public ReportGenerator(
            @Format(FormatType.JSON) Formatter jsonFormatter,
            @Format(FormatType.XML) Formatter xmlFormatter) {
        
        this.jsonFormatter = jsonFormatter;
        this.xmlFormatter = xmlFormatter;
    }
    
    public void generateReports(String data) {
        String json = jsonFormatter.format(data);
        String xml = xmlFormatter.format(data);
        // use both formatted outputs
    }
}

// With @Primary and constructor injection
@Component
@Primary
public class DefaultService implements BusinessService {
    // implementation
}

@Service
public class DefaultConsumer {
    
    private final BusinessService service;
    
    // No @Qualifier needed - @Primary is used
    @Autowired
    public DefaultConsumer(BusinessService service) {
        this.service = service;  // DefaultService injected (because of @Primary)
    }
}

Best Practice: Constructor injection with @Qualifier makes dependencies explicit and immutable. It's easier to test and ensures that required dependencies are provided at object creation time.

Benefits of Constructor Injection with @Qualifier

Immutability
  • Dependencies are final
  • Object state cannot change after construction
  • Thread-safe by design
  • No setter methods needed
Testability
  • Easy to mock dependencies in tests
  • No reflection needed for testing
  • Clear dependency requirements
  • Compile-time safety

Using @Qualifier with Setter Injection

Setter Injection with @Qualifier

Setter injection provides flexibility for optional dependencies or when you need to change dependencies at runtime. @Qualifier can be applied to setter method parameters. 


// Notification service implementations
@Component("emailNotification")
public class EmailNotificationService implements NotificationService {
    public void send(String message) {
        System.out.println("Email: " + message);
    }
}

@Component("smsNotification")  
public class SmsNotificationService implements NotificationService {
    public void send(String message) {
        System.out.println("SMS: " + message);
    }
}

@Component("pushNotification")
public class PushNotificationService implements NotificationService {
    public void send(String message) {
        System.out.println("Push: " + message);
    }
}

// Using @Qualifier with setter injection
@Service
public class NotificationManager {
    
    private NotificationService primaryNotification;
    private NotificationService secondaryNotification;
    private NotificationService emergencyNotification;
    
    // Setter injection with @Qualifier
    @Autowired
    public void setPrimaryNotification(@Qualifier("emailNotification") 
                                     NotificationService notification) {
        this.primaryNotification = notification;
    }
    
    @Autowired
    public void setSecondaryNotification(@Qualifier("smsNotification") 
                                       NotificationService notification) {
        this.secondaryNotification = notification;
    }
    
    @Autowired 
    public void setEmergencyNotification(@Qualifier("pushNotification") 
                                       NotificationService notification) {
        this.emergencyNotification = notification;
    }
    
    public void sendPrimaryNotification(String message) {
        primaryNotification.send(message);
    }
    
    public void sendSecondaryNotification(String message) {
        secondaryNotification.send(message);
    }
    
    public void sendEmergencyNotification(String message) {
        emergencyNotification.send(message);
    }
}

// Optional dependencies with setter injection
@Service
public class OrderProcessor {
    
    private NotificationService notificationService;
    
    // Optional dependency - won't fail if no NotificationService beans
    @Autowired(required = false)
    public void setNotificationService(@Qualifier("emailNotification") 
                                     NotificationService notificationService) {
        this.notificationService = notificationService;
    }
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        // process order logic
        
        // Only notify if notification service is available
        if (notificationService != null) {
            notificationService.send("Order processed: " + order.getId());
        }
    }
}

// Multiple setters for same type with different qualifiers
@Service
public class MultiChannelNotifier {
    
    private NotificationService channelA;
    private NotificationService channelB;
    
    @Autowired
    public void setChannelA(@Qualifier("emailNotification") 
                           NotificationService service) {
        this.channelA = service;
    }
    
    @Autowired
    public void setChannelB(@Qualifier("smsNotification") 
                           NotificationService service) {
        this.channelB = service;
    }
    
    public void broadcast(String message) {
        channelA.send(message);
