        channelB.send(message);
    }
}

When to Use Setter Injection with @Qualifier

Appropriate Use Cases
  • Optional dependencies
  • Circular dependency scenarios
  • Runtime dependency switching
  • Configuration changes after initialization
  • Legacy code integration
Considerations
  • Dependencies are mutable
  • Not thread-safe by default
  • More difficult to test than constructor injection
  • Can lead to partially initialized objects

@Qualifier Best Practices & Quick Reference

When to Use

  • Multiple beans of same type
  • Explicit bean selection needed
  • Different beans at different points
  • Working with third-party beans

Precedence Rules

  • @Qualifier (highest)
  • @Primary (medium)
  • Bean name matching (lowest)
  • Exception if unresolved

Injection Methods

  • Constructor parameters
  • Setter method parameters
  • Field injection
  • Method parameters

Critical Best Practices

  • Prefer constructor injection over setter injection
  • Use custom qualifiers for type safety
  • Combine @Primary with @Qualifier for flexible configurations
  • Avoid multiple @Primary beans for the same type
  • Ensure unique qualifier values across beans
  • Use meaningful qualifier names that describe the bean's purpose

Spring @Primary Annotation: Complete Guide with Examples

@Primary Annotation Overview

The @Primary annotation in Spring Framework is used to indicate that a particular bean should be given preference when multiple beans of the same type are available for dependency injection. It's a powerful mechanism for resolving bean conflicts and defining default implementations.

Core Concept: When Spring encounters multiple beans of the same type during dependency injection, @Primary tells the container which bean should be the default choice when no specific bean is requested using @Qualifier.

What is @Primary Annotation?

@Primary Annotation Definition

@Primary is a Spring annotation that can be applied at the class level or method level to indicate that a bean should be preferred when multiple candidates are available for autowiring. 


import org.springframework.context.annotation.Primary;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

// @Primary can be used with different stereotype annotations
@Primary
@Component
public class PrimaryDataSource implements DataSource {
    // This bean will be preferred when DataSource is autowired
}

@Component 
public class SecondaryDataSource implements DataSource {
    // This bean will not be used unless explicitly qualified
}

// Usage in service class
@Service
public class DataService {
    
    // PrimaryDataSource will be injected automatically
    @Autowired
    private DataSource dataSource;
}
Key Characteristics
  • Meta-annotation that can be used with component scanning
  • Works with @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Bean methods
  • Resolves ambiguity in dependency injection
  • Defines default bean implementation
Annotation Targets
  • Class level: With stereotype annotations
  • Method level: With @Bean methods in configuration
  • Cannot be used: On fields or parameters

@Primary Syntax and Usage Patterns


// PATTERN 1: With @Component and stereotypes
@Primary
@Component
public class EmailNotificationService implements NotificationService {
    public void send(String message) {
        System.out.println("Sending email: " + message);
    }
}

@Component
public class SmsNotificationService implements NotificationService {
    public void send(String message) {
        System.out.println("Sending SMS: " + message);
    }
}

// PATTERN 2: With @Bean methods in configuration
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    
    @Primary
    @Bean
    public DataSource primaryDataSource() {
        return new HikariDataSource();
    }
    
    @Bean
    public DataSource secondaryDataSource() {
        return new BasicDataSource();
    }
}

// PATTERN 3: With @Repository in persistence layer
@Primary
@Repository
public class JpaUserRepository implements UserRepository {
    // JPA implementation
}

@Repository  
public class JdbcUserRepository implements UserRepository {
    // JDBC implementation
}

// PATTERN 4: Multiple interfaces implementation
@Primary
@Service
public class ComprehensiveReportService implements 
    ReportService, ExportService, ValidationService {
    // Implements multiple interfaces, primary for all
}

When Should We Use @Primary?

Common Use Cases for @Primary

@Primary is particularly useful in several scenarios where you need to define default implementations or resolve bean conflicts in a clean, declarative way.

1. Default Implementation
// Default implementation for most cases
@Primary
@Service
public class DefaultPaymentService implements PaymentService {
    public void process(Payment payment) {
        // Default payment processing
    }
}

// Specialized implementation for specific cases
@Service
public class PayPalPaymentService implements PaymentService {
    public void process(Payment payment) {
        // PayPal specific processing
    }
}

// Most services will get DefaultPaymentService automatically
@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Autowired
    private PaymentService paymentService; // Gets DefaultPaymentService
}
2. Multiple Data Sources
// Primary datasource for most operations
@Primary
@Bean
public DataSource primaryDataSource() {
    return DataSourceBuilder.create()
        .url("jdbc:mysql://primary/db")
        .build();
}

// Secondary datasource for reporting
@Bean
public DataSource secondaryDataSource() {
    return DataSourceBuilder.create()
        .url("jdbc:mysql://secondary/db")
        .build();
}

// Most repositories use primary automatically
@Repository
public class UserRepository {
    // Uses primaryDataSource by default
}
3. Testing & Mocking
// Production implementation
@Primary  // Only in production config
@Bean
public PaymentService paymentService() {
    return new RealPaymentService();
}

// Test configuration
@TestConfiguration
public class TestConfig {
    
    @Primary  // Overrides production primary in tests
    @Bean
    public PaymentService mockPaymentService() {
        return new MockPaymentService();
    }
}

// Test class gets mock automatically
@SpringBootTest
class OrderServiceTest {
    
    @Autowired
    private PaymentService paymentService; // Gets mock
}
4. Feature Toggles & Profiles
// Old implementation
@Component
@Profile("legacy")
@Primary  // Primary only in legacy profile
public class LegacyReportGenerator implements ReportGenerator {
    // Legacy implementation
}

// New implementation  
@Component
@Profile("modern")
@Primary  // Primary only in modern profile
public class ModernReportGenerator implements ReportGenerator {
    // Modern implementation
}

// Service gets appropriate implementation based on active profile
@Service
public class ReportService {
    @Autowired
    private ReportGenerator generator; // Gets profile-specific primary
}

When NOT to Use @Primary

Avoid @Primary When:
  • Explicit control needed: Use @Qualifier instead
  • Multiple primary candidates: Causes NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
  • Complex dependency graphs: Can lead to confusion
  • Library code: Let consumers decide which bean to use
  • Conditional beans: Use @ConditionalOnProperty instead
Better Alternatives:
  • @Qualifier: For explicit bean selection
  • @Conditional: For conditional bean creation
  • @Profile: For environment-specific beans
  • Factory methods: For complex creation logic

How @Primary Resolves Bean Conflicts

Bean Resolution Mechanism

When Spring encounters multiple beans of the same type during dependency injection, it follows a specific resolution process where @Primary plays a key role. 


// Example scenario with multiple beans
@Primary
@Component
public class PrimaryService implements MyService {
    // Marked as primary
}

@Component
public class SecondaryService implements MyService {
    // Regular component
}

@Component  
public class AnotherService implements MyService {
    // Another regular component
}

// Spring's resolution process when autowiring:
@Service
public class ConsumerService {
    
    @Autowired
    private MyService service; // Which one gets injected?
    
    // RESOLUTION PROCESS:
    // 1. Find all beans of type MyService
    //    - PrimaryService (primary)
    //    - SecondaryService
    //    - AnotherService
    // 2. Check if any bean is marked with @Primary
    // 3. Found PrimaryService with @Primary
    // 4. Inject PrimaryService automatically
}

Resolution Flow: Spring first looks for @Primary beans. If exactly one primary bean exists, it's selected. If multiple primary beans exist, Spring throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException.

With @Primary Present
  1. Find all candidate beans
  2. Check for @Primary annotation
  3. If exactly one primary → Select it
  4. If multiple primary → Throw exception
  5. If no primary → Continue to other resolvers
Without @Primary
  1. Find all candidate beans
  2. No @Primary found
  3. Check for @Qualifier on injection point
  4. Check for bean names matching field name
  5. If still ambiguous → Throw exception

Conflict Resolution Examples

Successful Resolution
// Configuration with clear primary
@Primary
@Bean
public DataSource mainDataSource() {
    return createDataSource("main");
}

@Bean
public DataSource backupDataSource() {
    return createDataSource("backup");
}

// Successful injection
@Repository
public class UserRepository {
    @Autowired
    private DataSource dataSource; // Gets mainDataSource
    // ✅ Works: Exactly one primary bean
}
Failed Resolution
// ERROR: Multiple primary beans
@Primary  // ❌ PROBLEM: Multiple @Primary
@Bean
public DataSource firstDataSource() {
    return createDataSource("first");
}

@Primary  // ❌ PROBLEM: Multiple @Primary  
@Bean
public DataSource secondDataSource() {
    return createDataSource("second");
}

// This will throw:
// NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException: 
// No qualifying bean of type 'DataSource' available: 
// expected single matching bean but found 2: 
// firstDataSource,secondDataSource

Can We Have Multiple @Primary Beans?

Multiple @Primary Beans Restriction

No, you cannot have multiple @Primary beans of the same type in the same Spring context. When Spring detects multiple primary candidates for the same type, it throws a NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException because it cannot determine which one to use as the default. 


// ❌ INVALID: Multiple @Primary beans of same type
@Configuration
public class InvalidConfig {
    
    @Primary  // First primary bean
    @Bean
    public PaymentService creditCardService() {
        return new CreditCardService();
    }
    
    @Primary  // ❌ SECOND PRIMARY - CAUSES EXCEPTION
    @Bean  
    public PaymentService payPalService() {
        return new PayPalService();
    }
    
    @Bean
    public PaymentService bankTransferService() {
        return new BankTransferService();
    }
}

// When autowiring PaymentService:
@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Autowired
    private PaymentService paymentService; 
    // ❌ Throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException:
    // "No qualifying bean of type 'PaymentService' available: 
    //  expected single matching bean but found 3: 
    //  creditCardService,payPalService,bankTransferService"
}

Exception Message: The error clearly indicates that Spring found multiple beans but couldn't determine which one to use, even though some are marked as @Primary. This happens specifically when multiple beans have the @Primary annotation.

Workarounds for Multiple Default Scenarios

Solution 1: Use @Qualifier
// Define beans with qualifiers
@Bean
@Qualifier("creditCard")
public PaymentService creditCardService() {
    return new CreditCardService();
}

@Bean
@Qualifier("paypal")  
public PaymentService payPalService() {
    return new PayPalService();
}

@Bean
@Qualifier("bankTransfer")
public PaymentService bankTransferService() {
    return new BankTransferService();
}

// Use @Primary for real default
@Primary
@Bean
@Qualifier("default")
public PaymentService defaultPaymentService() {
    return creditCardService(); // Delegate to preferred one
}

// Explicit injection when needed
@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Autowired
    private PaymentService paymentService; // Gets default
    
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("paypal")
    private PaymentService paypalService; // Gets specific
}
Solution 2: Use Profiles
// Different primary for different environments
@Configuration
@Profile("production")
public class ProductionConfig {
    
    @Primary  // Primary only in production
    @Bean
    public PaymentService productionPaymentService() {
        return new CreditCardService();
    }
}

@Configuration
@Profile("development")  
public class DevelopmentConfig {
    
    @Primary  // Primary only in development
    @Bean
    public PaymentService developmentPaymentService() {
        return new MockPaymentService();
    }
}

// Only one primary active per profile
@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Autowired
    private PaymentService paymentService; 
    // Gets profile-specific primary
}
Solution 3: Conditional Beans
// Conditional primary based on properties
@Configuration
public class ConditionalConfig {
    
    @Primary
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnProperty(
        name = "payment.provider", 
        havingValue = "stripe"
    )
    public PaymentService stripePaymentService() {
        return new StripeService();
    }
    
    @Primary
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnProperty(
        name = "payment.provider",
        havingValue = "paypal",
        matchIfMissing = true  // Default if property missing
    )
    public PaymentService payPalPaymentService() {
        return new PayPalService();
    }
}

// Only one condition will be true, so only one primary
@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Autowired
    private PaymentService paymentService; 
    // Gets conditional primary
}
Solution 4: Factory Pattern
// Factory that decides which implementation to use
@Component
public class PaymentServiceFactory {
    
    @Autowired
    private CreditCardService creditCard;
    
    @Autowired
    private PayPalService paypal;
    
    @Autowired
    private BankTransferService bankTransfer;
    
    public PaymentService getDefaultPaymentService() {
        // Custom logic to determine default
        return creditCard; // Your decision logic here
    }
}

// Single primary service that uses factory
@Primary
@Component
public class DefaultPaymentService implements PaymentService {
    
    @Autowired
    private PaymentServiceFactory factory;
    
    private PaymentService delegate;
    
    @PostConstruct
    public void init() {
        delegate = factory.getDefaultPaymentService();
    }
    
    public void process(Payment payment) {
        delegate.process(payment);
    }
}

What Takes Precedence - @Qualifier or @Primary?

@Qualifier vs @Primary Precedence

@Qualifier always takes precedence over @Primary. When both annotations are present, Spring will use the bean specified by @Qualifier, completely ignoring the @Primary annotation. 


// Bean definitions
@Primary  // Marked as primary
@Component
public class PrimaryService implements MyService {
    public void execute() {
        System.out.println("Primary service executed");
    }
}

@Qualifier("secondary")
@Component
public class SecondaryService implements MyService {
    public void execute() {
        System.out.println("Secondary service executed");
    }
}

@Qualifier("tertiary")  
@Component
public class TertiaryService implements MyService {
    public void execute() {
        System.out.println("Tertiary service executed");
    }
}

// Different injection scenarios
@Service
public class ConsumerService {
    
    // CASE 1: No qualifier - uses @Primary
    @Autowired
    private MyService service1; 
    // Injects: PrimaryService (because it's primary)
    
    // CASE 2: With @Qualifier - ignores @Primary
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("secondary")
    private MyService service2; 
    // Injects: SecondaryService (qualifier takes precedence)
    
    // CASE 3: Another qualifier
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("tertiary")
    private MyService service3; 
    // Injects: TertiaryService (qualifier takes precedence)
}

// Output when methods are called:
// service1.execute() -> "Primary service executed"
// service2.execute() -> "Secondary service executed"  
// service3.execute() -> "Tertiary service executed"

Resolution Order: Spring first checks if a @Qualifier is specified. If yes, it looks for a bean with that qualifier. Only when no qualifier is specified does Spring consider @Primary beans.

Practical Precedence Examples

Constructor Injection
// Beans with primary and qualifiers
@Primary
@Bean
public DataSource mainDataSource() {
    return createDataSource("main");
}

@Bean
@Qualifier("reporting")
public DataSource reportingDataSource() {
    return createDataSource("reporting");
}

// Constructor injection examples
@Service
public class UserService {
    
    private final DataSource dataSource;
    
    // No qualifier - gets primary
    public UserService(DataSource dataSource) {
        this.dataSource = dataSource; // mainDataSource
    }
}

@Service
public class ReportService {
    
    private final DataSource dataSource;
    
    // With qualifier - gets specific bean
    public ReportService(
            @Qualifier("reporting") DataSource dataSource) {
        this.dataSource = dataSource; // reportingDataSource
    }
}
Method Parameter Injection
// Configuration with multiple message services
@Primary
@Bean
public MessageService emailService() {
    return new EmailService();
}

@Bean
@Qualifier("sms")
public MessageService smsService() {
    return new SmsService();
}

@Bean
@Qualifier("push")
public MessageService pushService() {
    return new PushNotificationService();
}

// Method parameter injection
@Service
public class NotificationService {
    
    // Qualifier on parameter overrides primary
    public void sendSmsAlert(
            @Qualifier("sms") MessageService messageService) {
        messageService.send("Alert!"); // Uses smsService
    }
    
    // No qualifier uses primary
    public void sendEmail(MessageService messageService) {
        messageService.send("Newsletter"); // Uses emailService
    }
}

Difference Between @Primary and Bean Ordering

@Primary vs @Order vs @Priority Comparison

Annotation Purpose Usage Precedence Use Case
@Primary Default bean selection Bean definitions High (but below @Qualifier) Single default implementation
@Order Execution order in collections Beans in List/array injection Collection ordering only Ordered processors, interceptors
@Priority JSR-250 priority standard Similar to @Order Collection ordering only Standard Java EE ordering
@Primary Example
// @Primary selects a single bean
@Primary
@Service
public class PrimaryService implements MyService {
    // This bean is selected for single injection
}

@Service
public class SecondaryService implements MyService {
    // Not selected unless explicitly qualified
}

// Single bean injection
@Service
public class Consumer {
    @Autowired
    private MyService service; // Gets PrimaryService
}
@Order Example
// @Order affects collection order
@Order(1)
@Service
public class FirstService implements MyService {
    // Executed first in collection
}

@Order(2)  
@Service
public class SecondService implements MyService {
    // Executed second in collection
}

@Order(3)
@Service
public class ThirdService implements MyService {
    // Executed third in collection
}

// Collection injection with order
@Service
public class Consumer {
    @Autowired
    private List<MyService> services; 
    // Order: [FirstService, SecondService, ThirdService]
}

Key Differences Summary

@Primary Characteristics
  • Single bean selection: Chooses one bean from multiple candidates
  • Dependency injection: Affects @Autowired on single fields
  • Default behavior: Defines the default implementation
  • Mutual exclusion: Only one primary per type allowed
  • Override by: @Qualifier takes precedence
@Order/@Priority Characteristics
  • Collection ordering: Affects order in Lists/arrays
  • Multiple beans: All beans are injected, just ordered
  • Execution order: Determines processing sequence
  • No mutual exclusion: Multiple beans can have order
  • Different purpose: Doesn't affect single bean selection
Important Note

@Primary and ordering annotations (@Order, @Priority) serve completely different purposes. @Primary is for selecting a single bean, while ordering annotations are for arranging multiple beans in collections. They can be used together without conflict.

@Primary Best Practices & Quick Reference

When to Use

  • Default implementations
  • Multiple data sources
  • Testing configurations
  • Profile-specific defaults
  • Feature toggles

When to Avoid

  • Multiple primary candidates
  • Explicit control needed
  • Library development
  • Complex dependency graphs
  • Conditional bean creation

Precedence Rules

  • @Qualifier > @Primary
  • Bean name matching > @Primary
  • Only one @Primary per type
  • @Order doesn't affect @Primary

Critical Rules to Remember

  • @Primary defines the default bean when no specific bean is requested
  • @Qualifier always takes precedence over @Primary
  • Only one @Primary bean is allowed per type in the same context
  • @Primary doesn't affect collection injection order - use @Order for that
  • Use profiles or conditions to have different primary beans in different environments
  • Always test bean resolution to ensure the correct bean is being injected

Spring @Resource Annotation: Complete Guide with Examples

What is @Resource Annotation?

The @Resource annotation is part of the Java EE (now Jakarta EE) specification and is used for dependency injection in Spring applications. It provides a standardized way to inject dependencies by name or by type, offering an alternative to Spring's native @Autowired annotation.

Key Fact: @Resource is part of JSR-250 (Common Annotations) and follows JNDI lookup semantics, making it familiar to Java EE developers while being fully supported in Spring.

@Resource Annotation Overview

Basic @Resource Usage

@Resource can be applied to fields, setter methods, and even constructor parameters (with some limitations). Here's how to use it in different scenarios: 


import javax.annotation.Resource;

// Service beans
@Service
public class UserService {
    public String getUserInfo() {
        return "User Information";
    }
}

@Service  
public class OrderService {
    public String getOrderInfo() {
        return "Order Information";
    }
}

// Client class using @Resource
@Component
public class ClientService {
    
    // 1. Field injection - by type
    @Resource
    private UserService userService;
    
    // 2. Field injection - by name
    @Resource(name = "orderService")
    private OrderService orderService;
    
    private AuditService auditService;
    
    // 3. Setter injection
    @Resource
    public void setAuditService(AuditService auditService) {
        this.auditService = auditService;
    }
    
    // 4. Constructor injection (limited support)
    private final PaymentService paymentService;
    
    public ClientService(@Resource PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }
    
    public void process() {
        System.out.println(userService.getUserInfo());
        System.out.println(orderService.getOrderInfo());
    }
}

// Configuration to enable @Resource
@Configuration
@ComponentScan(basePackages = "com.example")
public class AppConfig {
    // No special configuration needed for @Resource
}

Note: While @Resource can be used on constructors, this is less common and has limitations compared to field and setter injection.

What is the Default Behavior of @Resource?

The @Resource annotation follows a specific lookup strategy when no explicit name is provided. Understanding this default behavior is crucial for effective dependency injection. 


@Component
public class DefaultBehaviorExample {
    
    // CASE 1: No name specified - uses field name
    @Resource
    private UserRepository userRepository;
    // Lookup: by name "userRepository" first, then by type UserRepository
    
    // CASE 2: Field name matches bean name
    @Resource
    private OrderService orderService;
    // Lookup: bean named "orderService" (matches field name)
    
    // CASE 3: Field name doesn't match any bean - falls back to type
    @Resource
    private SomeService myCustomService;
    // Lookup: 
    // 1. First tries bean named "myCustomService" (field name)
    // 2. If not found, looks for bean of type SomeService
    // 3. If multiple beans of type, throws exception
    
    // CASE 4: Interface type with multiple implementations
    @Resource
    private NotificationService notificationService;
    // This will fail if multiple NotificationService implementations exist
    // unless one is marked as @Primary
}

// Multiple implementations scenario
interface NotificationService {
    void sendNotification();
}

@Service("emailService")
public class EmailService implements NotificationService {
    public void sendNotification() {
        System.out.println("Sending email");
    }
}

@Service("smsService") 
public class SmsService implements NotificationService {
    public void sendNotification() {
        System.out.println("Sending SMS");
    }
}

@Component
public class NotificationClient {
    
    // This will FAIL - multiple NotificationService implementations
    @Resource
    private NotificationService notificationService;
    
    // Solutions:
    // 1. Use explicit name
    @Resource(name = "emailService")
    private NotificationService emailService;
    
    // 2. Use @Primary on one implementation
    // 3. Use @Qualifier with @Autowired instead
}
Default Lookup Strategy
  1. Match by name (using field/method name)
  2. Fall back to type matching
  3. Throw exception if ambiguous
Key Characteristics
  • Name-based by default
  • JNDI-style lookup semantics
  • Standard Java EE annotation
  • Works with any Spring bean

Difference between @Resource and @Autowired

@Resource vs @Autowired Comparison

Aspect @Resource @Autowired
Origin Java EE (JSR-250) Spring Framework
Default Lookup ByName → ByType ByType → ByName
Required Always required Optional (required=false)
Name Specification name attribute @Qualifier annotation
Constructor Support Limited Excellent
Primary Resolution Supports @Primary Supports @Primary
Package javax.annotation org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation

Practical Comparison Examples


// Service definitions
@Service("userService")
public class UserServiceImpl implements UserService {
    // implementation
}

@Service("alternativeUserService") 
public class AlternativeUserService implements UserService {
    // alternative implementation
}

@Service
@Primary
public class PrimaryUserService implements UserService {
    // primary implementation
}

// CLIENT CLASS SHOWING DIFFERENCES
@Component
public class InjectionComparison {
    
    // ========== @Resource EXAMPLES ==========
    
    // 1. @Resource with default behavior
    @Resource
    private UserService userService;
    // Lookup: by name "userService" → finds UserServiceImpl
    // If no "userService" bean, looks by type → finds PrimaryUserService (@Primary)
    
    // 2. @Resource with explicit name
    @Resource(name = "alternativeUserService")
    private UserService alternativeService;
    // Direct lookup by name "alternativeUserService"
    
    // 3. @Resource with type-only (no matching name)
    @Resource
    private UserService someService;
    // Lookup: 
    // - First by name "someService" (not found)
    // - Then by type UserService → finds PrimaryUserService (@Primary)
    
    // ========== @Autowired EXAMPLES ==========
    
    // 1. @Autowired with default behavior
    @Autowired
    private UserService userService;
    // Lookup: by type UserService → finds PrimaryUserService (@Primary)
    // If multiple without @Primary, uses field name "userService" as fallback
    
    // 2. @Autowired with @Qualifier
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("alternativeUserService")
    private UserService qualifiedService;
    // Direct lookup by qualifier name
    
    // 3. @Autowired with required=false
    @Autowired(required = false)
    private OptionalService optionalService;
    // Injects if available, null otherwise
    // @Resource doesn't have this feature
    
    // ========== CONSTRUCTOR INJECTION ==========
    
    // @Autowired works excellently with constructors
    private final UserService constructorInjected;
    
    @Autowired
    public InjectionComparison(UserService userService) {
        this.constructorInjected = userService;
    }
    
    // @Resource on constructors is possible but limited
    private final UserService resourceConstructor;
    
    public InjectionComparison(@Resource UserService userService) {
        this.resourceConstructor = userService;
    }
}

// SPECIAL CASE: Multiple beans without @Primary
@Service("serviceA")
public class ServiceA implements CommonService { }

@Service("serviceB") 
public class ServiceB implements CommonService { }

@Component
public class AmbiguousInjection {
    
    // @Resource behavior
    @Resource
    private CommonService commonService;
    // Throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException immediately
    // because field name "commonService" doesn't match any bean
    
    // @Autowired behavior  
    @Autowired
    private CommonService commonService;
    // Also throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
    // because multiple CommonService implementations
    
    // Solutions for both:
    // 1. Use explicit name/qualifier
    @Resource(name = "serviceA")
    private CommonService serviceA;
    
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("serviceB")
    private CommonService serviceB;
    
    // 2. Use @Primary on one implementation
    // 3. Use List injection for all implementations
    @Resource
    private List<CommonService> allServices;
}
@Resource Advantages
  • Standard Java EE annotation
  • Clear name-based semantics
  • Familiar to Java EE developers
  • Good for by-name injection
@Autowired Advantages
  • More flexible (required=false)
  • Better constructor support
  • Spring-native solution
  • Better for by-type injection

When to Use @Resource vs @Autowired?

Usage Guidelines and Best Practices

Choosing between @Resource and @Autowired depends on your specific use case, team preferences, and application requirements.

Use @Resource When...
  • You want name-based injection:
    When bean names are meaningful and you prefer explicit naming.
  • Working in Java EE environments:
    When your team is familiar with Java EE standards.
  • Migrating from Java EE:
    When porting existing Java EE applications to Spring.
  • Clear bean identification:
    When bean names clearly identify their purpose. 
// Good @Resource use case
@Resource(name = "emailNotificationService")
private NotificationService emailService;

@Resource(name = "smsNotificationService")  
private NotificationService smsService;
Use @Autowired When...
  • You prefer type-based injection:
    When you care more about types than names.
  • Using constructor injection:
    For better immutability and testability.
  • Optional dependencies:
    When you need required=false.
  • Pure Spring applications:
    When building new Spring-based systems. 
// Good @Autowired use cases
@Autowired(required = false)
private OptionalService optionalService;

@Autowired
public MyService(@Qualifier("specific") Dependency dep) {
    this.dependency = dep;
}
Team Consistency is Key

The most important factor is consistency within your team and project. Choose one approach and stick with it throughout your codebase. Mixing both annotations arbitrarily can lead to confusion and maintenance issues.

Real-World Usage Scenarios


// SCENARIO 1: Multiple Data Sources - @Resource works well
@Configuration
public class DataSourceConfig {
    
    @Bean(name = "primaryDataSource")
    public DataSource primaryDataSource() {
        return DataSourceBuilder.create().build();
    }
    
    @Bean(name = "secondaryDataSource") 
    public DataSource secondaryDataSource() {
        return DataSourceBuilder.create().build();
    }
}

@Component
public class DataSourceUser {
    
    // Clear and explicit with @Resource
    @Resource(name = "primaryDataSource")
    private DataSource mainDataSource;
    
    @Resource(name = "secondaryDataSource")
    private DataSource backupDataSource;
    
    // Equivalent with @Autowired
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("primaryDataSource")
    private DataSource mainDataSource;
    
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("secondaryDataSource") 
    private DataSource backupDataSource;
}

// SCENARIO 2: Service with multiple implementations - @Autowired may be better
public interface PaymentProcessor {
    void processPayment(BigDecimal amount);
}

@Service
@Primary
public class CreditCardProcessor implements PaymentProcessor {
    public void processPayment(BigDecimal amount) {
        // credit card processing
    }
}

@Service
public class PayPalProcessor implements PaymentProcessor {
    public void processPayment(BigDecimal amount) {
        // PayPal processing
    }
}

@Component
public class PaymentService {
    
    // @Autowired better here - we usually want the primary
    @Autowired
    private PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor; // Gets CreditCardProcessor
    
    // If we need specific one, both work:
    @Resource(name = "payPalProcessor")
    private PaymentProcessor payPalProcessor;
    
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("payPalProcessor")
    private PaymentProcessor alsoPayPalProcessor;
}

// SCENARIO 3: Optional dependencies - @Autowired only
@Component
public class ReportingService {
    
    // This only works with @Autowired
    @Autowired(required = false)
    private AdvancedAnalyticsService analyticsService;
    
    public void generateReport() {
        // analyticsService might be null
        if (analyticsService != null) {
            analyticsService.enhanceReport();
        }
        // generate basic report
    }
}

// SCENARIO 4: Constructor injection - @Autowired preferred
@Component
public class OrderProcessingService {
    
    private final PaymentService paymentService;
    private final InventoryService inventoryService;
    private final NotificationService notificationService;
    
    // @Autowired is idiomatic for constructor injection
    @Autowired
    public OrderProcessingService(
            PaymentService paymentService,
            InventoryService inventoryService, 
            NotificationService notificationService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
        this.inventoryService = inventoryService;
        this.notificationService = notificationService;
    }
}

How does @Resource perform dependency lookup?

@Resource Dependency Lookup Process

The @Resource annotation follows a specific, well-defined lookup process that combines name-based and type-based resolution strategies.

@Resource Lookup Algorithm
1
Check name attribute
If name specified, lookup by that name
▼
2
No name - use default name
Use field name or property name
▼
3
Name lookup fails
Fall back to type-based lookup
▼
4
Type lookup with @Primary
Resolve using @Primary if multiple

@Component
public class LookupProcessDemo {
    
    // CASE 1: Explicit name - direct lookup
    @Resource(name = "specificBeanName")
    private MyService service1;
    // Step 1: Look for bean named "specificBeanName"
    // If found → inject, if not → exception
    
    // CASE 2: No name - use field name
    @Resource
    private MyService myService;
    // Step 1: Look for bean named "myService" (field name)
    // If found → inject
    
    // Step 2: If no "myService" bean found
    // Fall back to type lookup for MyService
    // If single MyService bean → inject
    // If multiple → check for @Primary
    // If no @Primary → exception
    
    // CASE 3: Setter method
    private AnotherService anotherService;
    
    @Resource
    public void setAnotherService(AnotherService service) {
        this.anotherService = service;
    }
    // Step 1: Extract property name → "anotherService"
    // Look for bean named "anotherService"
    // If found → inject
    
    // Step 2: If no "anotherService" bean
    // Fall back to type lookup for AnotherService
}

// Detailed lookup implementation in Spring
public class CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor {
    
    protected Object autowireResource(BeanFactory factory, 
                                    Resource resource, 
                                    String suggestedName) {
        
        // 1. If name explicitly specified
        if (resource.name() != null && !resource.name().isEmpty()) {
            return factory.getBean(resource.name(), resource.type());
        }
        
        // 2. Use suggested name (field/property name)
        if (suggestedName != null) {
            try {
                return factory.getBean(suggestedName, resource.type());
            } catch (NoSuchBeanDefinitionException e) {
                // Name not found, continue to type lookup
            }
        }
        
        // 3. Type-based lookup
        return factory.getBean(resource.type());
    }
}

Can @Resource be used with name attribute?

Using @Resource with name Attribute

Yes, the name attribute is a fundamental feature of @Resource that allows explicit specification of the bean name for injection. This provides precise control over which specific bean gets injected. 


// Bean definitions with explicit names
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    
    @Bean(name = "primaryDataSource")
    public DataSource primaryDataSource() {
        return createDataSource("primary-url");
    }
    
    @Bean(name = "backupDataSource")
    public DataSource backupDataSource() {
        return createDataSource("backup-url");
    }
    
    @Bean(name = "reportingDataSource") 
    public DataSource reportingDataSource() {
        return createDataSource("reporting-url");
    }
}

// Service using named beans
@Service
public class DataService {
    
    // Explicit name matching - most precise
    @Resource(name = "primaryDataSource")
    private DataSource mainDataSource;
    
    @Resource(name = "backupDataSource")
    private DataSource secondaryDataSource;
    
    // Using with setter methods
    private DataSource reportingDataSource;
    
    @Resource(name = "reportingDataSource")
    public void setReportingDataSource(DataSource dataSource) {
        this.reportingDataSource = dataSource;
    }
}

// Multiple implementations of same interface
public interface MessageService {
    void sendMessage(String message);
}

@Service("emailMessageService")
public class EmailMessageService implements MessageService {
    public void sendMessage(String message) {
        // send email
    }
}

@Service("smsMessageService")
public class SmsMessageService implements MessageService {
    public void sendMessage(String message) {
        // send SMS
    }
}

@Service("pushMessageService") 
public class PushMessageService implements MessageService {
    public void sendMessage(String message) {
        // send push notification
    }
}

@Component
public class NotificationManager {
    
    // Inject specific implementations by name
    @Resource(name = "emailMessageService")
    private MessageService emailService;
    
    @Resource(name = "smsMessageService")
    private MessageService smsService;
    
    @Resource(name = "pushMessageService")
    private MessageService pushService;
    
    public void sendAllNotifications(String message) {
        emailService.sendMessage(message);
        smsService.sendMessage(message);
        pushService.sendMessage(message);
    }
}

// Dynamic bean names scenario
@Configuration
public class DynamicBeanConfig {
    
    @Bean(name = "summerDiscountStrategy")
    public DiscountStrategy summerDiscount() {
        return new SeasonalDiscountStrategy("SUMMER", 0.15);
    }
    
    @Bean(name = "winterDiscountStrategy")
    public DiscountStrategy winterDiscount() {
        return new SeasonalDiscountStrategy("WINTER", 0.20);
    }
    
    @Bean(name = "clearanceDiscountStrategy")
    public DiscountStrategy clearanceDiscount() {
        return new ClearanceDiscountStrategy(0.50);
    }
}

@Service
public class PricingService {
    
    // Inject specific strategy by name
    @Resource(name = "summerDiscountStrategy")
    private DiscountStrategy summerStrategy;
    
    @Resource(name = "winterDiscountStrategy") 
    private DiscountStrategy winterStrategy;
    
    @Resource(name = "clearanceDiscountStrategy")
    private DiscountStrategy clearanceStrategy;
    
    public BigDecimal calculatePrice(Product product, String season) {
        DiscountStrategy strategy = getStrategyForSeason(season);
        return strategy.applyDiscount(product.getPrice());
    }
    
    private DiscountStrategy getStrategyForSeason(String season) {
        switch (season.toUpperCase()) {
            case "SUMMER": return summerStrategy;
            case "WINTER": return winterStrategy;
            case "CLEARANCE": return clearanceStrategy;
            default: return summerStrategy;
        }
    }
}

Important: When using the name attribute, the bean must exist with that exact name. If no bean with the specified name is found, Spring will throw a NoSuchBeanDefinitionException. There is no fallback to type-based lookup when an explicit name is provided.

@Resource Annotation Quick Reference

Key Features

  • JSR-250 standard annotation
  • Name-based lookup by default
  • Fallback to type-based lookup
  • Works on fields and setters

Lookup Strategy

  1. Explicit name (if provided)
  2. Field/property name
  3. Type-based resolution

When to Use

  • Name-based injection preferred
  • Java EE compatibility needed
  • Multiple same-type beans
  • Explicit bean selection

Best Practices Summary

  • Use @Resource for clear name-based dependency injection
  • Prefer @Autowired for constructor injection and optional dependencies
  • Be consistent within your project - choose one primary approach
  • Use explicit names when working with multiple implementations of the same type
  • Understand the lookup fallback mechanism to avoid unexpected behavior

Spring @Configuration & @Bean: Complete Dependency Configuration Guide

Spring Configuration Overview

Spring's @Configuration and @Bean annotations provide powerful programmatic dependency configuration capabilities. They offer fine-grained control over bean creation and dependency wiring that goes beyond component scanning.

Core Concept: @Configuration classes are the modern replacement for XML configuration files, allowing you to define beans programmatically with full type safety and IDE support.

How to Configure Dependencies using @Configuration

@Configuration Class Structure

@Configuration classes are annotated with @Component and are processed by the Spring container to define bean definitions and dependencies. 


// Basic @Configuration class
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    
    // Bean definitions go here
    // These methods produce beans managed by Spring container
}

// Configuration with component scanning
@Configuration
@ComponentScan("com.example.services")
@PropertySource("classpath:application.properties")
@EnableJpaRepositories("com.example.repositories")
public class RootConfig {
    // Combines multiple configuration approaches
}

// Modular configuration
@Configuration
@Import({ DatabaseConfig.class, SecurityConfig.class, ServiceConfig.class })
public class MainConfig {
    // Imports other configuration classes
}

// Conditional configuration
@Configuration
@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "spring.datasource.url")
public class DatabaseConfig {
    // Only loaded if conditions are met
}

// Profile-specific configuration
@Configuration
@Profile("production")
public class ProductionConfig {
    // Only active when "production" profile is active
}

@Configuration
@Profile("development")  
public class DevelopmentConfig {
    // Only active when "development" profile is active
}
@Configuration Annotations
  • @ComponentScan - Enable component scanning
  • @PropertySource - Load property files
  • @Import - Import other config classes
  • @Profile - Profile-specific configuration
  • @Conditional - Conditional bean creation
Configuration Best Practices
  • Keep configurations focused and modular
  • Use meaningful class names
  • Group related beans together
  • Use profiles for environment-specific config
  • Document complex bean setups

Comprehensive @Configuration Example


@Configuration
@ComponentScan(basePackages = "com.example")
@PropertySource({
    "classpath:application.properties",
    "classpath:database.properties",
    "classpath:security.properties"
})
@EnableJpaRepositories(basePackages = "com.example.repositories")
@EnableTransactionManagement
@EnableCaching
@EnableAsync
public class ApplicationConfig {
    
    @Autowired
    private Environment env;
    
    // Database configuration
    @Bean
    @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "spring.datasource")
    public DataSource dataSource() {
        return DataSourceBuilder.create().build();
    }
    
    @Bean
    public LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean entityManagerFactory() {
        LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean em = new LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean();
        em.setDataSource(dataSource());
        em.setPackagesToScan("com.example.entities");
        
        JpaVendorAdapter vendorAdapter = new HibernateJpaVendorAdapter();
        em.setJpaVendorAdapter(vendorAdapter);
        em.setJpaProperties(additionalProperties());
        
        return em;
    }
    
    @Bean
    public PlatformTransactionManager transactionManager(EntityManagerFactory emf) {
        JpaTransactionManager transactionManager = new JpaTransactionManager();
        transactionManager.setEntityManagerFactory(emf);
        return transactionManager;
    }
    
    // Service layer beans
    @Bean
    public UserService userService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        return new UserServiceImpl(userRepository);
    }
    
    @Bean 
    public EmailService emailService() {
        return new EmailService(
            env.getProperty("email.host"),
            Integer.parseInt(env.getProperty("email.port"))
        );
    }
    
    // Utility beans
    @Bean
    public ObjectMapper objectMapper() {
        ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper();
        mapper.configure(DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, false);
        mapper.registerModule(new JavaTimeModule());
        return mapper;
    }
    
    @Bean
    public PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
        return new BCryptPasswordEncoder();
    }
    
    // Async configuration
    @Bean
    public TaskExecutor taskExecutor() {
        ThreadPoolTaskExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
        executor.setCorePoolSize(5);
        executor.setMaxPoolSize(10);
        executor.setQueueCapacity(25);
        executor.setThreadNamePrefix("async-");
        return executor;
    }
    
    // Helper method for properties
    private Properties additionalProperties() {
        Properties properties = new Properties();
        properties.setProperty("hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto", 
            env.getProperty("hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto"));
        properties.setProperty("hibernate.dialect", 
            env.getProperty("hibernate.dialect"));
        properties.setProperty("hibernate.show_sql", 
            env.getProperty("hibernate.show_sql", "false"));
        return properties;
    }
}

How @Bean Method Works for Dependency Injection

@Bean Method Execution & Caching

Spring intercepts @Bean method calls and ensures that beans are properly managed as singletons (by default) within the application context. 


@Configuration
public class BeanMechanicsConfig {
    
    private int creationCount = 0;
    
    // Singleton by default - Spring caches the result
    @Bean
    public MyService myService() {
        creationCount++;
        System.out.println("Creating MyService instance #" + creationCount);
        return new MyService();
    }
    
    // Prototype scope - new instance each time
    @Bean
    @Scope(ConfigurableBeanFactory.SCOPE_PROTOTYPE)
    public PrototypeService prototypeService() {
        creationCount++;
        System.out.println("Creating PrototypeService instance #" + creationCount);
        return new PrototypeService();
    }
    
    // Testing the mechanics
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ApplicationContext context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(BeanMechanicsConfig.class);
        
        // First call - creates the bean
        MyService service1 = context.getBean(MyService.class);
        
        // Second call - returns cached instance
        MyService service2 = context.getBean(MyService.class);
        
        // Output: "Creating MyService instance #1"
        // service1 == service2 (same instance)
        
        // Prototype beans create new instances
        PrototypeService proto1 = context.getBean(PrototypeService.class);
        PrototypeService proto2 = context.getBean(PrototypeService.class);
        
        // Output: 
        // "Creating PrototypeService instance #2"
        // "Creating PrototypeService instance #3"
        // proto1 != proto2 (different instances)
    }
}

// How Spring handles @Bean methods internally
/*
1. Spring creates CGLIB proxy for @Configuration classes
2. When @Bean method is called, Spring checks if bean already exists
3. For singleton beans, Spring caches the first result
4. Subsequent calls return the cached instance
5. For prototype beans, new instance created each time
*/
Singleton @Bean Behavior
  • Default scope - one instance per container
  • Cached result - method called only once
  • Thread-safe - Spring handles synchronization
  • Eager initialization - created at startup by default
Prototype @Bean Behavior
  • New instance each time - method called on each access
  • No caching - fresh object created
  • Use with caution - can impact performance
  • Manual dependency management - no automatic wiring

@Bean Method Interception & Lifecycle


@Configuration
public class BeanLifecycleConfig {
    
    // Spring enhances @Configuration classes with CGLIB
    // This allows method interception for bean management
    
    @Bean(initMethod = "initialize", destroyMethod = "cleanup")
    public DataSource dataSource() {
        HikariDataSource dataSource = new HikariDataSource();
        dataSource.setJdbcUrl("jdbc:h2:mem:testdb");
        dataSource.setUsername("sa");
        dataSource.setPassword("");
        return dataSource;
    }
    
    // Bean with custom name
    @Bean("mainEntityManager")
    public EntityManager entityManager(EntityManagerFactory emf) {
        return emf.createEntityManager();
    }
    
    // Lazy initialization
    @Bean
    @Lazy
    public ExpensiveService expensiveService() {
        System.out.println("Creating ExpensiveService...");
        return new ExpensiveService();
    }
    
    // Conditional bean creation
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    public CacheManager cacheManager() {
        return new SimpleCacheManager();
    }
    
    // Bean with dependencies on other @Bean methods
    @Bean
    public ServiceCoordinator serviceCoordinator() {
        // Spring ensures myService() is only called once due to interception
        return new ServiceCoordinator(myService(), expensiveService());
    }
    
    @Bean
    public MyService myService() {
        return new MyService();
    }
}

// Bean with lifecycle methods
class DataSourceWithLifecycle extends HikariDataSource {
    
    public void initialize() {
        System.out.println("DataSource initializing...");
        // Custom initialization logic
    }
    
    public void cleanup() {
        System.out.println("DataSource cleaning up...");
        this.close();
    }
}

// Demonstration of Spring's interception
class Demonstration {
    
    public static void showInterception() {
        ApplicationContext ctx = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(BeanLifecycleConfig.class);
        
        // Even though serviceCoordinator() calls myService() directly,
        // Spring intercepts and returns the singleton instance
        
        BeanLifecycleConfig config = ctx.getBean(BeanLifecycleConfig.class);
        
        // This would NOT work outside Spring context - 
        // would create multiple MyService instances
        // ServiceCoordinator coordinator = config.serviceCoordinator(); // DON'T DO THIS
    }
}

Important: Never call @Bean methods directly from your code. Always get beans from the Spring application context. Direct calls bypass Spring's interception and can create multiple instances or miss dependency injection.

Can @Bean Methods Have Parameters?

Parameterized @Bean Methods - Yes!

@Bean methods can absolutely have parameters! Spring automatically provides dependencies from the application context as method parameters, enabling flexible bean configuration. 


@Configuration
public class ParameterizedBeanConfig {
    
    // Basic parameter injection
    @Bean
    public UserService userService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        return new UserServiceImpl(userRepository);
    }
    
    // Multiple parameters
    @Bean
    public OrderService orderService(
            OrderRepository orderRepository,
            PaymentService paymentService,
            EmailService emailService) {
        
        return new OrderServiceImpl(orderRepository, paymentService, emailService);
    }
    
    // Optional parameters with @Nullable
    @Bean 
    public ReportService reportService(
            DataSource dataSource,
            @Nullable CacheManager cacheManager) {  // Optional dependency
        
        ReportService service = new ReportService(dataSource);
        if (cacheManager != null) {
            service.setCacheManager(cacheManager);
        }
        return service;
    }
    
    // Qualifier with parameters
    @Bean
    public ClientService clientService(
            @Qualifier("restTemplate") RestTemplate restTemplate,
            @Value("${api.timeout:5000}") long timeout) {
        
        return new ClientService(restTemplate, timeout);
    }
    
    // Environment and property injection
    @Bean
    public DataSource dataSource(Environment env) {
        HikariDataSource dataSource = new HikariDataSource();
        dataSource.setJdbcUrl(env.getProperty("spring.datasource.url"));
        dataSource.setUsername(env.getProperty("spring.datasource.username"));
        dataSource.setPassword(env.getProperty("spring.datasource.password"));
        return dataSource;
    }
    
    // Using @Value with parameters
    @Bean
    public CloudStorageService cloudStorageService(
            @Value("${cloud.storage.bucket}") String bucketName,
            @Value("${cloud.storage.region}") String region) {
        
        return new CloudStorageService(bucketName, region);
    }
    
    // Complex object construction with multiple dependencies
    @Bean
    public ServiceFacade serviceFacade(
            UserService userService,
            OrderService orderService,
            ProductService productService,
            @Value("${app.mode}") String appMode) {
        
        ServiceFacade facade = new ServiceFacade();
        facade.setUserService(userService);
        facade.setOrderService(orderService);
        facade.setProductService(productService);
        facade.setMode(appMode);
        return facade;
    }
}

// Advanced parameter scenarios
@Configuration
public class AdvancedParameterConfig {
    
    // Collection injection
    @Bean
    public PluginManager pluginManager(List<Plugin> plugins) {
        // Spring injects all beans of type Plugin
        return new PluginManager(plugins);
    }
    
    // Map injection with qualifiers as keys
    @Bean
    public Router router(Map<String, Handler> handlers) {
        // Keys are bean names, values are Handler instances
        return new Router(handlers);
    }
    
    // Provider injection for lazy access
    @Bean
    public LazyService lazyService(Provider<ExpensiveService> expensiveServiceProvider) {
        // ExpensiveService created only when needed
        return new LazyService(expensiveServiceProvider);
    }
    
    // ObjectProvider for more flexibility
    @Bean
    public FlexibleService flexibleService(ObjectProvider<Validator> validators) {
        // Can check availability, get ordered stream, etc.
        return new FlexibleService(validators);
    }
}
Supported Parameter Types
  • Other @Bean method return types
  • @Component annotated classes
  • Primitives and Strings with @Value
  • Environment for property access
  • Collections of beans
  • Maps with bean names as keys
Parameter Injection Benefits
  • Explicit dependency declaration
  • Compile-time safety
  • Easy testing with mock parameters
  • Flexible bean construction
  • Clean, readable configuration

How to Inject Dependencies in @Bean Methods

Dependency Injection Techniques in @Bean Methods

Spring provides multiple ways to inject dependencies into @Bean methods, from simple parameter injection to advanced techniques using @Autowired and field injection. 


@Configuration
public class DependencyInjectionConfig {
    
    // 1. METHOD PARAMETER INJECTION (Recommended)
    @Bean
    public OrderProcessor orderProcessor(
            OrderRepository orderRepo,
            PaymentService paymentService,
            @Qualifier("emailService") NotificationService notifier) {
        
        return new OrderProcessor(orderRepo, paymentService, notifier);
    }
    
    // 2. FIELD INJECTION in @Configuration class
    @Autowired
    private UserRepository userRepository;
    
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("advancedValidator")
    private Validator validator;
    
    @Value("${app.batch.size:100}")
    private int batchSize;
    
    @Bean
    public UserService userService() {
        // Use injected fields
        return new UserServiceImpl(userRepository, validator, batchSize);
    }
    
    // 3. CONFIGURATION PROPERTIES INJECTION
    @Autowired
    private DatabaseProperties dbProperties;
    
    @Bean
    public DataSource dataSource() {
        HikariDataSource ds = new HikariDataSource();
        ds.setJdbcUrl(dbProperties.getUrl());
        ds.setUsername(dbProperties.getUsername());
        ds.setPassword(dbProperties.getPassword());
        return ds;
    }
    
    // 4. CONDITIONAL DEPENDENCY INJECTION
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnBean(CacheManager.class)
    public CachedUserService cachedUserService(
            UserService userService,
            CacheManager cacheManager) {
        
        return new CachedUserService(userService, cacheManager);
    }
    
    // 5. PROGRAMMATIC DEPENDENCY LOOKUP
    @Bean
    public ServiceLocator serviceLocator(ApplicationContext context) {
        return new ServiceLocator(context);
    }
}

// Advanced dependency injection patterns
@Configuration
public class AdvancedDIConfig {
    
    // 6. FACTORY BEAN WITH DEPENDENCIES
    @Bean
    public FactoryBean<ComplexService> complexServiceFactory(
            SimpleService simpleService,
            MediumService mediumService) {
        
        return new FactoryBean<ComplexService>() {
            @Override
            public ComplexService getObject() {
                return new ComplexService(simpleService, mediumService);
            }
            
            @Override
            public Class<?> getObjectType() {
                return ComplexService.class;
            }
            
            @Override
            public boolean isSingleton() {
                return true;
            }
        };
    }
    
    // 7. BUILDER PATTERN WITH DEPENDENCIES
    @Bean
    public ProductService productService(
            ProductRepository productRepo,
            CategoryService categoryService,
            @Value("${product.cache.enabled:true}") boolean cacheEnabled) {
        
        ProductService.Builder builder = ProductService.builder()
            .productRepository(productRepo)
            .categoryService(categoryService);
            
        if (cacheEnabled) {
            builder.enableCaching();
        }
        
        return builder.build();
    }
    
    // 8. DEPENDENCY RESOLUTION WITH ObjectProvider
    @Bean
    public AdaptiveService adaptiveService(
            ObjectProvider<FeatureService> featureServices,
            Environment env) {
        
        // Get ordered list of FeatureService beans
        List<FeatureService> services = featureServices.orderedStream()
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
            
        return new AdaptiveService(services, env.getActiveProfiles());
    }
    
    // 9. CONDITIONAL DEPENDENCIES WITH @Autowired(required = false)
    @Autowired(required = false)
    private Optional<MetricsService> metricsService;
    
    @Bean
    public MonitoredService monitoredService(BaseService baseService) {
        MonitoredService service = new MonitoredService(baseService);
        
        // Add metrics if available
        metricsService.ifPresent(service::setMetricsService);
        
        return service;
    }
}

// Configuration properties class
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.database")
public class DatabaseProperties {
    private String url;
    private String username;
    private String password;
    private int poolSize = 10;
    
    // getters and setters
}
Recommended Approaches
  • Method Parameters: Most explicit and testable
  • Constructor Injection: For immutable dependencies
  • @ConfigurationProperties: For external configuration
  • ObjectProvider: For optional or ordered dependencies
Approaches to Avoid
  • Field Injection in @Bean methods: Less testable
  • Direct method calls: Bypasses Spring interception
  • Complex conditional logic: Hard to maintain
  • Static dependencies: Defeats DI purpose

Practical Dependency Injection Examples


@Configuration
public class PracticalExamplesConfig {
    
    // REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE: REST Client Configuration
    @Bean
    public RestTemplate restTemplate(
            RestTemplateBuilder builder,
            @Value("${api.connect.timeout:5000}") int connectTimeout,
            @Value("${api.read.timeout:10000}") int readTimeout) {
        
        return builder
            .setConnectTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(connectTimeout))
            .setReadTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(readTimeout))
            .additionalInterceptors(new LoggingInterceptor())
            .build();
    }
    
    // REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE: JPA Configuration with Dependencies
    @Bean
    public LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean entityManagerFactory(
            DataSource dataSource,
            JpaVendorAdapter jpaVendorAdapter,
            @Value("${hibernate.dialect}") String dialect) {
        
        LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean em = new LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean();
        em.setDataSource(dataSource);
        em.setJpaVendorAdapter(jpaVendorAdapter);
        em.setPackagesToScan("com.example.entities");
        
        Properties props = new Properties();
        props.setProperty("hibernate.dialect", dialect);
        props.setProperty("hibernate.show_sql", "false");
        em.setJpaProperties(props);
        
        return em;
    }
    
    // REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE: Security Configuration with Dependencies
    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(
            HttpSecurity http,
            UserDetailsService userDetailsService,
            PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder) throws Exception {
        
        return http
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/public/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                .anyRequest().authenticated()
            )
            .userDetailsService(userDetailsService)
            .formLogin(form -> form
                .loginPage("/login")
                .permitAll()
            )
            .logout(logout -> logout
                .logoutSuccessUrl("/login?logout")
                .permitAll()
            )
            .build();
    }
    
    // REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE: Async Configuration with Dependencies
    @Bean
    public ThreadPoolTaskExecutor taskExecutor(
            @Value("${async.core.pool.size:5}") int corePoolSize,
            @Value("${async.max.pool.size:10}") int maxPoolSize,
            @Value("${async.queue.capacity:25}") int queueCapacity) {
        
        ThreadPoolTaskExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
        executor.setCorePoolSize(corePoolSize);
        executor.setMaxPoolSize(maxPoolSize);
        executor.setQueueCapacity(queueCapacity);
        executor.setThreadNamePrefix("async-");
        executor.setRejectedExecutionHandler(new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
        executor.initialize();
        return executor;
    }
    
    // REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE: Cache Configuration with Dependencies
    @Bean
    public CacheManager cacheManager(
            RedisConnectionFactory redisConnectionFactory,
            ObjectMapper objectMapper,
            @Value("${cache.ttl.minutes:30}") long ttlMinutes) {
        
        RedisCacheConfiguration config = RedisCacheConfiguration.defaultCacheConfig()
            .entryTtl(Duration.ofMinutes(ttlMinutes))
            .serializeValuesWith(RedisSerializationContext.SerializationPair
                .fromSerializer(new GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer(objectMapper)));
        
        return RedisCacheManager.builder(redisConnectionFactory)
            .cacheDefaults(config)
            .build();
    }
}

Difference between @Bean and @Component for Dependency Management

@Bean vs @Component: Comprehensive Comparison

Aspect @Bean @Component
Definition Location @Configuration class methods Class-level annotation
Bean Creation Control Full programmatic control Spring creates via reflection
Third-party Classes Perfect for external libraries Requires class modification
Complex Initialization Easy with custom logic Limited to @PostConstruct
Conditional Logic Flexible conditional creation Limited conditional support
Dependency Injection Method parameters or @Autowired Field/constructor/setter injection
Testing Easy to test configuration Standard Spring testing
Bean Naming Explicit via method name or @Bean("name") Implicit via class name

Practical Comparison: When to Use Each


// SCENARIO 1: THIRD-PARTY LIBRARY CONFIGURATION
// @Bean APPROACH (Recommended for external classes)
@Configuration
public class ThirdPartyConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public ObjectMapper objectMapper() {
        ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper();
        mapper.configure(DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, false);
        mapper.registerModule(new JavaTimeModule());
        return mapper;
    }
    
    @Bean
    public RestTemplate restTemplate() {
        return new RestTemplateBuilder()
            .setConnectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
            .setReadTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
            .build();
    }
}

// @Component APPROACH (Not possible - can't annotate third-party classes)
// ObjectMapper and RestTemplate are from libraries, can't add @Component

// SCENARIO 2: CUSTOM BUSINESS SERVICE
// @Component APPROACH (Recommended for your own classes)
@Service
public class UserService {
    
    private final UserRepository userRepository;
    
    @Autowired
    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
    }
    
    // business methods...
}

// @Bean APPROACH (Also works, but more verbose)
@Configuration
public class ServiceConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public UserService userService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        return new UserService(userRepository);
    }
}

// SCENARIO 3: COMPLEX BEAN WITH CONDITIONAL LOGIC
// @Bean APPROACH (Perfect for complex setup)
@Configuration
public class ComplexBeanConfig {
    
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "cache.enabled", havingValue = "true")
    public UserService cachedUserService(UserRepository userRepository, CacheManager cacheManager) {
        return new CachedUserService(userRepository, cacheManager);
    }
    
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "cache.enabled", havingValue = "false", matchIfMissing = true)
    public UserService simpleUserService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        return new SimpleUserService(userRepository);
    }
}

// @Component APPROACH (Limited for complex conditions)
@Service
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "cache.enabled", havingValue = "true")
public class CachedUserService implements UserService {
    // implementation...
}

@Service
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "cache.enabled", havingValue = "false", matchIfMissing = true)  
public class SimpleUserService implements UserService {
    // implementation...
}

// SCENARIO 4: MULTIPLE BEANS OF SAME TYPE
// @Bean APPROACH (Explicit naming and configuration)
@Configuration
public class MultipleBeansConfig {
    
    @Bean("primaryDataSource")
    @Primary
    public DataSource primaryDataSource() {
        return DataSourceBuilder.create()
            .url("jdbc:mysql://primary-host:3306/db")
            .username("user1")
            .build();
    }
    
    @Bean("secondaryDataSource") 
    public DataSource secondaryDataSource() {
        return DataSourceBuilder.create()
            .url("jdbc:mysql://secondary-host:3306/db")
            .username("user2")
            .build();
    }
}

// @Component APPROACH (More limited for multiple instances)
// Would require separate configuration classes or qualifiers

// SCENARIO 5: BEAN WITH CUSTOM INITIALIZATION
// @Bean APPROACH (Full control over initialization)
@Configuration
public class CustomInitConfig {
    
    @Bean(initMethod = "initialize", destroyMethod = "cleanup")
    public ExpensiveResource expensiveResource() {
        ExpensiveResource resource = new ExpensiveResource();
        resource.setTimeout(5000);
        return resource;
    }
    
    @Bean
    public AnotherService anotherService() {
        AnotherService service = new AnotherService();
        // Complex setup logic
        service.configure(loadConfiguration());
        service.validate();
        return service;
    }
    
    private Configuration loadConfiguration() {
        // Complex configuration loading
        return new Configuration();
    }
}

// @Component APPROACH (Limited to @PostConstruct)
@Component
public class ExpensiveResource {
    
    @PostConstruct
    public void initialize() {
        // Initialization logic
    }
    
    @PreDestroy  
    public void cleanup() {
        // Cleanup logic
    }
}
Use @Bean When...
  • Configuring third-party library classes
  • Need complex initialization logic
  • Conditional bean creation based on multiple factors
  • Creating multiple instances of the same type
  • Need programmatic control over bean creation
  • Working with factory patterns
Use @Component When...
  • Your own application classes
  • Simple dependency injection needs
  • Standard Spring lifecycle is sufficient
  • Component scanning makes sense
  • Minimal configuration required
  • Following convention-over-configuration

Hybrid Approach: Combining @Bean and @Component

In real-world applications, you'll often use both approaches together, leveraging the strengths of each. 


@Configuration
@ComponentScan("com.example.services")  // Scan for @Component classes
@EnableJpaRepositories("com.example.repositories") // Scan for repositories  
public class HybridApplicationConfig {
    
    // @Bean for third-party and complex configuration
    @Bean
    public ObjectMapper objectMapper() {
        return new ObjectMapper()
            .registerModule(new JavaTimeModule())
            .configure(DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, false);
    }
    
    @Bean
    public RestTemplate restTemplate(RestTemplateBuilder builder) {
        return builder
            .setConnectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
            .setReadTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
            .build();
    }
    
    @Bean
    public DataSource dataSource() {
        return DataSourceBuilder.create()
            .url("jdbc:h2:mem:testdb")
            .username("sa")
            .password("")
            .build();
    }
    
    // @Bean for conditional services
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "features.advanced-logging", havingValue = "true")
    public LoggingService advancedLoggingService() {
        return new AdvancedLoggingService();
    }
    
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean(LoggingService.class)
    public LoggingService defaultLoggingService() {
        return new SimpleLoggingService();
    }
}

// @Component for business services (scanned automatically)
@Service
public class UserService {
    // Business logic with @Autowired dependencies
}

@Repository  
public class UserRepository {
    // Data access with @Autowired EntityManager
}

@Component
public class EmailService {
    // Utility service with @Value properties
}

Configuration & Bean Management Quick Reference

@Configuration Usage

  • Programmatic bean definition
  • Third-party library configuration
  • Complex initialization logic
  • Conditional bean creation
  • Multiple bean instances

@Bean Method Features

  • Parameter injection for dependencies
  • Singleton scope by default
  • Method interception for caching
  • Custom init/destroy methods
  • Explicit bean naming

@Component Usage

  • Your own application classes
  • Simple dependency injection
  • Component scanning approach
  • Standard Spring lifecycle
  • Convention over configuration

Critical Best Practices

  • Use method parameter injection for @Bean methods when possible
  • Prefer @Component for your own classes, @Bean for third-party
  • Never call @Bean methods directly - use application context
  • Keep @Configuration classes focused and modular
  • Use meaningful bean names with @Bean("name")
  • Implement proper error handling in @Bean methods
  • Test @Configuration classes with @SpringBootTest

Spring Dependency Injection: Complete Best Practices Guide

Dependency Injection Fundamentals

Dependency Injection (DI) is a core principle of the Spring Framework that promotes loose coupling, testability, and maintainability. Proper implementation of DI patterns is crucial for building robust and scalable Spring applications.

Core Principle: Dependency Injection implements Inversion of Control (IoC) by delegating dependency management to the Spring container, rather than having components create their own dependencies.

Dependency Injection Best Practices

Spring DI Best Practices Hierarchy

Constructor Injection
Primary choice for mandatory dependencies
▼
Setter Injection
Optional dependencies, configuration
▼
Field Injection
Avoid in production code
Single Responsibility
Interface Segregation
Testing Strategy

Why Constructor Injection is Preferred

Benefits of Constructor Injection

Constructor injection is the recommended approach for mandatory dependencies in Spring applications. It provides several key advantages over other injection methods. 


// GOOD: Constructor injection
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;
    private final PaymentService paymentService;
    private final NotificationService notificationService;
    
    // Single constructor - Spring automatically uses it for DI
    public OrderService(OrderRepository orderRepository,
                       PaymentService paymentService,
                       NotificationService notificationService) {
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
        this.notificationService = notificationService;
    }
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        orderRepository.save(order);
        paymentService.processPayment(order);
        notificationService.sendConfirmation(order);
    }
}

// BAD: Field injection (avoid this)
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    @Autowired
    private OrderRepository orderRepository;
    
    @Autowired
    private PaymentService paymentService;
    
    @Autowired
    private NotificationService notificationService;
    
    // Hidden dependencies, harder to test
}
Immutability

Dependencies can be declared final, ensuring they're set once and never changed. This prevents accidental modification and makes the class thread-safe.

Testability

Dependencies are explicitly declared, making unit testing straightforward without reflection or Spring context.

Clear Contracts

Constructor makes dependencies explicit. The class cannot be instantiated without providing all required dependencies.

Circular Dependency Detection

Constructor injection immediately reveals circular dependencies at startup, rather than discovering them at runtime.

No Reflection Required

Unlike field injection, constructor injection doesn't rely on reflection, making it more performant and compatible with ahead-of-time compilation.

Constructor Injection in Practice


// Modern Spring (5+) - No @Autowired needed on constructor
@Service
public class CustomerService {
    
    private final CustomerRepository customerRepository;
    private final AddressValidator addressValidator;
    private final EmailService emailService;
    
    // Spring automatically uses this constructor for dependency injection
    public CustomerService(CustomerRepository customerRepository,
                          AddressValidator addressValidator,
                          EmailService emailService) {
        this.customerRepository = customerRepository;
        this.addressValidator = addressValidator;
        this.emailService = emailService;
    }
    
    public Customer registerCustomer(CustomerRegistrationRequest request) {
        if (!addressValidator.isValid(request.getAddress())) {
            throw new InvalidAddressException("Invalid address provided");
        }
        
        Customer customer = new Customer(request);
        Customer savedCustomer = customerRepository.save(customer);
        emailService.sendWelcomeEmail(savedCustomer);
        
        return savedCustomer;
    }
}

// With Lombok - Even more concise
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class ProductService {
    
    private final ProductRepository productRepository;
    private final InventoryService inventoryService;
    private final PriceCalculator priceCalculator;
    
    // Lombok generates constructor with all final fields
    // Spring uses it for dependency injection
    
    public Product createProduct(ProductCreateRequest request) {
        Product product = new Product(request);
        product.setPrice(priceCalculator.calculatePrice(request));
        return productRepository.save(product);
    }
}

// Testing constructor-injected classes is straightforward
class CustomerServiceTest {
    
    private CustomerRepository customerRepository;
    private AddressValidator addressValidator;
    private EmailService emailService;
    private CustomerService customerService;
    
    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
        customerRepository = mock(CustomerRepository.class);
        addressValidator = mock(AddressValidator.class);
        emailService = mock(EmailService.class);
