        // Easy instantiation without Spring context
        customerService = new CustomerService(
            customerRepository, addressValidator, emailService);
    }
    
    @Test
    void shouldRegisterCustomerWithValidAddress() {
        // Test implementation
        when(addressValidator.isValid(any())).thenReturn(true);
        when(customerRepository.save(any())).thenReturn(new Customer());
        
        Customer result = customerService.registerCustomer(validRequest);
        
        assertNotNull(result);
        verify(emailService).sendWelcomeEmail(any());
    }
}

How to Avoid Overusing @Autowired

Problems with @Autowired Overuse

While @Autowired is convenient, overusing it—especially with field injection—leads to several maintainability and testability issues. 


// ANTI-PATTERN: Overusing @Autowired
@Service
public class OrderProcessingService {
    
    @Autowired
    private OrderRepository orderRepository;
    
    @Autowired
    private PaymentService paymentService;
    
    @Autowired
    private InventoryService inventoryService;
    
    @Autowired
    private ShippingService shippingService;
    
    @Autowired
    private NotificationService notificationService;
    
    @Autowired
    private AuditService auditService;
    
    @Autowired
    private DiscountService discountService;
    
    @Autowired
    private TaxCalculationService taxCalculationService;
    
    // 8 dependencies! This class has too many responsibilities
    // Hidden dependencies make testing difficult
    // No clear contract about what's required
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        // Complex method that does too much
    }
}

// PROBLEM: Testing this class is painful
class OrderProcessingServiceTest {
    
    @InjectMocks
    private OrderProcessingService service;
    
    @Mock
    private OrderRepository orderRepository;
    
    @Mock
    private PaymentService paymentService;
    
    @Mock
    private InventoryService inventoryService;
    
    @Mock
    private ShippingService shippingService;
    
    @Mock
    private NotificationService notificationService;
    
    @Mock
    private AuditService auditService;
    
    @Mock
    private DiscountService discountService;
    
    @Mock
    private TaxCalculationService taxCalculationService;
    
    // 8 mocks to set up! Tests become brittle and hard to maintain
}

Dependency Explosion: When a class has too many @Autowired dependencies, it's often a sign that the class has too many responsibilities and violates the Single Responsibility Principle.

Solutions for @Autowired Overuse


// SOLUTION 1: Use constructor injection and refactor
@Service
public class OrderProcessingService {
    
    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;
    private final OrderOrchestrator orderOrchestrator;
    
    // Reduced from 8 dependencies to 2
    public OrderProcessingService(OrderRepository orderRepository,
                                 OrderOrchestrator orderOrchestrator) {
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
        this.orderOrchestrator = orderOrchestrator;
    }
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        orderRepository.save(order);
        orderOrchestrator.orchestrateOrderProcessing(order);
    }
}

// Extract complex orchestration into its own class
@Service
public class OrderOrchestrator {
    
    private final PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor;
    private final InventoryManager inventoryManager;
    private final ShippingCoordinator shippingCoordinator;
    private final NotificationDispatcher notificationDispatcher;
    
    public OrderOrchestrator(PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor,
                            InventoryManager inventoryManager,
                            ShippingCoordinator shippingCoordinator,
                            NotificationDispatcher notificationDispatcher) {
        this.paymentProcessor = paymentProcessor;
        this.inventoryManager = inventoryManager;
        this.shippingCoordinator = shippingCoordinator;
        this.notificationDispatcher = notificationDispatcher;
    }
    
    public void orchestrateOrderProcessing(Order order) {
        paymentProcessor.processPayment(order);
        inventoryManager.reserveInventory(order);
        shippingCoordinator.scheduleShipping(order);
        notificationDispatcher.sendOrderNotifications(order);
    }
}

// SOLUTION 2: Use @Configuration classes to group related beans
@Configuration
public class OrderProcessingConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public OrderOrchestrator orderOrchestrator(PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor,
                                              InventoryManager inventoryManager,
                                              ShippingCoordinator shippingCoordinator,
                                              NotificationDispatcher notificationDispatcher) {
        return new OrderOrchestrator(
            paymentProcessor, inventoryManager, shippingCoordinator, notificationDispatcher);
    }
    
    @Bean
    public PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor(PaymentService paymentService,
                                           TaxCalculationService taxService,
                                           DiscountService discountService) {
        return new PaymentProcessor(paymentService, taxService, discountService);
    }
}

// SOLUTION 3: Use method injection for complex object creation
@Service
public class ReportService {
    
    private final DataSource dataSource;
    private final TemplateEngine templateEngine;
    
    public ReportService(DataSource dataSource, TemplateEngine templateEngine) {
        this.dataSource = dataSource;
        this.templateEngine = templateEngine;
    }
    
    // Method injection for prototype-scoped beans
    @Autowired
    public void setReportGenerator(ReportGenerator reportGenerator) {
        this.reportGenerator = reportGenerator;
    }
}

// SOLUTION 4: Use @Qualifier for multiple beans of same type
@Configuration
public class NotificationConfig {
    
    @Bean
    @Qualifier("email")
    public NotificationService emailNotificationService() {
        return new EmailNotificationService();
    }
    
    @Bean
    @Qualifier("sms")
    public NotificationService smsNotificationService() {
        return new SmsNotificationService();
    }
}

@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    private final NotificationService emailNotificationService;
    private final NotificationService smsNotificationService;
    
    public OrderService(@Qualifier("email") NotificationService emailNotificationService,
                       @Qualifier("sms") NotificationService smsNotificationService) {
        this.emailNotificationService = emailNotificationService;
        this.smsNotificationService = smsNotificationService;
    }
}
Refactoring Strategies
  • Group related dependencies into facade services
  • Extract business logic into domain services
  • Use @Configuration classes for complex wiring
  • Apply Single Responsibility Principle rigorously
When to Use @Autowired
  • Optional dependencies with setter methods
  • Configuration methods in @Configuration classes
  • Field injection in @ConfigurationProperties
  • Legacy code migration (temporarily)

When to Use Setter Injection

Appropriate Use Cases for Setter Injection

Setter injection is suitable for optional dependencies or when you need to reconfigure beans after instantiation. It should be used judiciously alongside constructor injection. 


// GOOD: Mixed constructor and setter injection
@Service
public class CachingUserService {
    
    private final UserRepository userRepository;
    private CacheManager cacheManager; // Optional dependency
    private MetricsCollector metricsCollector; // Optional dependency
    
    // Constructor for mandatory dependencies
    public CachingUserService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
    }
    
    // Setter for optional dependency with default
    @Autowired(required = false)
    public void setCacheManager(CacheManager cacheManager) {
        this.cacheManager = cacheManager;
    }
    
    // Setter for optional dependency with default implementation
    @Autowired(required = false)
    public void setMetricsCollector(MetricsCollector metricsCollector) {
        this.metricsCollector = metricsCollector != null 
            ? metricsCollector 
            : new NoOpMetricsCollector();
    }
    
    public User findUser(Long userId) {
        // Use cache if available, otherwise fall back to repository
        if (cacheManager != null) {
            User cached = cacheManager.get(userId, User.class);
            if (cached != null) {
                return cached;
            }
        }
        
        User user = userRepository.findById(userId).orElseThrow();
        
        if (cacheManager != null) {
            cacheManager.put(userId, user);
        }
        
        if (metricsCollector != null) {
            metricsCollector.recordUserLookup();
        }
        
        return user;
    }
}

// GOOD: Setter injection for configuration
@Component
public class EmailService {
    
    private String fromAddress;
    private int retryAttempts = 3;
    private long timeoutMs = 5000;
    
    // No constructor injection - configured via setters
    @Autowired
    public void setFromAddress(@Value("${email.from.address}") String fromAddress) {
        this.fromAddress = fromAddress;
    }
    
    @Autowired
    public void setRetryAttempts(@Value("${email.retry.attempts:3}") int retryAttempts) {
        this.retryAttempts = retryAttempts;
    }
    
    @Autowired
    public void setTimeoutMs(@Value("${email.timeout.ms:5000}") long timeoutMs) {
        this.timeoutMs = timeoutMs;
    }
}

// GOOD: Setter injection for circular dependency resolution
@Service
public class ServiceA {
    
    private ServiceB serviceB;
    
    public ServiceA() {
        // Default constructor
    }
    
    @Autowired
    public void setServiceB(ServiceB serviceB) {
        this.serviceB = serviceB;
    }
}

@Service
public class ServiceB {
    
    private ServiceA serviceA;
    
    public ServiceB() {
        // Default constructor
    }
    
    @Autowired
    public void setServiceA(ServiceA serviceA) {
        this.serviceA = serviceA;
    }
}
Appropriate Setter Injection Use Cases
  • Optional dependencies with fallback behavior
  • Configuration properties that may change
  • Circular dependency resolution (though better to avoid)
  • Legacy code that can't use constructor injection
  • Dependencies with reasonable defaults
Setter Injection Anti-Patterns
  • Using for mandatory dependencies
  • Creating mutable state unnecessarily
  • Overusing instead of constructor injection
  • Creating hidden dependencies

Organizing Dependencies for Better Maintainability

Dependency Organization Strategies

Well-organized dependencies make your code more maintainable, testable, and understandable. Proper organization follows clear architectural patterns and principles. 


// LAYERED ARCHITECTURE ORGANIZATION

// 1. Domain Layer (no Spring dependencies)
public interface UserRepository {
    Optional<User> findById(Long id);
    User save(User user);
}

// 2. Infrastructure Layer (Spring Data)
@Repository
public interface JpaUserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long>, UserRepository {
    // Implementation provided by Spring Data
}

// 3. Service Layer (business logic)
@Service
@Transactional
public class UserService {
    
    private final UserRepository userRepository;
    private final PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder;
    private final EmailService emailService;
    
    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository,
                      PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder,
                      EmailService emailService) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
        this.passwordEncoder = passwordEncoder;
        this.emailService = emailService;
    }
    
    public User registerUser(UserRegistrationRequest request) {
        // Business logic here
        User user = createUserFromRequest(request);
        return userRepository.save(user);
    }
}

// 4. Configuration Layer (dependency wiring)
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
        return new BCryptPasswordEncoder();
    }
    
    @Bean
    public EmailService emailService(@Value("${smtp.host}") String host,
                                    @Value("${smtp.port}") int port) {
        return new SmtpEmailService(host, port);
    }
}

// MODULAR ORGANIZATION BY FEATURE

// Feature: User Management
@Configuration
public class UserManagementConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public UserService userService(UserRepository userRepository,
                                  PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder,
                                  EmailService emailService) {
        return new UserService(userRepository, passwordEncoder, emailService);
    }
    
    @Bean
    public UserController userController(UserService userService) {
        return new UserController(userService);
    }
}

// Feature: Order Management  
@Configuration
public class OrderManagementConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public OrderService orderService(OrderRepository orderRepository,
                                    PaymentService paymentService,
                                    InventoryService inventoryService) {
        return new OrderService(orderRepository, paymentService, inventoryService);
    }
}

// USING @COMPONENTSCAN EFFECTIVELY
@SpringBootApplication
@ComponentScan(basePackages = {
    "com.example.application",
    "com.example.domain", 
    "com.example.infrastructure"
},
excludeFilters = @ComponentScan.Filter(
    type = FilterType.REGEX, 
    pattern = "com.example.legacy.*"
))
public class Application {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args);
    }
}

// DEPENDENCY GROUPING WITH FACADES
@Service
public class OrderProcessingFacade {
    
    private final OrderValidator orderValidator;
    private final PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor;
    private final InventoryManager inventoryManager;
    private final ShippingCoordinator shippingCoordinator;
    
    public OrderProcessingFacade(OrderValidator orderValidator,
                                PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor, 
                                InventoryManager inventoryManager,
                                ShippingCoordinator shippingCoordinator) {
        this.orderValidator = orderValidator;
        this.paymentProcessor = paymentProcessor;
        this.inventoryManager = inventoryManager;
        this.shippingCoordinator = shippingCoordinator;
    }
    
    public OrderProcessingResult processOrder(Order order) {
        // Coordinate complex process with multiple dependencies
        orderValidator.validate(order);
        PaymentResult payment = paymentProcessor.process(order);
        InventoryReservation inventory = inventoryManager.reserve(order);
        ShippingConfirmation shipping = shippingCoordinator.schedule(order);
        
        return new OrderProcessingResult(payment, inventory, shipping);
    }
}
Organization Strategies
  • Layered Architecture: Separate by concerns (domain, service, infrastructure)
  • Feature-based: Group by business capabilities
  • Module-based: Use Java modules or Spring profiles
  • Facade Pattern: Group related dependencies
Maintenance Benefits
  • Clear dependency boundaries
  • Easier testing and mocking
  • Better separation of concerns
  • Simplified refactoring
  • Reduced coupling between components

Single Responsibility Principle in Dependency Injection

Applying SRP to Dependency Injection

The Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) states that a class should have only one reason to change. In DI context, this translates to having focused dependencies that align with the class's single responsibility. 


// VIOLATION: Class with too many responsibilities and dependencies
@Service
public class OrderManager {
    
    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;
    private final PaymentService paymentService;
    private final InventoryService inventoryService;
    private final ShippingService shippingService;
    private final EmailService emailService;
    private final SmsService smsService;
    private final ReportGenerator reportGenerator;
    private final AnalyticsService analyticsService;
    
    // 8 dependencies! This class does too much:
    // - Order management
    // - Payment processing  
    // - Inventory management
    // - Shipping coordination
    // - Customer notifications
    // - Reporting
    // - Analytics
    // This violates SRP
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        // Does everything related to orders
    }
}

// APPLYING SRP: Split into focused classes
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;
    
    public OrderService(OrderRepository orderRepository) {
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
    }
    
    // Focused responsibility: basic order operations
    public Order createOrder(OrderRequest request) {
        return orderRepository.save(new Order(request));
    }
    
    public Order findOrder(Long orderId) {
        return orderRepository.findById(orderId).orElseThrow();
    }
}

@Service
public class OrderPaymentService {
    
    private final PaymentService paymentService;
    
    public OrderPaymentService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }
    
    // Focused responsibility: payment-related operations
    public PaymentResult processOrderPayment(Order order) {
        return paymentService.processPayment(order);
    }
}

@Service
public class OrderFulfillmentService {
    
    private final InventoryService inventoryService;
    private final ShippingService shippingService;
    
    public OrderFulfillmentService(InventoryService inventoryService,
                                  ShippingService shippingService) {
        this.inventoryService = inventoryService;
        this.shippingService = shippingService;
    }
    
    // Focused responsibility: order fulfillment
    public FulfillmentResult fulfillOrder(Order order) {
        inventoryService.reserveItems(order);
        return shippingService.scheduleDelivery(order);
    }
}

@Service
public class OrderNotificationService {
    
    private final EmailService emailService;
    private final SmsService smsService;
    
    public OrderNotificationService(EmailService emailService,
                                   SmsService smsService) {
        this.emailService = emailService;
        this.smsService = smsService;
    }
    
    // Focused responsibility: customer notifications
    public void sendOrderNotifications(Order order) {
        emailService.sendOrderConfirmation(order);
        smsService.sendTrackingNotification(order);
    }
}

// COORDINATION: Use a facade or orchestrator for complex workflows
@Service
public class OrderOrchestrator {
    
    private final OrderService orderService;
    private final OrderPaymentService orderPaymentService;
    private final OrderFulfillmentService orderFulfillmentService;
    private final OrderNotificationService orderNotificationService;
    
    public OrderOrchestrator(OrderService orderService,
                            OrderPaymentService orderPaymentService,
                            OrderFulfillmentService orderFulfillmentService,
                            OrderNotificationService orderNotificationService) {
        this.orderService = orderService;
        this.orderPaymentService = orderPaymentService;
        this.orderFulfillmentService = orderFulfillmentService;
        this.orderNotificationService = orderNotificationService;
    }
    
    // Orchestrates the process without implementing business logic
    public Order processOrder(OrderRequest request) {
        Order order = orderService.createOrder(request);
        orderPaymentService.processOrderPayment(order);
        orderFulfillmentService.fulfillOrder(order);
        orderNotificationService.sendOrderNotifications(order);
        return order;
    }
}

SRP Benefits in DI: When each class has a single responsibility, it naturally has fewer, more focused dependencies. This makes classes easier to test, maintain, and understand. It also reduces the risk of changes in one dependency affecting unrelated functionality.

SRP Violation Indicators in Dependency Injection

Code Smells
  • Classes with 5+ dependencies
  • Dependencies from unrelated domains
  • Methods that use only some dependencies
  • Frequent changes due to different reasons
  • Large test setup with many mocks
SRP Compliance Signs
  • 2-4 focused dependencies per class
  • All dependencies used in most methods
  • Clear, single responsibility
  • Easy to describe purpose in one sentence
  • Simple test setup

Testing Dependencies Effectively

Effective Dependency Testing Strategies

Proper dependency injection enables comprehensive testing through isolation, mocking, and clear test boundaries. Well-designed dependencies are easy to test. 


// UNIT TESTING WITH CONSTRUCTOR INJECTION
class UserServiceTest {
    
    private UserRepository userRepository;
    private PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder;
    private EmailService emailService;
    private UserService userService;
    
    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
        userRepository = mock(UserRepository.class);
        passwordEncoder = mock(PasswordEncoder.class);
        emailService = mock(EmailService.class);
        
        // Easy instantiation - no Spring context needed
        userService = new UserService(userRepository, passwordEncoder, emailService);
    }
    
    @Test
    void shouldRegisterUserWithHashedPassword() {
        // Given
        UserRegistrationRequest request = new UserRegistrationRequest(
            "john@example.com", "plainPassword");
        
        when(passwordEncoder.encode("plainPassword")).thenReturn("hashedPassword");
        when(userRepository.save(any(User.class))).thenAnswer(inv -> inv.getArgument(0));
        
        // When
        User result = userService.registerUser(request);
        
        // Then
        assertThat(result.getPassword()).isEqualTo("hashedPassword");
        verify(emailService).sendWelcomeEmail(result);
    }
    
    @Test
    void shouldFailWhenEmailAlreadyExists() {
        // Given
        UserRegistrationRequest request = new UserRegistrationRequest(
            "existing@example.com", "password");
        
        when(userRepository.findByEmail("existing@example.com"))
            .thenReturn(Optional.of(new User()));
        
        // When & Then
        assertThrows(DuplicateEmailException.class, 
            () -> userService.registerUser(request));
    }
}

// INTEGRATION TESTING WITH SPRING
@SpringBootTest
class UserServiceIntegrationTest {
    
    @Autowired
    private UserService userService;
    
    @Autowired
    private UserRepository userRepository;
    
    @Test
    void shouldPersistUserInDatabase() {
        // Given
        UserRegistrationRequest request = new UserRegistrationRequest(
            "test@example.com", "password");
        
        // When
        User result = userService.registerUser(request);
        
        // Then
        assertThat(userRepository.findById(result.getId())).isPresent();
    }
}

// TESTING OPTIONAL DEPENDENCIES
class CachingUserServiceTest {
    
    @Test
    void shouldUseCacheWhenAvailable() {
        UserRepository repo = mock(UserRepository.class);
        CacheManager cache = mock(CacheManager.class);
        UserService service = new UserService(repo); // No cache in constructor
        
        // Inject cache via setter
        service.setCacheManager(cache);
        
        when(cache.get(1L, User.class)).thenReturn(new User(1L, "cached"));
        
        User result = service.findUser(1L);
        
        assertThat(result.getName()).isEqualTo("cached");
        verify(repo, never()).findById(any()); // Cache was used
    }
    
    @Test
    void shouldFallbackToRepositoryWhenNoCache() {
        UserRepository repo = mock(UserRepository.class);
        UserService service = new UserService(repo); // No cache set
        
        when(repo.findById(1L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(new User(1L, "from_db")));
        
        User result = service.findUser(1L);
        
        assertThat(result.getName()).isEqualTo("from_db");
        // No cache interaction expected
    }
}

// TEST CONFIGURATION CLASSES
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class AppConfigTest {
    
    @Mock
    private UserRepository userRepository;
    
    @Mock
    private PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder;
    
    @Mock
    private EmailService emailService;
    
    @Test
    void shouldCreateUserServiceWithDependencies() {
        AppConfig config = new AppConfig();
        
        UserService userService = config.userService(userRepository, passwordEncoder, emailService);
        
        assertThat(userService).isNotNull();
        // The service should be properly wired
    }
}

// TESTING WITH TEST-SPECIFIC CONFIGURATION
@TestConfiguration
public class TestConfig {
    
    @Bean
    @Primary
    public PasswordEncoder testPasswordEncoder() {
        return new PlainTextPasswordEncoder(); // Fast for tests
    }
    
    @Bean
    @Primary
    public EmailService testEmailService() {
        return new MockEmailService(); // Doesn't send real emails
    }
}

@SpringBootTest
@Import(TestConfig.class)
class UserServiceWithTestConfigTest {
    
    @Autowired
    private UserService userService;
    
    @Autowired
    private EmailService emailService;
    
    @Test
    void shouldUseTestDependencies() {
        // Uses test-specific beans from TestConfig
        User user = userService.registerUser(validRequest);
        
        verify(emailService).sendWelcomeEmail(user);
    }
}
Testing Benefits of Good DI
  • Isolation: Test one component at a time
  • Mocking: Easy to substitute dependencies
  • No Spring Context: Faster unit tests
  • Clear Boundaries: Know exactly what to test
  • Test Data: Controlled dependency responses
Testing Strategies
  • Unit Tests: No Spring, manual dependency injection
  • Integration Tests: Spring context with real beans
  • Test Configuration: Override specific beans for testing
  • Mocking Frameworks: Use Mockito for dependency simulation
  • Test Profiles: Use different configurations for testing

Common Anti-patterns in Spring Dependency Injection

Dependency Injection Anti-patterns

Recognizing and avoiding common DI anti-patterns is crucial for maintaining clean, testable, and maintainable Spring applications. 


// ANTI-PATTERN 1: God Class with too many dependencies
@Service
public class ApplicationManager { // What does this even do?
    
    @Autowired private UserService userService;
    @Autowired private ProductService productService;
    @Autowired private OrderService orderService;
    @Autowired private ReportService reportService;
    @Autowired private AnalyticsService analyticsService;
    @Autowired private EmailService emailService;
    @Autowired private SmsService smsService;
    @Autowired private FileService fileService;
    // ... and 10 more
    
    // This class probably violates SRP and does everything
}

// ANTI-PATTERN 2: Service Locator pattern disguised as DI
@Component
public class ServiceLocator {
    
    @Autowired
    private ApplicationContext applicationContext;
    
    public <T> T getBean(Class<T> beanType) {
        return applicationContext.getBean(beanType);
    }
}

@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    @Autowired
    private ServiceLocator serviceLocator;
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        // Hidden dependencies - what does this method need?
        PaymentService payment = serviceLocator.getBean(PaymentService.class);
        InventoryService inventory = serviceLocator.getBean(InventoryService.class);
        // Dependencies are not explicit in the constructor
    }
}

// ANTI-PATTERN 3: Circular dependencies
@Service
public class ServiceA {
    
    @Autowired
    private ServiceB serviceB; // Depends on ServiceB
    
    public void doA() {
        serviceB.doB();
    }
}

@Service
public class ServiceB {
    
    @Autowired
    private ServiceA serviceA; // Depends on ServiceA - circular!
    
    public void doB() {
        serviceA.doA();
    }
}

// ANTI-PATTERN 4: Using @Autowired on fields in production code
@Service
public class ProductService {
    
    @Autowired
    private ProductRepository productRepository; // Hard to test
    
    @Autowired
    private PriceCalculator priceCalculator; // Hidden dependency
    
    // No constructor - dependencies are not obvious
}

// ANTI-PATTERN 5: Constructor with too many parameters
@Service
public class OrderProcessingService {
    
    public OrderProcessingService(OrderRepository orderRepository,
                                 PaymentService paymentService,
                                 InventoryService inventoryService,
                                 ShippingService shippingService,
                                 EmailService emailService,
                                 SmsService smsService,
                                 AuditService auditService,
                                 DiscountService discountService,
                                 TaxService taxService,
                                 ReportService reportService) {
        // 10 parameters! This is hard to read and maintain
    }
}

// ANTI-PATTERN 6: Mixing business logic with dependency wiring
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public OrderService orderService() {
        OrderService service = new OrderService();
        
        // Business logic in configuration - wrong place!
        if (isProduction()) {
            service.setEmailService(productionEmailService());
        } else {
            service.setEmailService(mockEmailService());
        }
        
        return service;
    }
}

// ANTI-PATTERN 7: Using static methods to access Spring beans
@Component
public class ApplicationContextHolder implements ApplicationContextAware {
    
    private static ApplicationContext context;
    
    @Override
    public void setApplicationContext(ApplicationContext applicationContext) {
        context = applicationContext;
    }
    
    public static <T> T getBean(Class<T> beanClass) {
        return context.getBean(beanClass);
    }
}

// Somewhere in the code - static access to beans
public void someMethod() {
    UserService userService = ApplicationContextHolder.getBean(UserService.class);
    // This bypasses dependency injection and makes testing hard
}
Anti-pattern Solutions
  • God Class: Split into focused services
  • Service Locator: Use constructor injection
  • Circular Dependencies: Refactor or use setter injection
  • Field Injection: Convert to constructor injection
  • Many Parameters: Group related dependencies
  • Mixed Configuration: Separate wiring from logic
  • Static Access: Use proper dependency injection
Detection Strategies
  • Code reviews focusing on dependencies
  • Static analysis tools
  • Test difficulty as an indicator
  • Architecture reviews
  • Monitoring class responsibility counts

Dependency Injection Quick Reference

Constructor Injection

  • Mandatory dependencies
  • Immutable dependencies
  • Best for testability
  • Spring 5+ auto-wires

Setter Injection

  • Optional dependencies
  • Configuration changes
  • Circular dependencies
  • Use sparingly

Field Injection

  • Avoid in production
  • Hard to test
  • Hidden dependencies
  • No immutability

Organization

  • Follow SRP
  • Group by feature
  • Use configuration classes
  • Monitor dependency count

Critical DI Rules

  • Always prefer constructor injection for mandatory dependencies
  • Avoid field injection in production code
  • Keep dependency count per class under 5
  • Apply Single Responsibility Principle rigorously
  • Make dependencies explicit and immutable when possible
  • Design for testability from the beginning
  • Use @Configuration classes for complex wiring

Spring Boot Dependency Injection: Complete Guide & Advanced Patterns

Spring Dependency Injection Overview

Dependency Injection (DI) is the core principle of the Spring Framework, enabling loose coupling, testability, and maintainability. Spring Boot builds upon Spring Framework's DI capabilities with auto-configuration and convention-over-configuration approaches.

Core Concept: Dependency Injection is a design pattern where objects receive their dependencies from an external source rather than creating them internally, following the Inversion of Control (IoC) principle.

How Dependency Injection Works in Spring Boot

Spring Boot DI Process Flow

Spring Boot enhances Spring's DI with auto-configuration, component scanning, and conditional bean creation.

Spring Boot DI Process

1. Component Scanning
@SpringBootApplication triggers scanning
▼
2. Bean Definition
@Component, @Service, @Repository classes found
▼
3. Auto-Configuration
Conditional beans created based on classpath
▼
4. Dependency Injection
@Autowired, constructor injection wires dependencies
▼
5. Bean Post-Processing
AOP proxies, @PostConstruct methods executed

// Spring Boot Application
@SpringBootApplication
public class MyApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(MyApplication.class, args);
    }
}

// Service Bean
@Service
public class UserService {
    private final UserRepository userRepository;
    
    // Constructor Injection (Recommended)
    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
    }
    
    public User findUser(Long id) {
        return userRepository.findById(id).orElse(null);
    }
}

// Repository Bean  
@Repository
public class UserRepository {
    // Spring Data JPA automatically provides implementation
}

// Configuration with conditional beans
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnClass(name = "com.example.ExternalService")
    @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "external.service.enabled", havingValue = "true")
    public ExternalService externalService() {
        return new ExternalService();
    }
}

// Controller with dependency injection
@RestController
public class UserController {
    private final UserService userService;
    
    // Spring automatically injects UserService
    public UserController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/users/{id}")
    public User getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findUser(id);
    }
}

Dependency Injection Types in Spring Boot

Constructor Injection

Recommended approach for required dependencies

@Service
public class MyService {
    private final MyRepository repo;
    
    public MyService(MyRepository repo) {
        this.repo = repo;
    }
}
Setter Injection

For optional dependencies

@Service
public class MyService {
    private MyRepository repo;
    
    @Autowired
    public void setRepo(MyRepository repo) {
        this.repo = repo;
    }
}
Field Injection

Less testable, use sparingly

@Service
public class MyService {
    @Autowired
    private MyRepository repo;
}

Spring Framework DI vs Spring Boot DI

Key Differences

Aspect Spring Framework Spring Boot
Configuration XML or JavaConfig explicit configuration Auto-configuration with sensible defaults
Component Scanning Manual @ComponentScan configuration Automatic with @SpringBootApplication
Bean Discovery Explicit @Bean methods or XML Auto-detection + conditional beans
Dependency Management Manual dependency versions Starter POMs with managed versions
Property Injection Manual PropertySources configuration Auto-loaded from application.properties
Testing @ContextConfiguration @SpringBootTest with full context 

// SPRING FRAMEWORK - Explicit Configuration
@Configuration
@ComponentScan("com.example")
@PropertySource("classpath:app.properties")
public class AppConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public DataSource dataSource() {
        // Manual configuration
        return new DriverManagerDataSource(url, username, password);
    }
    
    @Bean 
    public JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate(DataSource dataSource) {
        return new JdbcTemplate(dataSource);
    }
}

// Application initialization
AnnotationConfigApplicationContext context = 
    new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class);
                            

// SPRING BOOT - Auto Configuration
@SpringBootApplication
public class Application {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args);
    }
}

// Auto-configured beans automatically available
@RestController
public class MyController {
    
    // JdbcTemplate auto-configured by Spring Boot
    private final JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate;
    
    public MyController(JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate) {
        this.jdbcTemplate = jdbcTemplate;
    }
}

// application.properties
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost/mydb
spring.datasource.username=user
spring.datasource.password=pass

ObjectFactory for Lazy Dependency Access

ObjectFactory Interface

ObjectFactory provides lazy access to dependencies, creating beans only when needed. Useful for expensive beans or circular dependency scenarios. 


import org.springframework.beans.factory.ObjectFactory;

@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    private final ObjectFactory<PaymentProcessor> paymentProcessorFactory;
    private final ObjectFactory<EmailService> emailServiceFactory;
    
    // Inject ObjectFactory instead of actual dependencies
    public OrderService(ObjectFactory<PaymentProcessor> paymentProcessorFactory,
                       ObjectFactory<EmailService> emailServiceFactory) {
        this.paymentProcessorFactory = paymentProcessorFactory;
        this.emailServiceFactory = emailServiceFactory;
    }
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        // Process order logic...
        
        // Lazily get PaymentProcessor only when needed
        PaymentProcessor processor = paymentProcessorFactory.getObject();
        processor.processPayment(order);
        
        // Email service created only if notification is needed
        if (order.isNotifyCustomer()) {
            EmailService emailService = emailServiceFactory.getObject();
            emailService.sendOrderConfirmation(order);
        }
    }
    
    // Useful for prototype-scoped beans
    public void createMultipleProcessors() {
        for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
            PaymentProcessor processor = paymentProcessorFactory.getObject();
            // Each getObject() returns a new instance for prototype scope
            processor.processBatch(i);
        }
    }
}

// Configuration with prototype beans
@Configuration
public class ProcessorConfig {
    
    @Bean
    @Scope(ConfigurableBeanFactory.SCOPE_PROTOTYPE)
    public PaymentProcessor paymentProcessor() {
        // Expensive initialization
        System.out.println("Creating new PaymentProcessor instance...");
        return new PaymentProcessor();
    }
    
    @Bean
    @Scope(ConfigurableBeanFactory.SCOPE_PROTOTYPE) 
    public EmailService emailService() {
        return new EmailService();
    }
}

// Expensive service that should be created lazily
@Component
@Lazy  // Marks the bean for lazy initialization
public class ExpensiveService {
    
    public ExpensiveService() {
        System.out.println("ExpensiveService constructor - heavy initialization");
        // Simulate expensive operation
        try {
            Thread.sleep(2000);
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }
    
    public void performOperation() {
        System.out.println("Performing expensive operation...");
    }
}

@Service
public class ClientService {
    
    private final ObjectFactory<ExpensiveService> expensiveServiceFactory;
    
    public ClientService(ObjectFactory<ExpensiveService> expensiveServiceFactory) {
        this.expensiveServiceFactory = expensiveServiceFactory;
    }
    
    public void doWork() {
        // ExpensiveService is created only when actually needed
        if (needsExpensiveOperation()) {
            ExpensiveService service = expensiveServiceFactory.getObject();
            service.performOperation();
        }
    }
    
    private boolean needsExpensiveOperation() {
        // Some condition to determine if expensive operation is needed
        return Math.random() > 0.5;
    }
}

// Usage in a web controller
@RestController
public class OrderController {
    
    private final ObjectFactory<OrderService> orderServiceFactory;
    
    public OrderController(ObjectFactory<OrderService> orderServiceFactory) {
        this.orderServiceFactory = orderServiceFactory;
    }
    
    @PostMapping("/orders")
    public ResponseEntity<Order> createOrder(@RequestBody Order order) {
        // Get a fresh OrderService instance for each request
        OrderService orderService = orderServiceFactory.getObject();
        orderService.processOrder(order);
        return ResponseEntity.ok(order);
    }
}
ObjectFactory Benefits
  • Lazy initialization of expensive beans
  • Prototype bean creation on demand
  • Circular dependency resolution
  • Reduced application startup time
Use Cases
  • Expensive-to-create services
  • Prototype-scoped beans
  • Optional dependencies
  • Request-scoped beans in singleton context

Provider Interface for Dependency Injection

javax.inject.Provider Interface

The Provider interface (from JSR-330) provides a standard way for lazy dependency access. Similar to ObjectFactory but part of the Java standard. 


import javax.inject.Provider;

@Service
public class ShoppingCartService {
    
    private final Provider<PaymentGateway> paymentGatewayProvider;
    private final Provider<InventoryService> inventoryServiceProvider;
    
    // Inject Provider instead of direct dependency
    public ShoppingCartService(Provider<PaymentGateway> paymentGatewayProvider,
                              Provider<InventoryService> inventoryServiceProvider) {
        this.paymentGatewayProvider = paymentGatewayProvider;
        this.inventoryServiceProvider = inventoryServiceProvider;
    }
    
    public CheckoutResult checkout(ShoppingCart cart) {
        // Verify inventory first
        InventoryService inventoryService = inventoryServiceProvider.get();
        if (!inventoryService.checkAvailability(cart.getItems())) {
            return CheckoutResult.outOfStock();
        }
        
        // Process payment only if inventory is available
        PaymentGateway paymentGateway = paymentGatewayProvider.get();
        PaymentResult paymentResult = paymentGateway.processPayment(cart);
        
        if (paymentResult.isSuccess()) {
            inventoryService.updateStock(cart.getItems());
            return CheckoutResult.success();
        } else {
            return CheckoutResult.paymentFailed();
        }
    }
}

// Prototype-scoped service with state
@Component
@Scope(ConfigurableBeanFactory.SCOPE_PROTOTYPE)
public class PaymentGateway {
    
    private final String transactionId;
    private final LocalDateTime createdAt;
    
    public PaymentGateway() {
        this.transactionId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        this.createdAt = LocalDateTime.now();
    }
    
    public PaymentResult processPayment(ShoppingCart cart) {
        System.out.println("Processing payment with transaction: " + transactionId);
        // Payment processing logic
        return new PaymentResult(Math.random() > 0.1); // 90% success rate
    }
    
    public String getTransactionId() {
        return transactionId;
    }
}

// Service with request-scoped dependency
@Service
public class UserSessionService {
    
    private final Provider<UserPreferences> userPreferencesProvider;
    
    public UserSessionService(Provider<UserPreferences> userPreferencesProvider) {
        this.userPreferencesProvider = userPreferencesProvider;
    }
    
    public void updateUserSettings(UserSettings settings) {
        // Get current request's UserPreferences
        UserPreferences preferences = userPreferencesProvider.get();
        preferences.updateFrom(settings);
    }
    
    public UserPreferences getCurrentPreferences() {
        return userPreferencesProvider.get();
    }
}

// Request-scoped bean
@Component
@Scope(value = WebApplicationContext.SCOPE_REQUEST, proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)
public class UserPreferences {
    
    private String theme = "light";
    private String language = "en";
    private final String sessionId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
    
    public void updateFrom(UserSettings settings) {
        this.theme = settings.getTheme();
        this.language = settings.getLanguage();
    }
    
    // getters and setters
}

// Advanced usage with multiple instances
@Service
public class BatchProcessor {
    
    private final Provider<ItemProcessor> itemProcessorProvider;
    
    public BatchProcessor(Provider<ItemProcessor> itemProcessorProvider) {
        this.itemProcessorProvider = itemProcessorProvider;
    }
    
    public void processBatch(List<Item> items) {
        List<Future<ProcessResult>> futures = new ArrayList<>();
        
        ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(5);
        
        for (Item item : items) {
            futures.add(executor.submit(() -> {
                // Each thread gets its own ItemProcessor instance
                ItemProcessor processor = itemProcessorProvider.get();
                return processor.process(item);
            }));
        }
        
        // Wait for completion and handle results
        futures.forEach(future -> {
            try {
                ProcessResult result = future.get();
                System.out.println("Processed: " + result);
            } catch (Exception e) {
                System.err.println("Processing failed: " + e.getMessage());
            }
        });
        
        executor.shutdown();
    }
}

// Prototype processor with thread-specific state
@Component
@Scope(ConfigurableBeanFactory.SCOPE_PROTOTYPE)
public class ItemProcessor {
    
    private final String processorId;
    private final Thread creatingThread;
    
    public ItemProcessor() {
        this.processorId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        this.creatingThread = Thread.currentThread();
    }
    
    public ProcessResult process(Item item) {
        System.out.println("Processing item " + item.getId() + 
                          " with processor " + processorId + 
                          " on thread " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
        return new ProcessResult(item.getId(), true);
    }
}
Provider vs ObjectFactory
  • Provider: JSR-330 standard, simpler API
  • ObjectFactory: Spring-specific, more features
  • Both provide lazy access to dependencies
  • Choose based on standardization needs
When to Use Provider
  • JSR-330 compliance required
  • Working with different DI frameworks
  • Simple lazy dependency access
  • Prototype bean management

Programmatic Dependency Lookup

Manual Dependency Lookup

Programmatic lookup allows manually retrieving beans from the ApplicationContext. Useful for dynamic bean selection or when dependency injection is not feasible. 


@Service
public class NotificationService {
    
    @Autowired
    private ApplicationContext applicationContext;
    
    public void sendNotification(NotificationRequest request) {
        // Dynamically select notifier based on type
        Notifier notifier = getNotifier(request.getType());
        notifier.send(request.getMessage(), request.getRecipient());
    }
    
    private Notifier getNotifier(NotificationType type) {
        String beanName = type.name().toLowerCase() + "Notifier";
        
        // Programmatic lookup by bean name
        return applicationContext.getBean(beanName, Notifier.class);
    }
    
    // Get all beans of a type
    public List<Notifier> getAllNotifiers() {
        Map<String, Notifier> notifierBeans = 
            applicationContext.getBeansOfType(Notifier.class);
        return new ArrayList<>(notifierBeans.values());
    }
    
    // Check if bean exists
    public boolean isNotifierAvailable(NotificationType type) {
        String beanName = type.name().toLowerCase() + "Notifier";
        return applicationContext.containsBean(beanName);
    }
}

// Different notifier implementations
@Component("emailNotifier")
public class EmailNotifier implements Notifier {
    public void send(String message, String recipient) {
        System.out.println("Sending email to " + recipient + ": " + message);
    }
}

@Component("smsNotifier")  
public class SmsNotifier implements Notifier {
    public void send(String message, String recipient) {
        System.out.println("Sending SMS to " + recipient + ": " + message);
    }
}

@Component("pushNotifier")
public class PushNotifier implements Notifier {
    public void send(String message, String recipient) {
        System.out.println("Sending push to " + recipient + ": " + message);
    }
}

// Factory pattern with programmatic lookup
@Service
public class PaymentProcessorFactory {
    
    @Autowired
    private ApplicationContext applicationContext;
    
    public PaymentProcessor getProcessor(PaymentMethod method) {
        String beanName = method.getProcessorBeanName();
        
        try {
            return applicationContext.getBean(beanName, PaymentProcessor.class);
        } catch (NoSuchBeanDefinitionException e) {
            throw new UnsupportedPaymentMethodException(
                "No processor found for method: " + method, e);
        }
    }
    
    // Get bean with constructor arguments
    public PaymentProcessor createProcessorWithConfig(PaymentMethod method, 
                                                     ProcessorConfig config) {
        String beanName = method.getProcessorBeanName();
        PaymentProcessor processor = applicationContext.getBean(beanName, PaymentProcessor.class);
        processor.configure(config);
        return processor;
    }
}

// Using BeanFactory for more control
@Service
public class AdvancedLookupService {
    
    @Autowired
    private BeanFactory beanFactory;
    
    public Object getBeanWithCustomCreation(String beanName, Object... args) {
        // Use BeanFactory for more advanced scenarios
        return beanFactory.getBean(beanName, args);
    }
    
    public <T> T getBean(Class<T> requiredType, Object... args) {
        return beanFactory.getBean(requiredType, args);
    }
    
    // Check bean scope
    public boolean isSingleton(String beanName) {
        return beanFactory.isSingleton(beanName);
    }
    
    // Get bean definition details
    public String[] getBeanDefinitionNames() {
        if (beanFactory instanceof ListableBeanFactory) {
            return ((ListableBeanFactory) beanFactory).getBeanDefinitionNames();
        }
        return new String[0];
    }
}

// Dynamic service resolver
@Service
public class ServiceResolver {
    
    @Autowired
    private ApplicationContext applicationContext;
    
    private final Map<Class<?>, Object> cachedServices = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    
    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public <T> T resolve(Class<T> serviceType) {
        return (T) cachedServices.computeIfAbsent(serviceType, type -> {
            Map<String, T> beans = applicationContext.getBeansOfType((Class<T>) type);
            
            if (beans.isEmpty()) {
                throw new NoSuchBeanDefinitionException(type, "No bean found for type: " + type);
            }
            
            if (beans.size() > 1) {
                // Handle multiple beans - could use @Primary or other strategies
                String primaryBeanName = findPrimaryBean(beans);
                return beans.get(primaryBeanName);
            }
            
            return beans.values().iterator().next();
        });
    }
    
    private <T> String findPrimaryBean(Map<String, T> beans) {
        return beans.keySet().stream()
            .filter(beanName -> {
                BeanDefinition definition = ((ListableBeanFactory) applicationContext)
                    .getBeanDefinition(beanName);
                return definition.isPrimary();
            })
            .findFirst()
            .orElseThrow(() -> new NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException(
                "Multiple beans found but no primary specified"));
    }
}
Use Cases
  • Dynamic bean selection at runtime
  • Plugin architecture implementations
  • Factory patterns with multiple implementations
  • Conditional bean usage
Considerations
  • Breaks inversion of control principle
  • Harder to test than dependency injection
  • Use sparingly when DI is not feasible
  • Consider ServiceLocator pattern as alternative

ApplicationContextAware for Manual Dependency Lookup

ApplicationContextAware Interface

ApplicationContextAware allows beans to get access to the ApplicationContext programmatically. Useful for framework components or when you need context awareness. 


import org.springframework.context.ApplicationContext;
import org.springframework.context.ApplicationContextAware;

// Component that needs awareness of application context
@Component
public class ServiceLocator implements ApplicationContextAware {
    
    private static ApplicationContext context;
    
    @Override
    public void setApplicationContext(ApplicationContext applicationContext) 
            throws BeansException {
        // Store the application context
        context = applicationContext;
    }
    
    // Static method to get beans from anywhere
    public static <T> T getBean(Class<T> beanClass) {
        if (context == null) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("ApplicationContext not initialized");
        }
        return context.getBean(beanClass);
    }
    
    public static <T> T getBean(String beanName, Class<T> beanClass) {
        if (context == null) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("ApplicationContext not initialized");
        }
        return context.getBean(beanName, beanClass);
    }
    
    public static Object getBean(String beanName) {
        if (context == null) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("ApplicationContext not initialized");
        }
        return context.getBean(beanName);
    }
    
    // Get all beans of a type
    public static <T> Map<String, T> getBeansOfType(Class<T> type) {
        if (context == null) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("ApplicationContext not initialized");
        }
        return context.getBeansOfType(type);
    }
}

// Usage in non-Spring managed classes
public class UtilityClass {
    
    public void doSomething() {
        // Get Spring bean from non-Spring class
        UserService userService = ServiceLocator.getBean(UserService.class);
        userService.doSomething();
    }
}

// Advanced context-aware component
@Component
public class DynamicFeatureManager implements ApplicationContextAware, 
                                              ApplicationListener<ContextRefreshedEvent> {
    
    private ApplicationContext applicationContext;
    private Map<String, Feature> availableFeatures;
    
    @Override
    public void setApplicationContext(ApplicationContext applicationContext) 
            throws BeansException {
        this.applicationContext = applicationContext;
    }
    
    @Override
    public void onApplicationEvent(ContextRefreshedEvent event) {
        // Initialize when context is refreshed
        loadAvailableFeatures();
    }
    
    private void loadAvailableFeatures() {
        availableFeatures = applicationContext.getBeansOfType(Feature.class);
        System.out.println("Loaded " + availableFeatures.size() + " features");
    }
    
    public Feature getFeature(String featureName) {
        return availableFeatures.get(featureName);
    }
    
    public void enableFeature(String featureName) {
        Feature feature = availableFeatures.get(featureName);
        if (feature != null) {
            feature.enable();
        }
    }
    
    // Check if a feature bean exists
    public boolean isFeatureAvailable(String featureName) {
        return applicationContext.containsBean(featureName);
    }
}

// Feature interface and implementations
public interface Feature {
    void enable();
    void disable();
    boolean isEnabled();
}

@Component("advancedSearch")
public class AdvancedSearchFeature implements Feature {
    private boolean enabled = false;
    
    public void enable() { this.enabled = true; }
    public void disable() { this.enabled = false; }
    public boolean isEnabled() { return enabled; }
}

@Component("darkMode")
public class DarkModeFeature implements Feature {
    private boolean enabled = false;
    
    public void enable() { this.enabled = true; }
    public void disable() { this.enabled = false; }
    public boolean isEnabled() { return enabled; }
}

// Bean that needs to publish events
@Component
public class EventPublisher implements ApplicationContextAware {
    
    private ApplicationContext applicationContext;
    
    @Override
    public void setApplicationContext(ApplicationContext applicationContext) 
            throws BeansException {
        this.applicationContext = applicationContext;
    }
    
    public void publishUserCreatedEvent(User user) {
        UserCreatedEvent event = new UserCreatedEvent(this, user);
        applicationContext.publishEvent(event);
    }
    
    public void publishCustomEvent(Object source, String message) {
        CustomApplicationEvent event = new CustomApplicationEvent(source, message);
        applicationContext.publishEvent(event);
    }
}

// Custom application event
public class CustomApplicationEvent extends ApplicationEvent {
    private final String message;
    
    public CustomApplicationEvent(Object source, String message) {
        super(source);
        this.message = message;
    }
    
    public String getMessage() {
        return message;
    }
}

// Event listener
@Component
public class CustomEventListener {
    
    @EventListener
    public void handleCustomEvent(CustomApplicationEvent event) {
        System.out.println("Received custom event: " + event.getMessage());
    }
}

// Factory that creates beans programmatically
@Component
public class PrototypeBeanFactory implements ApplicationContextAware {
    
    private ApplicationContext applicationContext;
    
    @Override
    public void setApplicationContext(ApplicationContext applicationContext) 
            throws BeansException {
        this.applicationContext = applicationContext;
    }
    
    public <T> T createPrototypeBean(Class<T> beanType, Object... constructorArgs) {
        // Use ApplicationContext to create prototype beans with arguments
        return applicationContext.getBean(beanType, constructorArgs);
    }
    
    public Object createBean(String beanName, Object... constructorArgs) {
        return applicationContext.getBean(beanName, constructorArgs);
    }
}
Benefits
  • Access Spring context from non-managed classes
  • Dynamic bean lookup and creation
  • Event publishing capabilities
  • Framework component development
Cautions
  • Breaks pure dependency injection
  • Harder to test (mocking ApplicationContext)
  • Use only when necessary
  • Consider alternatives first

Dependency Injection with AOP Proxies

AOP Proxies in Dependency Injection

Spring uses AOP proxies to implement cross-cutting concerns like transactions, security, and caching. Understanding how proxies affect dependency injection is crucial. 


// Service with transactional methods
@Service
public class UserService {
    
    private final UserRepository userRepository;
    
    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
    }
    
    @Transactional
    public User createUser(User user) {
        // This method is proxied for transaction management
        return userRepository.save(user);
    }
    
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public User findUser(Long id) {
        return userRepository.findById(id).orElse(null);
    }
    
    // Non-transactional method
    public void validateUser(User user) {
        // No proxy interception for this method
        if (user.getEmail() == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Email is required");
        }
    }
}

// Understanding proxy behavior
@Service
public class ProxyAwareService {
    
    @Autowired
    private UserService userService; // This is actually a proxy!
    
    @PostConstruct
    public void checkProxy() {
        System.out.println("UserService class: " + userService.getClass().getName());
        // Output: UserService class: com.example.UserService$$EnhancerBySpringCGLIB$$...
        
        // Check if it's a proxy
        boolean isProxy = AopUtils.isAopProxy(userService);
        boolean isCglib = AopUtils.isCglibProxy(userService);
        boolean isJdk = AopUtils.isJdkDynamicProxy(userService);
        
        System.out.println("Is proxy: " + isProxy);
        System.out.println("Is CGLIB: " + isCglib);
        System.out.println("Is JDK: " + isJdk);
    }
    
    public void demonstrateProxyBehavior() {
        // Internal call bypasses proxy!
        userService.validateUser(new User()); // No transaction
        
        // External call goes through proxy
        userService.createUser(new User()); // Transactional
    }
}

// Service with self-injection problem
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;
    
    @Autowired
    private OrderService self; // Self-reference for proxy awareness
    
    public OrderService(OrderRepository orderRepository) {
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
    }
    
    @Transactional
    public Order createOrder(Order order) {
        // This works through proxy
        return orderRepository.save(order);
    }
    
    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        // Internal call that needs transaction
        // WRONG: this.createOrder(order) - bypasses proxy!
        
        // CORRECT: use self-injected proxy
        self.createOrder(order); // Goes through proxy, transaction works
    }
}

// AOP aspect for custom cross-cutting concern
@Aspect
@Component
public class LoggingAspect {
    
    private static final Logger logger = LoggerFactory.getLogger(LoggingAspect.class);
    
    @Around("@annotation(LogExecution)")
    public Object logExecutionTime(ProceedingJoinPoint joinPoint) throws Throwable {
        long start = System.currentTimeMillis();
        
        try {
            Object result = joinPoint.proceed();
            long duration = System.currentTimeMillis() - start;
            
            logger.info("Method {} executed in {} ms", 
                       joinPoint.getSignature(), duration);
            return result;
        } catch (Exception e) {
            logger.error("Method {} failed with exception: {}", 
                        joinPoint.getSignature(), e.getMessage());
            throw e;
        }
    }
}

// Custom annotation for AOP
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface LogExecution {
}

// Service using custom AOP
@Service
public class ProductService {
    
    @LogExecution
    public Product createProduct(Product product) {
        // This method will be intercepted by LoggingAspect
        // The injected ProductService in other beans will be a proxy
        return product; // simplified
    }
}

// Configuration for AOP
@Configuration
@EnableAspectJAutoProxy
public class AopConfig {
    // Enables @Aspect support
}

// Understanding proxy limitations
@Service
public class ProxyLimitationService {
    
    private String internalState = "initial";
    
    @Transactional
    public void transactionalMethod() {
        internalState = "modified";
        internalMethod(); // Bypasses proxy!
    }
    
    private void internalMethod() {
        // This method is not proxied, even if called from transactional method
        System.out.println("Internal state: " + internalState);
    }
    
    // Final methods cannot be proxied
    @Transactional
    public final void finalMethod() {
        // This will NOT be transactional in CGLIB proxy!
        // JDK proxies can't proxy final methods at all
    }
}

// Testing AOP proxies
@SpringBootTest
class UserServiceTest {
    
    @Autowired
    private UserService userService;
    
    @Test
    void testProxyBehavior() {
        // Verify that userService is actually a proxy
        assertTrue(AopUtils.isAopProxy(userService));
        
        // Test transactional behavior
        User user = new User("test@example.com");
        User saved = userService.createUser(user);
        
        assertNotNull(saved.getId());
    }
    
    @Test
    void testInternalCallLimitation() {
        // This demonstrates the proxy limitation
        User user = new User("test@example.com");
        
        // Internal validation call (no transaction)
        userService.validateUser(user);
        
        // The validation works, but note it bypasses any AOP interception
        // that might be applied to validateUser if it were called externally
    }
}
Proxy Types
  • JDK Dynamic Proxy: Interface-based proxies
  • CGLIB Proxy: Class-based proxies (default in Spring Boot)
  • Both enable AOP interception
  • Affect how beans are injected
Proxy Limitations
  • Internal method calls bypass proxy
  • Final methods can't be proxied (CGLIB)
  • Private methods are not proxied
  • Self-injection needed for internal calls

CGLIB Proxies Effect on Dependency Injection

CGLIB Proxies in Spring

CGLIB proxies are the default in Spring Boot for AOP. They create subclass-based proxies that can affect constructor injection and bean behavior. 


// Spring Boot default: CGLIB proxies
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableAspectJAutoProxy(proxyTargetClass = true) // Default in Spring Boot
public class Application {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args);
    }
}

// Service that will be CGLIB-proxied
@Service
@Transactional
public class AccountService {
    
    private final AccountRepository accountRepository;
    
    // Constructor injection with CGLIB proxy
    public AccountService(AccountRepository accountRepository) {
        this.accountRepository = accountRepository;
        System.out.println("AccountService constructor called");
        System.out.println("Actual class: " + this.getClass().getName());
    }
    
    @Transactional
    public Account createAccount(Account account) {
        return accountRepository.save(account);
    }
    
    // Final method - cannot be overridden by CGLIB
    public final String getServiceType() {
        return "ACCOUNT_SERVICE";
    }
    
    // Private method - not proxied
    private void internalProcessing() {
        System.out.println("Internal processing");
    }
}

// Understanding CGLIB proxy creation
@Component
public class ProxyInspector {
    
    @Autowired
    private AccountService accountService;
    
    @PostConstruct
    public void inspectProxy() {
        System.out.println("=== CGLIB Proxy Inspection ===");
        System.out.println("Injected class: " + accountService.getClass().getName());
        System.out.println("Is CGLIB proxy: " + AopUtils.isCglibProxy(accountService));
        System.out.println("Is JDK proxy: " + AopUtils.isJdkDynamicProxy(accountService));
        System.out.println("Is AOP proxy: " + AopUtils.isAopProxy(accountService));
        
        // Get target class (original class)
        Class targetClass = AopProxyUtils.ultimateTargetClass(accountService);
        System.out.println("Target class: " + targetClass.getName());
        
        // Check method availability
        try {
            // CGLIB proxies can expose final methods but can't intercept them
            System.out.println("Service type: " + accountService.getServiceType());
        } catch (Exception e) {
            System.out.println("Error calling final method: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

// Configuration to control proxy behavior
@Configuration
@EnableTransactionManagement(proxyTargetClass = true) // Force CGLIB for transactions
@EnableAspectJAutoProxy(proxyTargetClass = true)     // Force CGLIB for aspects
public class ProxyConfig {
    
    @Bean
    @Scope(proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS) // CGLIB for scoped proxies
    public SessionData sessionData() {
        return new SessionData();
    }
}

// Scoped bean with CGLIB proxy
@Component
@Scope(value = WebApplicationContext.SCOPE_REQUEST, proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)
public class SessionData {
    
    private final String sessionId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
    private final LocalDateTime created = LocalDateTime.now();
    
    public String getSessionInfo() {
        return "Session: " + sessionId + " created at: " + created;
    }
}

// Service using scoped proxy
@Service
public class WebService {
    
    private final SessionData sessionData; // Actually a CGLIB proxy
    
    public WebService(SessionData sessionData) {
        this.sessionData = sessionData;
    }
    
    public void handleRequest() {
        // The proxy will delegate to the actual request-scoped bean
        System.out.println(sessionData.getSessionInfo());
    }
}

// CGLIB proxy limitations and workarounds
@Service
public class ProxyAwareService {
    
    private final AccountService accountService;
    
    // Self-injection for proxy awareness
    @Autowired
    private ProxyAwareService self;
    
    public ProxyAwareService(AccountService accountService) {
        this.accountService = accountService;
    }
    
    public void processWithTransaction() {
        // WRONG: direct call bypasses transaction proxy
        // accountService.createAccount(new Account());
        
        // CORRECT: use injected proxy (but we can't change AccountService)
        // Instead, ensure transactional methods are called from external classes
        performTransactionalOperation();
    }
    
    @Transactional
    public void performTransactionalOperation() {
        // This will be properly proxied when called from external classes
        accountService.createAccount(new Account());
    }
    
    public void internalCallNeedingTransaction() {
        // WRONG: bypasses proxy
        // performTransactionalOperation();
        
        // CORRECT: use self-injected proxy
        self.performTransactionalOperation();
    }
}

// Testing CGLIB proxies
@SpringBootTest
class CglibProxyTest {
    
    @Autowired
    private AccountService accountService;
    
    @Autowired
    private ApplicationContext context;
    
    @Test
    void testCglibProxyInjection() {
        // Verify it's a CGLIB proxy
        assertTrue(AopUtils.isCglibProxy(accountService));
        assertFalse(AopUtils.isJdkDynamicProxy(accountService));
        
        // Verify the underlying target class
        Class targetClass = AopProxyUtils.ultimateTargetClass(accountService);
        assertEquals(AccountService.class, targetClass);
    }
    
    @Test
    void testFinalMethodOnProxy() {
        // Final methods work on CGLIB proxies (but can't be intercepted)
        String serviceType = accountService.getServiceType();
        assertEquals("ACCOUNT_SERVICE", serviceType);
    }
    
    @Test
    void testBeanDefinition() {
        // Check how the bean is defined in context
        BeanDefinition beanDefinition = context.getBeanDefinition("accountService");
        System.out.println("Bean definition: " + beanDefinition);
    }
}

// Advanced: Custom CGLIB configuration
@Configuration
public class AdvancedProxyConfig implements ImportAware {
    
    @Override
    public void setImportMetadata(AnnotationMetadata importMetadata) {
        // Custom proxy configuration if needed
    }
    
    @Bean
    public DefaultAopProxyFactory aopProxyFactory() {
        return new DefaultAopProxyFactory();
    }
}
CGLIB Advantages
  • Works with class-based proxies (no interfaces needed)
  • Default in Spring Boot
  • Better performance in some scenarios
  • Can proxy package-visible methods
CGLIB Limitations
  • Requires no-arg constructor (for some cases)
  • Cannot proxy final methods
  • More complex class loading
  • Larger memory footprint

Dependencies in Parent-Child Contexts

Hierarchical Application Contexts

Spring supports hierarchical contexts where child contexts can access beans from parent contexts, but parent contexts cannot access child beans. Common in web applications. 


// Parent context configuration (root application context)
@Configuration
@ComponentScan(basePackages = "com.example.core")
@PropertySource("classpath:application.properties")
public class RootConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public DataSource dataSource() {
        // Core infrastructure beans in parent context
        return new EmbeddedDatabaseBuilder()
            .setType(EmbeddedDatabaseType.H2)
            .build();
    }
    
    @Bean
    public JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate(DataSource dataSource) {
        return new JdbcTemplate(dataSource);
    }
    
    @Bean 
    public PlatformTransactionManager transactionManager(DataSource dataSource) {
        return new DataSourceTransactionManager(dataSource);
    }
}

// Child context configuration (web application context)
@Configuration
@ComponentScan(basePackages = "com.example.web")
@EnableWebMvc
public class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
    
    // Child context can access parent beans
    @Autowired
    private JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate;
    
    @Bean
    public UserController userController() {
        // This can use jdbcTemplate from parent context
        return new UserController(jdbcTemplate);
    }
    
    // Bean only available in child context
    @Bean
    public ViewResolver viewResolver() {
        InternalResourceViewResolver resolver = new InternalResourceViewResolver();
        resolver.setPrefix("/WEB-INF/views/");
        resolver.setSuffix(".jsp");
        return resolver;
    }
}

// Service in parent context
@Service
public class CoreService {
    
    private final JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate;
    
    public CoreService(JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate) {
        this.jdbcTemplate = jdbcTemplate;
    }
    
    public String getApplicationName() {
        return "My Application";
    }
}

// Controller in child context
@RestController
public class UserController {
    
    private final JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate;
    
    // Can inject parent context beans
    @Autowired
    private CoreService coreService;
    
    public UserController(JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate) {
        this.jdbcTemplate = jdbcTemplate;
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/info")
    public String getInfo() {
        return coreService.getApplicationName(); // From parent context
    }
}

// Bean that needs to be aware of context hierarchy
@Component
public class ContextAwareBean implements ApplicationContextAware {
    
    private ApplicationContext applicationContext;
    
    @Override
    public void setApplicationContext(ApplicationContext applicationContext) 
            throws BeansException {
        this.applicationContext = applicationContext;
    }
    
    public void checkContextHierarchy() {
        ApplicationContext parent = applicationContext.getParent();
        
        if (parent != null) {
            System.out.println("This is a child context");
            System.out.println("Parent context: " + parent.getDisplayName());
            
            // Check if we can access parent beans
            try {
                CoreService coreService = parent.getBean(CoreService.class);
                System.out.println("Accessed parent bean: " + coreService.getApplicationName());
            } catch (Exception e) {
                System.out.println("Cannot access parent bean: " + e.getMessage());
            }
        } else {
            System.out.println("This is a root context");
        }
    }
    
    // Get bean from parent context explicitly
    public <T> T getBeanFromParent(Class<T> requiredType) {
        ApplicationContext parent = applicationContext.getParent();
        if (parent != null) {
            return parent.getBean(requiredType);
        }
        return null;
    }
}

// Manual context hierarchy setup
public class ManualContextHierarchy {
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Create parent context
        AnnotationConfigApplicationContext parentContext = 
            new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(RootConfig.class);
        
        // Create child context with parent
        AnnotationConfigApplicationContext childContext = 
            new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext();
        childContext.setParent(parentContext);
        childContext.register(WebConfig.class);
        childContext.refresh();
        
        // Child can access parent beans
        UserController controller = childContext.getBean(UserController.class);
        System.out.println(controller.getInfo());
        
        // Parent cannot access child beans
        try {
            UserController fromParent = parentContext.getBean(UserController.class);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            System.out.println("Parent cannot access child beans: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        
        childContext.close();
        parentContext.close();
    }
}

// Spring Boot with multiple contexts (less common)
@SpringBootApplication
public class MultiContextApplication {
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication application = new SpringApplication(MultiContextApplication.class);
        
        // In Spring Boot, hierarchical contexts are handled automatically
        // Web context is child of root context
        application.run(args);
    }
}

// Testing hierarchical contexts
@SpringBootTest
@ContextHierarchy({
    @ContextConfiguration(classes = RootConfig.class, name = "parent"),
    @ContextConfiguration(classes = WebConfig.class, name = "child")
})
class HierarchicalContextTest {
    
    @Autowired
    private ApplicationContext applicationContext;
    
    @Test
    void testContextHierarchy() {
        ApplicationContext parent = applicationContext.getParent();
        assertNotNull(parent);
        
        // Verify parent context beans are available
        JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate = applicationContext.getBean(JdbcTemplate.class);
        assertNotNull(jdbcTemplate);
        
        // Verify child context beans are available
        UserController controller = applicationContext.getBean(UserController.class);
        assertNotNull(controller);
    }
}

// Bean definition overriding in child context
@Configuration
public class ChildConfig {
    
    @Bean
    @Primary // Override parent bean definition
    public DataSource dataSource() {
        // Child-specific data source
        return new DriverManagerDataSource("jdbc:h2:mem:childdb");
    }
}

// Conditional bean creation based on context
@Configuration
public class ConditionalBeanConfig {
    
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean // Only create if not already defined in parent
    public FallbackService fallbackService() {
        return new FallbackService();
    }
}
Context Hierarchy Benefits
