  • Separation of concerns (core vs web beans)
  • Bean definition overriding in child contexts
  • Modular application architecture
  • Independent context lifecycle
Considerations
  • Parent cannot access child beans
  • Complex debugging and testing
  • Potential for bean definition conflicts
  • Understand context lifecycle

BeanFactory Role in Dependency Injection

BeanFactory - The Core DI Engine

BeanFactory is the actual dependency injection engine in Spring. ApplicationContext extends BeanFactory and adds enterprise features. Understanding BeanFactory helps understand Spring's core DI mechanism. 


// Using BeanFactory directly (rare in application code)
public class BeanFactoryExample {
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Create BeanFactory (not commonly used directly)
        DefaultListableBeanFactory beanFactory = new DefaultListableBeanFactory();
        
        // Register bean definitions
        RootBeanDefinition serviceDef = new RootBeanDefinition(MyService.class);
        beanFactory.registerBeanDefinition("myService", serviceDef);
        
        RootBeanDefinition repoDef = new RootBeanDefinition(MyRepository.class);
        beanFactory.registerBeanDefinition("myRepository", repoDef);
        
        // Manual dependency injection setup
        ConstructorArgumentValues cav = new ConstructorArgumentValues();
        cav.addGenericArgumentValue(new RuntimeBeanReference("myRepository"));
        serviceDef.setConstructorArgumentValues(cav);
        
        // Get bean from BeanFactory
        MyService service = beanFactory.getBean(MyService.class);
        service.doSomething();
    }
}

// Bean that uses BeanFactory for advanced scenarios
@Component
public class AdvancedBeanManager implements BeanFactoryAware {
    
    private BeanFactory beanFactory;
    
    @Override
    public void setBeanFactory(BeanFactory beanFactory) throws BeansException {
        this.beanFactory = beanFactory;
    }
    
    // Programmatic bean creation with BeanFactory
    public <T> T createBean(Class<T> beanClass, Object... constructorArgs) {
        if (beanFactory instanceof DefaultListableBeanFactory) {
            DefaultListableBeanFactory listableBeanFactory = 
                (DefaultListableBeanFactory) beanFactory;
            
            // Create bean definition
            RootBeanDefinition beanDefinition = new RootBeanDefinition(beanClass);
            
            // Register with unique name
            String beanName = beanClass.getSimpleName() + "#" + UUID.randomUUID();
            listableBeanFactory.registerBeanDefinition(beanName, beanDefinition);
            
            // Get the bean (will be created and initialized)
            return listableBeanFactory.getBean(beanName, beanClass);
        }
        throw new IllegalStateException("BeanFactory is not a DefaultListableBeanFactory");
    }
    
    // Check bean existence and type
    public boolean containsBean(String beanName) {
        return beanFactory.containsBean(beanName);
    }
    
    public boolean isSingleton(String beanName) {
        return beanFactory.isSingleton(beanName);
    }
    
    public Class<?> getType(String beanName) {
        return beanFactory.getType(beanName);
    }
    
    // Get all beans of a type
    public <T> Map<String, T> getBeansOfType(Class<T> type) {
        if (beanFactory instanceof ListableBeanFactory) {
            return ((ListableBeanFactory) beanFactory).getBeansOfType(type);
        }
        return Collections.emptyMap();
    }
    
    // Get bean names
    public String[] getBeanNamesForType(Class<?> type) {
        if (beanFactory instanceof ListableBeanFactory) {
            return ((ListableBeanFactory) beanFactory).getBeanNamesForType(type);
        }
        return new String[0];
    }
}

// Custom BeanPostProcessor for DI customization
@Component
public class CustomBeanPostProcessor implements BeanPostProcessor {
    
    @Override
    public Object postProcessBeforeInitialization(Object bean, String beanName) 
            throws BeansException {
        // Called before @PostConstruct
        System.out.println("Before initialization: " + beanName);
        return bean;
    }
    
    @Override
    public Object postProcessAfterInitialization(Object bean, String beanName) 
            throws BeansException {
        // Called after @PostConstruct
        System.out.println("After initialization: " + beanName);
        
        // Example: wrap specific beans with proxies
        if (bean instanceof MyService) {
            return enhanceService((MyService) bean);
        }
        
        return bean;
    }
    
    private MyService enhanceService(MyService service) {
        // Custom enhancement logic
        return service;
    }
}

// BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext understanding
@Component
public class ContainerComparison {
    
    @Autowired
    private ApplicationContext applicationContext;
    
    @Autowired
    private BeanFactory beanFactory;
    
    @PostConstruct
    public void compareContainers() {
        System.out.println("=== BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext ===");
        
        // Both can get beans
        MyService fromAppContext = applicationContext.getBean(MyService.class);
        MyService fromBeanFactory = beanFactory.getBean(MyService.class);
        
        System.out.println("Same bean instance: " + (fromAppContext == fromBeanFactory));
        
        // ApplicationContext has additional features
        System.out.println("ApplicationContext class: " + applicationContext.getClass().getName());
        System.out.println("BeanFactory class: " + beanFactory.getClass().getName());
        
        // ApplicationContext extends BeanFactory
        System.out.println("Is ApplicationContext a BeanFactory: " + 
                          (applicationContext instanceof BeanFactory));
    }
}

// Using BeanFactory for low-level DI control
@Service
public class LowLevelDIControl {
    
    @Autowired
    private BeanFactory beanFactory;
    
    public void demonstrateBeanLifecycle() {
        // Get bean definition
        if (beanFactory instanceof ListableBeanFactory) {
            ListableBeanFactory listable = (ListableBeanFactory) beanFactory;
            
            String[] beanNames = listable.getBeanDefinitionNames();
            for (String beanName : beanNames) {
                BeanDefinition definition = listable.getBeanDefinition(beanName);
                System.out.println("Bean: " + beanName + 
                                 ", Scope: " + definition.getScope() +
                                 ", Lazy: " + definition.isLazyInit());
            }
        }
    }
    
    // Manual dependency resolution
    public void resolveDependencies() {
        if (beanFactory instanceof DefaultListableBeanFactory) {
            DefaultListableBeanFactory factory = (DefaultListableBeanFactory) beanFactory;
            
            // Resolve dependencies programmatically
            String[] dependencies = factory.getDependenciesForBean("myService");
            System.out.println("Dependencies for myService: " + Arrays.toString(dependencies));
        }
    }
}

// Custom scope registration with BeanFactory
@Component
public class CustomScopeRegistrar implements BeanFactoryAware {
    
    private BeanFactory beanFactory;
    
    @Override
    public void setBeanFactory(BeanFactory beanFactory) throws BeansException {
        this.beanFactory = beanFactory;
        registerCustomScopes();
    }
    
    private void registerCustomScopes() {
        if (beanFactory instanceof ConfigurableBeanFactory) {
            ConfigurableBeanFactory configurableFactory = (ConfigurableBeanFactory) beanFactory;
            
            // Register custom scope
            configurableFactory.registerScope("thread", new SimpleThreadScope());
            configurableFactory.registerScope("custom", new CustomScope());
        }
    }
}

// Custom scope implementation
public class CustomScope implements Scope {
    
    private final Map<String, Object> scopedObjects = Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>());
    private final Map<String, Runnable> destructionCallbacks = Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>());
    
    @Override
    public Object get(String name, ObjectFactory<?> objectFactory) {
        return scopedObjects.computeIfAbsent(name, k -> objectFactory.getObject());
    }
    
    @Override
    public Object remove(String name) {
        destructionCallbacks.remove(name);
        return scopedObjects.remove(name);
    }
    
    @Override
    public void registerDestructionCallback(String name, Runnable callback) {
        destructionCallbacks.put(name, callback);
    }
    
    @Override
    public Object resolveContextualObject(String key) {
        return null;
    }
    
    @Override
    public String getConversationId() {
        return "custom";
    }
}

// Bean with custom scope
@Component
@Scope("custom")
public class CustomScopedBean {
    private final String id = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
    
    public String getId() {
        return id;
    }
}

Spring AOP: Complete Aspect-Oriented Programming Guide

Aspect-Oriented Programming Overview

Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP) is a programming paradigm that aims to increase modularity by allowing the separation of cross-cutting concerns. It complements Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) by providing another way of thinking about program structure.

Core Concept: AOP provides the ability to add behavior to existing code without modifying the code itself. This is achieved through aspects that can be "woven" into the program at compile-time, load-time, or runtime.

What is Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP)?

AOP Definition & Purpose

AOP is a programming paradigm that aims to increase modularity by allowing the separation of cross-cutting concerns. It does this by adding additional behavior to existing code without modifying the code itself.

Without AOP
public class UserService {
    public User createUser(User user) {
        // Logging - Cross-cutting concern
        logger.info("Creating user: " + user.getUsername());
        
        // Security - Cross-cutting concern  
        if (!securityContext.hasPermission("CREATE_USER")) {
            throw new SecurityException("No permission");
        }
        
        // Transaction - Cross-cutting concern
        Transaction tx = beginTransaction();
        try {
            // Business logic
            validateUser(user);
            user.setCreatedDate(new Date());
            User savedUser = userRepository.save(user);
            
            tx.commit();
            logger.info("User created: " + savedUser.getId());
            return savedUser;
        } catch (Exception e) {
            tx.rollback();
            logger.error("User creation failed", e);
            throw e;
        }
    }
}
With AOP
public class UserService {
    public User createUser(User user) {
        // Pure business logic
        validateUser(user);
        user.setCreatedDate(new Date());
        return userRepository.save(user);
    }
}

// Cross-cutting concerns handled by aspects
@Aspect
@Component
public class LoggingAspect {
    @Before("execution(* UserService.createUser(..))")
    public void logMethodCall(JoinPoint joinPoint) {
        logger.info("Creating user: " + 
            joinPoint.getArgs()[0]);
    }
}
Key Characteristics of AOP
  • Separation of Concerns: Isolates cross-cutting functionality from business logic
  • Modularity: Cross-cutting concerns are encapsulated in separate modules (aspects)
  • Reusability: Aspects can be applied to multiple parts of the application
  • Maintainability: Changes to cross-cutting concerns are made in one place
  • Transparency: Business code remains unaware of aspect application

Advantages of Using AOP

Cleaner Code

Business logic remains focused on core functionality without being cluttered with cross-cutting concerns like logging, security, and transactions.

Better Modularity

Cross-cutting concerns are encapsulated in separate aspects, making the system more modular and easier to understand and maintain.

Easier Maintenance

Changes to cross-cutting concerns are made in one place (the aspect) rather than scattered throughout the codebase.

Reusability

Aspects can be applied to multiple classes and methods across the application, promoting code reuse and consistency.

Reduced Code Duplication

Common functionality that would otherwise be duplicated across multiple methods is centralized in aspects.

Improved Testability

Business logic can be tested independently of cross-cutting concerns, and aspects can be tested in isolation.

Key AOP Concepts

Aspect

A modularization of a concern that cuts across multiple classes. It contains advice and pointcuts. 

@Aspect
public class LoggingAspect {
    // Contains advice methods
}

Join Point

A point during the execution of a program, such as method execution or exception handling. 

method execution
constructor call
field access
exception handling

Advice

Action taken by an aspect at a particular join point. Different types include Before, After, Around. 

@Before
@After
@Around
@AfterReturning
@AfterThrowing

Pointcut

A predicate that matches join points. Advice is associated with a pointcut expression. 

@Pointcut("execution(* com.example.*.*(..))")
public void allMethods() {}

Weaving

The process of linking aspects with other application types to create an advised object. 

Compile-time weaving
Load-time weaving
Runtime weaving (Spring AOP)

Target Object

Object being advised by one or more aspects. Also known as the proxied object. 

public class UserService {
    // Target object for aspects
}

Concern vs Cross-cutting Concern

Understanding Concerns in Software Development

Core Concern

The primary functionality of a module or component. This is the main reason the module exists.

  • UserService: User management logic
  • OrderService: Order processing logic
  • ProductService: Product catalog management
  • PaymentService: Payment processing logic
// Core concern - Business logic
public class UserService {
    public User createUser(User user) {
        validateUser(user);
        return userRepository.save(user);
    }
}
Cross-cutting Concern

Functionality that affects multiple modules and cannot be cleanly decomposed from the rest of the system.

  • Logging: Applied to all service methods
  • Security: Authentication and authorization
  • Transactions: Database transaction management
  • Caching: Performance optimization
  • Error Handling: Consistent exception handling
// Cross-cutting concern - Logging
@Aspect
public class LoggingAspect {
    @Before("execution(* com.example.service.*.*(..))")
    public void logMethodCall(JoinPoint jp) {
        logger.info("Executing: " + jp.getSignature());
    }
}
Visual Representation
Traditional Application Structure
UserService + Logging + Security + Transactions
OrderService + Logging + Security + Transactions
ProductService + Logging + Security + Transactions
Code duplication and tight coupling
→
AOP Application Structure
UserService | OrderService | ProductService
Aspects
Logging
Security
Transactions
Clean separation and modularity

Spring AOP Advice Types

@Before Advice

Executes before a join point. Cannot prevent the method execution unless it throws an exception. 


@Aspect
@Component
public class SecurityAspect {
    
    private static final Logger logger = LoggerFactory.getLogger(SecurityAspect.class);
    
    @Before("execution(* com.example.service.*.*(..))")
    public void checkSecurity(JoinPoint joinPoint) {
        String methodName = joinPoint.getSignature().getName();
        Object[] args = joinPoint.getArgs();
        
        logger.info("Security check for method: " + methodName);
        
        // Check authentication
        if (!SecurityContext.isAuthenticated()) {
            throw new SecurityException("User not authenticated");
        }
        
        // Check authorization based on method name
        if (methodName.startsWith("delete") || methodName.startsWith("update")) {
            if (!SecurityContext.hasRole("ADMIN")) {
                throw new SecurityException("Insufficient privileges");
            }
        }
        
        logger.info("Security check passed for: " + methodName);
    }
    
    // More specific pointcut
    @Before("execution(* com.example.service.UserService.deleteUser(..)) && args(userId)")
    public void checkDeletePermission(JoinPoint joinPoint, Long userId) {
        if (!SecurityContext.hasPermission("DELETE_USER", userId)) {
            throw new SecurityException("No permission to delete user: " + userId);
        }
    }
}

// Usage example
@Service
public class UserService {
    // This method will have security check applied automatically
    public void deleteUser(Long userId) {
        userRepository.deleteById(userId);
    }
}
Use Cases
  • Security checks
  • Parameter validation
  • Logging method entry
  • Audit trail recording
Limitations
  • Cannot modify method parameters
  • Cannot prevent execution (except by exception)
  • No access to return value

@After Advice

Executes after a join point completes, regardless of whether it completed normally or threw an exception. Similar to a finally block. 


@Aspect
@Component
public class ResourceCleanupAspect {
    
    private static final Logger logger = LoggerFactory.getLogger(ResourceCleanupAspect.class);
    
    @After("execution(* com.example.service.*.*(..))")
    public void cleanupResources(JoinPoint joinPoint) {
        String methodName = joinPoint.getSignature().getName();
        String className = joinPoint.getTarget().getClass().getSimpleName();
        
        logger.info("Cleaning up resources for {}.{}", className, methodName);
        
        // Clean up thread-local variables
        ThreadLocalContext.clear();
        
        // Close any open resources
        ResourceManager.cleanup();
        
        // Reset any context variables
        RequestContext.reset();
    }
    
    // More specific cleanup for database operations
    @After("execution(* com.example.repository.*.*(..))")
    public void cleanupDatabaseResources(JoinPoint joinPoint) {
        logger.debug("Cleaning up database resources");
        
        // Close any open database connections in thread-local
        DatabaseConnectionManager.closeThreadConnections();
        
        // Clear any session data
        HibernateUtil.clearSession();
    }
}

@Service
public class FileProcessingService {
    public void processLargeFile(String filePath) {
        // This method might open file handles, network connections, etc.
        // The @After advice ensures cleanup happens regardless of success/failure
    }
}
Use Cases
  • Resource cleanup
  • Resetting thread-local variables
  • Releasing locks
  • Final logging
Important Notes
  • Runs regardless of success or exception
  • No access to return value or exception
  • Similar to finally block behavior

@AfterReturning Advice

Executes after a join point completes normally (without throwing an exception). Has access to the return value. 


@Aspect
@Component
public class AuditAspect {
    
    private static final Logger logger = LoggerFactory.getLogger(AuditAspect.class);
    
    @AfterReturning(
        pointcut = "execution(* com.example.service.UserService.*(..))",
        returning = "result"
    )
    public void auditSuccessfulOperation(JoinPoint joinPoint, Object result) {
        String methodName = joinPoint.getSignature().getName();
        Object[] args = joinPoint.getArgs();
        
        logger.info("Method {} executed successfully with result: {}", methodName, result);
        
        // Log to audit trail
        AuditEntry auditEntry = new AuditEntry(
            SecurityContext.getCurrentUser(),
            methodName,
            args,
            result,
            LocalDateTime.now()
        );
        auditRepository.save(auditEntry);
        
        // Send notification for specific operations
        if (methodName.equals("createUser") && result instanceof User) {
            User newUser = (User) result;
            notificationService.sendUserCreatedNotification(newUser);
        }
    }
    
    // Type-safe version with specific return type
    @AfterReturning(
        pointcut = "execution(* com.example.service.UserService.findByEmail(..))",
        returning = "user"
    )
    public void auditUserLookup(JoinPoint joinPoint, User user) {
        if (user != null) {
            logger.info("User found by email: {}", user.getEmail());
            userAccessRepository.logAccess(user.getId(), "EMAIL_LOOKUP");
        }
    }
}

@Service
public class UserService {
    public User createUser(User user) {
        // After this method returns successfully, the audit aspect will trigger
        return userRepository.save(user);
    }
}
Use Cases
  • Audit logging
  • Result processing
  • Success notifications
  • Cache population
Features
  • Access to return value via 'returning' parameter
  • Only executes on successful completion
  • Can modify return value (but not recommended)

@AfterThrowing Advice

Executes when a join point exits by throwing an exception. Has access to the thrown exception. 


@Aspect
@Component
public class ExceptionHandlingAspect {
    
    private static final Logger logger = LoggerFactory.getLogger(ExceptionHandlingAspect.class);
    
    @AfterThrowing(
        pointcut = "execution(* com.example.service.*.*(..))",
        throwing = "ex"
    )
    public void handleServiceExceptions(JoinPoint joinPoint, Exception ex) {
        String methodName = joinPoint.getSignature().getName();
        String className = joinPoint.getTarget().getClass().getSimpleName();
        
        logger.error("Exception in {}.{}: {}", className, methodName, ex.getMessage(), ex);
        
        // Convert to user-friendly exception
        if (ex instanceof DataAccessException) {
            throw new ServiceUnavailableException("Service temporarily unavailable", ex);
        }
        
        // Log to error tracking system
        ErrorTracker.trackError(className, methodName, ex);
        
        // Send alert for critical errors
        if (ex instanceof OutOfMemoryError || ex instanceof StackOverflowError) {
            alertService.sendCriticalAlert("Critical error in " + methodName, ex);
        }
    }
    
    // Specific exception handling
    @AfterThrowing(
        pointcut = "execution(* com.example.service.PaymentService.*(..))",
        throwing = "paymentEx"
    )
    public void handlePaymentExceptions(JoinPoint joinPoint, PaymentException paymentEx) {
        logger.warn("Payment operation failed: {}", paymentEx.getMessage());
        
        // Update payment status
        PaymentFailedEvent event = new PaymentFailedEvent(
            paymentEx.getPaymentId(),
            paymentEx.getMessage()
        );
        eventPublisher.publishEvent(event);
    }
    
    // Handle specific exception types
    @AfterThrowing(
        pointcut = "execution(* com.example.repository.*.*(..))",
        throwing = "ex"
    )
    public void handleDatabaseExceptions(JoinPoint joinPoint, DataAccessException ex) {
        logger.error("Database error in method: {}", joinPoint.getSignature().getName());
        
        // Retry logic for transient errors
        if (isTransientError(ex)) {
            scheduleRetry(joinPoint, joinPoint.getArgs());
        }
    }
}

@Service
public class PaymentService {
    public void processPayment(PaymentRequest request) {
        // If this method throws PaymentException, the aspect will handle it
        paymentGateway.process(request);
    }
}
Use Cases
  • Exception logging and tracking
  • Exception translation
  • Error notification
  • Retry logic initiation
Important Notes
  • Only executes when exception is thrown
  • Access to exception via 'throwing' parameter
  • Can re-throw same or different exception
  • Does not prevent exception propagation

@Around Advice

The most powerful advice that surrounds a join point. It can control whether the method executes, modify parameters, handle exceptions, and modify the return value. 


@Aspect
@Component
public class PerformanceAspect {
    
    private static final Logger logger = LoggerFactory.getLogger(PerformanceAspect.class);
    
    @Around("execution(* com.example.service.*.*(..))")
    public Object measureExecutionTime(ProceedingJoinPoint joinPoint) throws Throwable {
        String methodName = joinPoint.getSignature().getName();
        long startTime = System.currentTimeMillis();
        
        logger.info("Starting execution of: {}", methodName);
        
        try {
            // Execute the target method
            Object result = joinPoint.proceed();
            
            long executionTime = System.currentTimeMillis() - startTime;
            logger.info("Method {} executed in {} ms", methodName, executionTime);
            
            // Log slow methods
            if (executionTime > 1000) {
                logger.warn("Slow method detected: {} took {} ms", methodName, executionTime);
            }
            
            return result;
            
        } catch (Exception ex) {
            long executionTime = System.currentTimeMillis() - startTime;
            logger.error("Method {} failed after {} ms", methodName, executionTime, ex);
            throw ex;
        }
    }
    
    // Caching aspect
    @Around("@annotation(Cacheable)")
    public Object handleCaching(ProceedingJoinPoint joinPoint) throws Throwable {
        String cacheKey = generateCacheKey(joinPoint);
        
        // Check cache first
        Object cachedValue = cacheManager.get(cacheKey);
        if (cachedValue != null) {
            logger.debug("Cache hit for key: {}", cacheKey);
            return cachedValue;
        }
        
        // Execute method and cache result
        Object result = joinPoint.proceed();
        cacheManager.put(cacheKey, result);
        logger.debug("Cached result for key: {}", cacheKey);
        
        return result;
    }
    
    // Retry aspect for unreliable operations
    @Around("execution(* com.example.integration.*.*(..))")
    public Object handleRetries(ProceedingJoinPoint joinPoint) throws Throwable {
        int maxRetries = 3;
        int retryCount = 0;
        Exception lastException = null;
        
        while (retryCount < maxRetries) {
            try {
                return joinPoint.proceed();
            } catch (TransientException ex) {
                lastException = ex;
                retryCount++;
                logger.warn("Transient error, retry {}/{}", retryCount, maxRetries);
                
                if (retryCount < maxRetries) {
                    Thread.sleep(1000 * retryCount); // Exponential backoff
                }
            }
        }
        
        throw new ServiceUnavailableException("Operation failed after " + maxRetries + " retries", lastException);
    }
    
    // Security with method execution control
    @Around("execution(* com.example.service.AdminService.*(..))")
    public Object checkAdminAccess(ProceedingJoinPoint joinPoint) throws Throwable {
        if (!SecurityContext.hasRole("ADMIN")) {
            logger.warn("Unauthorized access attempt to admin method: {}", 
                       joinPoint.getSignature().getName());
            throw new SecurityException("Admin access required");
        }
        
        return joinPoint.proceed();
    }
}

// Custom annotation for caching
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface Cacheable {
    String value() default "";
    int ttl() default 3600;
}

@Service
public class ReportService {
    @Cacheable("reports")
    public Report generateReport(String reportType) {
        // This method result will be cached
        return reportGenerator.generate(reportType);
    }
}
Use Cases
  • Performance monitoring
  • Caching
  • Retry logic
  • Transaction management
  • Security with full control
Power Features
  • Full control over method execution
  • Can modify parameters and return value
  • Can prevent method execution
  • Can handle exceptions and retry
  • Most flexible but most complex

JoinPoint and Pointcut

JoinPoint

A JoinPoint represents a point in the execution of the program where an aspect can be plugged in. This point could be a method being called, an exception being thrown, or even a field being modified. 

public interface JoinPoint {
    String toString();         // Returns String representation
    String toShortString();    // Returns abbreviated String representation
    String toLongString();     // Returns long String representation
    
    Object getThis();          // Returns the currently executing object
    Object getTarget();        // Returns the target object
    
    Object[] getArgs();        // Returns the method arguments
    Signature getSignature();  // Returns the signature at the join point
    
    SourceLocation getSourceLocation(); // Returns source location
    String getKind();          // Returns the kind of join point
    
    StaticPart getStaticPart(); // Returns the static part
}

// ProceedingJoinPoint (for @Around advice)
public interface ProceedingJoinPoint extends JoinPoint {
    Object proceed() throws Throwable;
    Object proceed(Object[] args) throws Throwable;
}
Common JoinPoint Usage
@Before("execution(* com.example.service.*.*(..))")
public void beforeAdvice(JoinPoint joinPoint) {
    // Get method signature
    String methodName = joinPoint.getSignature().getName();
    String className = joinPoint.getSignature().getDeclaringTypeName();
    
    // Get method arguments
    Object[] args = joinPoint.getArgs();
    
    // Get target object
    Object target = joinPoint.getTarget();
    
    logger.info("Executing {}.{} with args: {}", 
                className, methodName, Arrays.toString(args));
}

Pointcut

A Pointcut is a predicate that matches join points. It is used to define where advice should be applied. Pointcuts use expressions to match method executions. 

// Pointcut expression patterns
execution(modifiers-pattern? 
          return-type-pattern 
          declaring-type-pattern? 
          method-name-pattern(parameters-pattern)
          throws-pattern?)

// Examples:
execution(public * *(..))                    // Any public method
execution(* set*(..))                        // Any method starting with "set"
execution(* com.example.service.*.*(..))     // Any method in service package
execution(* com.example.service..*.*(..))    // Any method in service package or sub-packages

// Combining pointcuts
@Pointcut("execution(* com.example.dao.*.*(..))")
public void dataAccessOperation() {}

@Pointcut("execution(* com.example.service.*.*(..))")
public void businessService() {}

@Pointcut("dataAccessOperation() || businessService()")
public void allServiceOperations() {}
Pointcut Designators
execution(* *(..))                    // Method execution
within(com.example.service.*)         // Within types
this(com.example.Service)             // Bean reference is instance of
target(com.example.Service)           // Target object is instance of
args(java.io.Serializable)            // Method arguments
@target(org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional) // Class annotation
@within(org.springframework.stereotype.Service) // Class annotation
@annotation(org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional) // Method annotation
@args(com.example.Valid)              // Parameter annotation
bean(dataSource)                      // Spring bean name

Spring AOP vs AspectJ AOP

Comparison: Spring AOP vs AspectJ

Feature Spring AOP AspectJ
Weaving Mechanism Runtime weaving using proxies Compile-time, post-compile, or load-time weaving
Performance Slower due to proxy overhead Faster, woven directly into bytecode
Join Points Only method execution Method exec, constructor, field access, etc.
Dependency Part of Spring Framework Separate dependency
Complexity Simpler, uses proxy pattern More complex, full AOP implementation
Target Objects Only Spring beans Any Java object
Configuration XML or annotations AspectJ language or annotations
When to Use Spring AOP
  • Simple cross-cutting concerns (logging, security, transactions)
  • When you're already using Spring Framework
  • When performance overhead is acceptable
  • When you only need method execution join points
  • For quick prototyping and development
When to Use AspectJ
  • Need fine-grained join points (field access, constructor calls)
  • Performance-critical applications
  • Complex cross-cutting concerns
  • When you need to advise objects not managed by Spring
  • For production systems where performance is crucial

Weaving in AOP

Understanding Weaving

Weaving is the process of applying aspects to target objects to create advised objects. This can happen at different stages in the application lifecycle.

Compile-time Weaving

Aspects are woven into the target classes at compile time using a special compiler (AspectJ compiler). 

// Using AspectJ compiler
// ajc -aspectpath aspects.jar 
//     -outjar myapp.jar 
//     MyClass.java MyAspect.aj
  • Pros: Best performance, no runtime overhead
  • Cons: Requires special build process
  • Tools: AspectJ compiler (ajc)
Load-time Weaving

Aspects are woven when the target classes are loaded by the classloader. 

// Spring configuration
@EnableLoadTimeWeaving

// Or in XML
<context:load-time-weaver/>

// JVM argument
-javaagent:path/to/spring-instrument.jar
  • Pros: No build-time changes, good performance
  • Cons: Requires JVM agent configuration
  • Tools: Spring LoadTimeWeaver, AspectJ weaver
Runtime Weaving

Aspects are applied at runtime using dynamic proxies (Spring AOP default). 

// Spring AOP uses runtime weaving
// Creates proxies for target beans

// JDK dynamic proxies (for interfaces)
// CGLIB proxies (for classes without interfaces)
  • Pros: Simple configuration, no special setup
  • Cons: Performance overhead, limited join points
  • Tools: Spring AOP, JDK proxies, CGLIB
Weaving Process Visualization
Target Class + Aspect → Weaving → Advised Class
Target Class
Business Logic
+
Aspect
Cross-cutting Logic
→
Advised Class
Enhanced Behavior

Spring AOP Quick Reference

Advice Types

  • @Before - Before method execution
  • @After - After method (finally)
  • @AfterReturning - After success
  • @AfterThrowing - After exception
  • @Around - Surround method

Key Concepts

  • Aspect: Modular cross-cutting concern
  • JoinPoint: Execution point in program
  • Pointcut: Predicate for join points
  • Advice: Action taken at join point
  • Weaving: Applying aspects to code

Pointcut Expressions

  • execution(* *(..)) - Any method
  • within(com.example..*) - Within package
  • @annotation(Annotation) - Method annotation
  • bean(service*) - Spring bean name

Best Practices

  • Use for true cross-cutting concerns
  • Keep aspects focused and simple
  • Avoid business logic in aspects
  • Use meaningful pointcut names
  • Test aspects thoroughly

Common AOP Pitfalls

  • Overusing AOP for non-cross-cutting concerns
  • Creating overly complex pointcut expressions
  • Ignoring performance implications of runtime weaving
  • Not testing aspects with different scenarios
  • Forgetting that @Transactional uses AOP internally
  • Creating circular dependencies with self-invocation

Spring MVC: Complete Guide to Web Framework Architecture

What is Spring MVC?

Spring MVC (Model-View-Controller) is a powerful and flexible web framework built on the Spring Framework. It provides a comprehensive programming model for building robust, scalable web applications following the MVC architectural pattern.

Core Concept: Spring MVC separates application concerns into three main components: Model (data), View (presentation), and Controller (business logic), enabling clean separation of concerns and easier maintenance.

Key Features

  • Powerful configuration options (XML, Java Config, annotations)
  • Flexible view resolution (JSP, Thymeleaf, FreeMarker, etc.)
  • Comprehensive data binding and validation
  • RESTful web service support
  • Internationalization and localization
  • Theme and template support
  • Exception handling mechanisms

Benefits

  • Clean separation of concerns
  • Highly configurable and extensible
  • Integration with Spring ecosystem
  • Comprehensive testing support
  • Mature and widely adopted
  • Strong community support

Spring MVC Workflow

Spring MVC Request Processing Workflow

1
HTTP Request
Client sends request to DispatcherServlet
▼
2
Handler Mapping
Find appropriate Controller
▼
3
Controller Processing
Execute business logic
▼
4
View Resolution
Resolve view name to actual view
▼
5
HTTP Response
Send response back to client
Detailed Workflow Steps:
  1. Request Received: DispatcherServlet receives the HTTP request
  2. Handler Mapping: Determines which controller should handle the request
  3. Controller Execution: The mapped controller processes the request and returns ModelAndView
  4. View Resolution: ViewResolver maps logical view names to actual view implementations
  5. View Rendering: The view renders the response using model data
  6. Response Sent: The rendered response is sent back to the client

Workflow in Action - Code Example


// 1. Client sends request: GET /users/123

// 2. DispatcherServlet receives request and consults HandlerMapping
@Configuration
@EnableWebMvc
public class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
    // HandlerMapping configuration
}

// 3. HandlerMapping finds appropriate controller
@Controller
@RequestMapping("/users")
public class UserController {
    
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public String getUser(@PathVariable Long id, Model model) {
        // 4. Controller processes request
        User user = userService.findById(id);
        model.addAttribute("user", user);
        
        // 5. Returns view name
        return "user-details"; // Logical view name
    }
}

// 6. ViewResolver resolves "user-details" to actual view
@Configuration
public class ViewConfig {
    @Bean
    public ViewResolver viewResolver() {
        InternalResourceViewResolver resolver = new InternalResourceViewResolver();
        resolver.setPrefix("/WEB-INF/views/");
        resolver.setSuffix(".jsp");
        return resolver;
    }
}

// 7. View renders response: /WEB-INF/views/user-details.jsp
// 8. Response sent to client

What is DispatcherServlet?

DispatcherServlet - Front Controller

DispatcherServlet is the central dispatcher for HTTP request handlers/controllers in Spring MVC. It follows the Front Controller design pattern and coordinates all request processing activities. 


// web.xml configuration (Traditional)
<web-app>
    <servlet>
        <servlet-name>dispatcher</servlet-name>
        <servlet-class>
            org.springframework.web.servlet.DispatcherServlet
        </servlet-class>
        <init-param>
            <param-name>contextConfigLocation</param-name>
            <param-value>/WEB-INF/spring-mvc-config.xml</param-value>
        </init-param>
        <load-on-startup>1</load-on-startup>
    </servlet>
    
    <servlet-mapping>
        <servlet-name>dispatcher</servlet-name>
        <url-pattern>/</url-pattern>
    </servlet-mapping>
</web-app>

// Java Configuration (Spring Boot)
@SpringBootApplication
public class Application {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args);
    }
}

// DispatcherServlet is automatically configured in Spring Boot
Key Responsibilities:
  • Receives all incoming HTTP requests
  • Delegates requests to appropriate controllers
  • Manages view resolution process
  • Handles exception processing
  • Manages file uploads
  • Provides localization support
  • Handles theme resolution
Integration Points:
  • HandlerMapping - Finds appropriate controller
  • HandlerAdapter - Executes controller methods
  • ViewResolver - Resolves view names
  • HandlerExceptionResolver - Handles exceptions
  • MultipartResolver - Handles file uploads
  • LocaleResolver - Manages localization

What is ViewResolver?

ViewResolver - View Resolution Strategy

ViewResolver is responsible for resolving logical view names returned by controllers into actual View implementations. It provides a mapping between view names and actual view technologies. 


// Common ViewResolver Implementations

// 1. InternalResourceViewResolver - for JSP
@Bean
public ViewResolver jspViewResolver() {
    InternalResourceViewResolver resolver = new InternalResourceViewResolver();
    resolver.setPrefix("/WEB-INF/views/");
    resolver.setSuffix(".jsp");
    resolver.setViewClass(JstlView.class);
    return resolver;
}

// 2. ThymeleafViewResolver - for Thymeleaf
@Bean
public SpringResourceTemplateResolver templateResolver() {
    SpringResourceTemplateResolver resolver = new SpringResourceTemplateResolver();
    resolver.setPrefix("classpath:/templates/");
    resolver.setSuffix(".html");
    resolver.setTemplateMode(TemplateMode.HTML);
    return resolver;
}

// 3. FreeMarkerViewResolver - for FreeMarker
@Bean
public FreeMarkerConfigurer freeMarkerConfigurer() {
    FreeMarkerConfigurer configurer = new FreeMarkerConfigurer();
    configurer.setTemplateLoaderPath("classpath:/templates/");
    return configurer;
}

// 4. ContentNegotiatingViewResolver - for multiple view types
@Bean
public ViewResolver contentNegotiatingViewResolver() {
    ContentNegotiatingViewResolver resolver = new ContentNegotiatingViewResolver();
    resolver.setViewResolvers(Arrays.asList(
        jspViewResolver(),
        thymeleafViewResolver()
    ));
    return resolver;
}

// Controller returns logical view name
@Controller
public class UserController {
    @GetMapping("/user")
    public String getUser(Model model) {
        model.addAttribute("user", new User());
        return "user-form"; // Resolved to /WEB-INF/views/user-form.jsp
    }
}
Common ViewResolver Types:
  • InternalResourceViewResolver: For JSP and JSTL
  • ThymeleafViewResolver: For Thymeleaf templates
  • FreeMarkerViewResolver: For FreeMarker templates
  • GroovyMarkupViewResolver: For Groovy templates
  • ContentNegotiatingViewResolver: For multiple view types
  • ResourceBundleViewResolver: From resource bundles
Configuration Options:
  • Prefix and suffix for view names
  • View class customization
  • Content negotiation
  • Multiple resolver chains
  • Ordering of resolvers
  • Default views

What is HandlerMapping?

HandlerMapping - Request to Controller Mapping

HandlerMapping is responsible for mapping incoming HTTP requests to appropriate handler methods (controllers). It determines which controller should handle a specific request based on URL patterns and other criteria. 


// Common HandlerMapping Strategies

// 1. RequestMappingHandlerMapping (Default in Spring MVC)
// Maps requests based on @RequestMapping annotations
@Controller
@RequestMapping("/users")
public class UserController {
    
    @GetMapping("/{id}")  // Maps to GET /users/123
    public String getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return "user-details";
    }
    
    @PostMapping("/")      // Maps to POST /users/
    public String createUser(@ModelAttribute User user) {
        return "redirect:/users/" + user.getId();
    }
}

// 2. SimpleUrlHandlerMapping - Explicit URL mappings
@Configuration
public class UrlMappingConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
    
    @Bean
    public SimpleUrlHandlerMapping simpleUrlHandlerMapping() {
        SimpleUrlHandlerMapping mapping = new SimpleUrlHandlerMapping();
        mapping.setUrlMap(Collections.singletonMap("/home", homeController()));
        mapping.setOrder(1);
        return mapping;
    }
}

// 3. BeanNameUrlHandlerMapping - Maps URLs to bean names
@Component("/welcome")
public class WelcomeController implements Controller {
    public ModelAndView handleRequest(HttpServletRequest request, 
                                     HttpServletResponse response) {
        return new ModelAndView("welcome");
    }
}

// 4. RouterFunctionMapping - For functional endpoints (WebFlux)
@Bean
public RouterFunction<ServerResponse> userRoutes() {
    return RouterFunctions.route()
        .GET("/users/{id}", this::getUser)
        .POST("/users", this::createUser)
        .build();
}
HandlerMapping Types:
  • RequestMappingHandlerMapping: For @RequestMapping (most common)
  • SimpleUrlHandlerMapping: Explicit URL mappings
  • BeanNameUrlHandlerMapping: Bean name based mapping
  • RouterFunctionMapping: Functional programming model
  • DefaultAnnotationHandlerMapping: Legacy annotation mapping
Mapping Strategies:
  • URL path patterns
  • HTTP methods (GET, POST, etc.)
  • Request parameters
  • Headers
  • Content type
  • Custom conditions

Difference between @Controller and @RestController

@Controller vs @RestController Comparison

Aspect @Controller @RestController
Purpose Traditional web MVC controller RESTful web service controller
Response Returns view name for rendering Returns data directly as response body
Annotations Needed Often requires @ResponseBody for data @ResponseBody is implicit
Use Case HTML web applications REST APIs, JSON/XML services
View Resolution Uses ViewResolver for templates No view resolution, direct data
Content Type Typically text/html application/json, application/xml

Code Examples

@Controller Example
@Controller
@RequestMapping("/web")
public class WebUserController {
    
    // Returns view name for HTML rendering
    @GetMapping("/users/{id}")
    public String getUser(@PathVariable Long id, Model model) {
        User user = userService.findById(id);
        model.addAttribute("user", user);
        return "user-details"; // Resolved to user-details.jsp
    }
    
    // Returns JSON but requires @ResponseBody
    @GetMapping("/api/users/{id}")
    @ResponseBody
    public User getUserJson(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id);
    }
}
@RestController Example
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api")
public class RestUserController {
    
    // Automatically returns JSON, no view resolution
    @GetMapping("/users/{id}")
    public User getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id);
    }
    
    @PostMapping("/users")
    public User createUser(@RequestBody User user) {
        return userService.save(user);
    }
    
    @PutMapping("/users/{id}")
    public User updateUser(@PathVariable Long id, 
                          @RequestBody User user) {
        return userService.update(id, user);
    }
    
    @DeleteMapping("/users/{id}")
    public void deleteUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        userService.delete(id);
    }
}

HTTP Method Annotations

@RequestMapping - Generic Request Mapping

@RequestMapping is the most general annotation for mapping web requests to specific handler classes and/or methods. It can be used at both class and method levels and supports various attributes for fine-grained mapping. 


@Controller
@RequestMapping("/products")  // Class-level mapping
public class ProductController {
    
    // Map multiple HTTP methods
    @RequestMapping(value = "/{id}", method = {RequestMethod.GET, RequestMethod.HEAD})
    public String getProduct(@PathVariable Long id, Model model) {
        model.addAttribute("product", productService.findById(id));
        return "product-details";
    }
    
    // Map with specific HTTP method
    @RequestMapping(value = "/", method = RequestMethod.POST)
    public String createProduct(@ModelAttribute Product product) {
        productService.save(product);
        return "redirect:/products/" + product.getId();
    }
    
    // Map with parameters condition
    @RequestMapping(value = "/search", method = RequestMethod.GET, 
                   params = "category")
    public String searchByCategory(@RequestParam String category, Model model) {
        model.addAttribute("products", productService.findByCategory(category));
        return "product-list";
    }
    
    // Map with headers condition
    @RequestMapping(value = "/special", method = RequestMethod.GET,
                   headers = "X-Special-Header=true")
    public String specialProducts(Model model) {
        model.addAttribute("products", productService.findSpecialProducts());
        return "special-products";
    }
    
    // Map with content type
    @RequestMapping(value = "/{id}", method = RequestMethod.GET,
                   produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
    @ResponseBody
    public Product getProductJson(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return productService.findById(id);
    }
}
Common Attributes
  • value/path - URL path mapping
  • method - HTTP methods (GET, POST, etc.)
  • params - Request parameter conditions
  • headers - Request header conditions
  • consumes - Request content type
  • produces - Response content type
Best Practices
  • Use specific method annotations when possible
  • Use class-level @RequestMapping for common paths
  • Specify produces/consumes for REST APIs
  • Use params for conditional mapping

HTTP Method Specific Annotations

Spring provides specialized annotations for each HTTP method, making code more readable and concise. These are composed annotations built on top of @RequestMapping. 


@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/books")
public class BookController {
    
    // GET - Retrieve resource(s)
    @GetMapping
    public List<Book> getAllBooks() {
        return bookService.findAll();
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public Book getBook(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return bookService.findById(id);
    }
    
    // POST - Create new resource
    @PostMapping
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)
    public Book createBook(@RequestBody Book book) {
        return bookService.save(book);
    }
    
    // PUT - Update/replace entire resource
    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    public Book updateBook(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody Book book) {
        book.setId(id);
        return bookService.save(book);
    }
    
    // PATCH - Partial update of resource
    @PatchMapping("/{id}")
    public Book patchBook(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody Map<String, Object> updates) {
        return bookService.patch(id, updates);
    }
    
    // DELETE - Remove resource
    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)
    public void deleteBook(@PathVariable Long id) {
        bookService.delete(id);
    }
    
    // HEAD - Same as GET but without response body
    @GetMapping(value = "/{id}", headers = "HEAD")
    public ResponseEntity<Void> headBook(@PathVariable Long id) {
        if (bookService.exists(id)) {
            return ResponseEntity.ok().build();
        }
        return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
    }
    
    // OPTIONS - Get supported operations
    @RequestMapping(value = "/{id}", method = RequestMethod.OPTIONS)
    public ResponseEntity<Void> optionsBook() {
        return ResponseEntity.ok()
            .header("Allow", "GET, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS")
            .build();
    }
}
Annotation HTTP Method Purpose Idempotent Safe
@GetMapping GET Retrieve resources Yes Yes
@PostMapping POST Create new resource No No
@PutMapping PUT Replace entire resource Yes No
@DeleteMapping DELETE Remove resource Yes No
@PatchMapping PATCH Partial update No No

Parameter Binding Annotations

@RequestParam - Query Parameters

Binds request parameters (query string or form data) to method parameters. Useful for optional or required query parameters in GET requests or form fields in POST requests. 

@RestController
public class SearchController {
    
    // Required parameter (default)
    // URL: /search?query=spring
    @GetMapping("/search")
    public List<Product> search(@RequestParam String query) {
        return productService.search(query);
    }
    
    // Optional parameter
    // URL: /search?query=spring&category=books
    @GetMapping("/search")
    public List<Product> search(
            @RequestParam String query,
            @RequestParam(required = false) String category) {
        return productService.search(query, category);
    }
    
    // Default value for missing parameter
    // URL: /products (page defaults to 0)
    @GetMapping("/products")
    public Page<Product> getProducts(
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "20") int size) {
        return productService.findAll(PageRequest.of(page, size));
    }
    
    // Multiple values for same parameter
    // URL: /products?categories=books&categories=electronics
    @GetMapping("/products")
    public List<Product> getProductsByCategories(
            @RequestParam List<String> categories) {
        return productService.findByCategories(categories);
    }
    
    // Map all parameters
    @GetMapping("/filter")
    public List<Product> filterProducts(
            @RequestParam Map<String, String> filters) {
        return productService.filter(filters);
    }
    
    // Custom parameter name
    @GetMapping("/users")
    public List<User> getUsers(
            @RequestParam("user_name") String username) {
        return userService.findByUsername(username);
    }
}
Key Attributes:
  • required - Whether parameter is required (default: true)
  • defaultValue - Default value if parameter is missing
  • name/value - Parameter name (defaults to method parameter name)

@PathVariable - URL Path Variables

Bends URI template variables to method parameters. Used for capturing values from the URL path, making URLs more RESTful and readable. 

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {
    
    // Single path variable
    // URL: /api/users/123
    @GetMapping("/{userId}")
    public User getUser(@PathVariable Long userId) {
        return userService.findById(userId);
    }
    
    // Multiple path variables
    // URL: /api/users/123/orders/456
    @GetMapping("/{userId}/orders/{orderId}")
    public Order getUserOrder(
            @PathVariable Long userId,
            @PathVariable Long orderId) {
        return orderService.findUserOrder(userId, orderId);
    }
    
    // Custom variable name
    // URL: /api/users/123
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public User getUser(@PathVariable("id") Long userId) {
        return userService.findById(userId);
    }
    
    // Optional path variable (Spring 4.3+)
    // URL: /api/users OR /api/users/123
    @GetMapping({"/", "/{userId}"})
    public List<User> getUsers(@PathVariable(required = false) Long userId) {
        if (userId != null) {
            return List.of(userService.findById(userId));
        }
        return userService.findAll();
    }
    
    // Regex in path variables
    // URL: /api/users/123-456
    @GetMapping("/{userId:[0-9]+-[0-9]+}")
    public User getUserWithComplexId(@PathVariable String userId) {
        String[] parts = userId.split("-");
        return userService.findByCompositeId(parts[0], parts[1]);
    }
    
    // Map all path variables
    @GetMapping("/{department}/{category}/{id}")
    public Product getProduct(@PathVariable Map<String, String> pathVars) {
        return productService.findByPath(
            pathVars.get("department"),
            pathVars.get("category"), 
            pathVars.get("id")
        );
    }
}
Best Practices:
  • Use for resource identifiers in RESTful URLs
  • Keep path variables simple and meaningful
  • Use regex constraints for validation
  • Consider optional path variables for flexibility

@RequestBody - Request Body Binding

Binds the HTTP request body to a method parameter. Used for reading JSON, XML, or other content from the request body, typically in POST, PUT, and PATCH requests. 

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/products")
public class ProductController {
    
    // Basic @RequestBody usage
    // POST /api/products with JSON body
    @PostMapping
    public Product createProduct(@RequestBody Product product) {
        return productService.save(product);
    }
    
    // With validation
    @PostMapping
    public Product createProductValid(
            @Valid @RequestBody Product product) {
        return productService.save(product);
    }
    
    // With specific content type
    @PostMapping(consumes = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
    public Product createProductJson(@RequestBody Product product) {
        return productService.save(product);
    }
    
    // Raw request body as String
    @PostMapping("/raw")
    public String processRawBody(@RequestBody String rawBody) {
        return "Received: " + rawBody.length() + " characters";
    }
    
    // Request body as byte array
    @PostMapping("/binary")
    public String processBinary(@RequestBody byte[] binaryData) {
        return "Received: " + binaryData.length + " bytes";
    }
    
    // Custom object with Jackson annotations
    @PostMapping("/custom")
    public void processCustom(@RequestBody CreateProductRequest request) {
        productService.createFromRequest(request);
    }
    
    // With HttpEntity for more control
    @PostMapping("/entity")
    public ResponseEntity<Product> createWithEntity(
            HttpEntity<Product> requestEntity) {
        Product product = requestEntity.getBody();
        HttpHeaders headers = requestEntity.getHeaders();
        
        Product saved = productService.save(product);
        return ResponseEntity.ok()
            .headers(headers)
            .body(saved);
    }
}

// DTO for request body
class CreateProductRequest {
    private String name;
    private String description;
    private BigDecimal price;
    private Long categoryId;
    
    // Jackson annotations for customization
    @JsonProperty("product_name")
    private String productName;
    
    @JsonFormat(shape = JsonFormat.Shape.STRING, pattern = "yyyy-MM-dd")
    private LocalDate manufactureDate;
    
    // getters and setters
}
Configuration:
  • Requires HttpMessageConverter (Jackson for JSON)
  • Configure ObjectMapper for custom serialization
  • Use @Valid for validation
  • Specify consumes for content type negotiation

@ResponseBody - Response Body Writing

Indicates that the method return value should be bound to the web response body. Bypasses view resolution and writes directly to the response output stream. 

@Controller
@RequestMapping("/web")
public class WebController {
    
    // @ResponseBody on method
    @GetMapping("/users/{id}/json")
    @ResponseBody
    public User getUserJson(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id);
    }
    
    // @ResponseBody on class (all methods)
    @Controller
    @ResponseBody
    @RequestMapping("/api/v1")
    public class ApiV1Controller {
        // All methods return response body
    }
    
    // Equivalent to @RestController
    @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody
}

// Manual response handling
@Controller
public class CustomResponseController {
    
    @GetMapping("/data")
    @ResponseBody
    public String getPlainText() {
        return "Hello, World!";
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/number")
    @ResponseBody
    public int getNumber() {
        return 42;
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/list")
    @ResponseBody
    public List<String> getList() {
        return Arrays.asList("A", "B", "C");
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/map")
    @ResponseBody
    public Map<String, Object> getMap() {
        Map<String, Object> map = new HashMap<>();
        map.put("name", "John");
        map.put("age", 30);
        return map;
    }
    
    // Custom content type
    @GetMapping(value = "/xml", produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_XML_VALUE)
    @ResponseBody
    public User getXml() {
        return userService.findById(1L);
    }
    
    // With ResponseEntity for full control
    @GetMapping("/custom")
    public ResponseEntity<String> getCustom() {
        HttpHeaders headers = new HttpHeaders();
        headers.setContentType(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN);
        headers.set("X-Custom-Header", "value");
        
        return new ResponseEntity<>("Custom Response", headers, HttpStatus.OK);
    }
}
Use Cases:
  • REST API endpoints returning JSON/XML
  • AJAX responses in web applications
  • File downloads with custom content
  • When you need full control over response

Model Attribute Annotations

@ModelAttribute - Model Data Binding

Binds a method parameter or method return value to a named model attribute, which can then be accessed in the view. Used for form data binding and pre-populating model data. 

@Controller
@RequestMapping("/products")
public class ProductController {
    
    // @ModelAttribute on method parameter (form binding)
    // POST /products with form data
    @PostMapping
    public String createProduct(@ModelAttribute Product product) {
        productService.save(product);
        return "redirect:/products/" + product.getId();
    }
    
    // @ModelAttribute with custom name
    @PostMapping
    public String createProduct(
            @ModelAttribute("newProduct") Product product) {
        productService.save(product);
        return "redirect:/products";
    }
    
    // @ModelAttribute on method (pre-populate model)
    @ModelAttribute("categories")
    public List<Category> populateCategories() {
        return categoryService.findAll();
    }
    
    @ModelAttribute("productTypes")
    public ProductType[] productTypes() {
        return ProductType.values();
    }
    
    // @ModelAttribute with request data
    @ModelAttribute
    public void addAttributes(Model model) {
        model.addAttribute("version", "1.0.0");
        model.addAttribute("currentYear", LocalDate.now().getYear());
    }
    
    // Form display with pre-populated data
    @GetMapping("/create")
    public String showCreateForm(Model model) {
        // The @ModelAttribute methods above will auto-execute
        // and add categories, productTypes to the model
        model.addAttribute("product", new Product());
        return "product-form";
    }
    
    // Binding result for validation
    @PostMapping
    public String createProductWithValidation(
            @Valid @ModelAttribute Product product,
            BindingResult result,
            Model model) {
        
        if (result.hasErrors()) {
            // Return to form with errors
            model.addAttribute("categories", categoryService.findAll());
            return "product-form";
        }
        
        productService.save(product);
        return "redirect:/products/" + product.getId();
    }
}

// Using @ModelAttribute in Thymeleaf template
/*
<form th:action="@{/products}" th:object="${product}" method="post">
    <input type="text" th:field="*{name}" />
    <select th:field="*{category}">
        <option th:each="category : ${categories}" 
                th:value="${category.id}" 
                th:text="${category.name}"></option>
    </select>
</form>
*/
Key Features:
  • Data binding from request parameters
  • Pre-population of model data
  • Form validation support
  • Automatic type conversion
  • Custom attribute names

@SessionAttributes - Session Storage

Declares session attributes used by a specific handler, storing model attributes in the HTTP session between requests. Useful for multi-step forms or wizard-style interfaces. 

@Controller
@RequestMapping("/order")
@SessionAttributes("order") // Store 'order' in session
public class OrderController {
    
    // Initialize order in session
    @ModelAttribute("order")
    public Order initializeOrder() {
        return new Order();
    }
    
    // Step 1: Customer information
    @GetMapping("/customer")
    public String showCustomerForm(@ModelAttribute("order") Order order) {
        return "order-customer-form";
    }
    
    @PostMapping("/customer")
    public String processCustomerInfo(
            @Valid @ModelAttribute("order") Order order,
            BindingResult result) {
        
        if (result.hasErrors()) {
            return "order-customer-form";
        }
        return "redirect:/order/shipping";
    }
    
    // Step 2: Shipping information
    @GetMapping("/shipping")
    public String showShippingForm(@ModelAttribute("order") Order order) {
        return "order-shipping-form";
    }
    
    @PostMapping("/shipping")
    public String processShippingInfo(
            @Valid @ModelAttribute("order") Order order,
            BindingResult result) {
        
        if (result.hasErrors()) {
            return "order-shipping-form";
        }
        return "redirect:/order/payment";
    }
    
    // Step 3: Payment information
    @GetMapping("/payment")
    public String showPaymentForm(@ModelAttribute("order") Order order) {
        return "order-payment-form";
    }
    
    @PostMapping("/payment")
    public String processPayment(
            @Valid @ModelAttribute("order") Order order,
            BindingResult result,
            SessionStatus sessionStatus) {
        
        if (result.hasErrors()) {
            return "order-payment-form";
        }
        
        // Save the complete order
        orderService.save(order);
        
        // Clear session attributes
        sessionStatus.setComplete();
        
        return "redirect:/order/confirmation";
    }
    
    // Confirmation page
    @GetMapping("/confirmation")
    public String showConfirmation() {
        return "order-confirmation";
    }
    
    // Clear specific session attribute
    @PostMapping("/cancel")
    public String cancelOrder(SessionStatus sessionStatus) {
        sessionStatus.setComplete();
        return "redirect:/order";
    }
}

// Using @SessionAttribute to access session data
@Controller
public class CartController {
    
    @GetMapping("/cart")
    public String viewCart(@SessionAttribute("cart") ShoppingCart cart) {
        return "cart-view";
    }
    
    @PostMapping("/cart/clear")
    public String clearCart(HttpSession session) {
        session.removeAttribute("cart");
        return "redirect:/cart";
    }
}
Best Practices:
  • Use for multi-step forms and wizards
  • Always call SessionStatus.setComplete() to clean up
  • Be mindful of session size and memory usage
  • Consider session timeout configurations
  • Use for small, temporary data only

Spring MVC Quick Reference

Core Components

  • DispatcherServlet - Front Controller
  • HandlerMapping - Request Mapping
  • Controller - Request Processing
  • ViewResolver - View Resolution

Annotations

  • @Controller / @RestController
  • @RequestMapping
  • @GetMapping / @PostMapping
  • @ResponseBody

Parameter Binding

  • @RequestParam - Query params
  • @PathVariable - URL variables
  • @RequestBody - Request body
  • @ModelAttribute - Form data

Session & Model

  • @SessionAttributes - Session storage
  • @ModelAttribute - Model data
  • Model interface
  • SessionStatus

Best Practices Summary

  • Use @RestController for REST APIs, @Controller for web pages
  • Prefer specific HTTP method annotations over generic @RequestMapping
  • Use @RequestParam for optional parameters, @PathVariable for resource IDs
  • Always validate @RequestBody and @ModelAttribute with @Valid
  • Clean up session attributes with SessionStatus.setComplete()
  • Use appropriate HTTP status codes and response types

Spring MVC: Complete Guide to Web Layer Components & Features

Spring MVC Architecture Overview

Spring MVC provides a comprehensive framework for building web applications with clear separation of concerns. Understanding its core components and features is essential for building robust, maintainable web applications.

Core Concept: Spring MVC follows the Model-View-Controller pattern with extensible interfaces for customization. Key components include interceptors, exception handlers, and powerful data binding capabilities.

HandlerInterceptor: Request/Response Interception

What is HandlerInterceptor?

HandlerInterceptor is an interface that allows custom pre-processing and post-processing of requests. It provides three methods to intercept the execution of a handler (controller method). 


public interface HandlerInterceptor {
    
    // Called before handler execution
    default boolean preHandle(HttpServletRequest request, 
                             HttpServletResponse response, 
                             Object handler) throws Exception;
    
    // Called after handler execution but before view rendering
    default void postHandle(HttpServletRequest request, 
                           HttpServletResponse response, 
                           Object handler,
                           ModelAndView modelAndView) throws Exception;
    
    // Called after complete request completion
    default void afterCompletion(HttpServletRequest request, 
                                HttpServletResponse response, 
                                Object handler, 
                                Exception ex) throws Exception;
}
preHandle
Before controller execution
postHandle
After controller, before view
afterCompletion
After complete request

HandlerInterceptor Implementation Examples


@Component
public class LoggingInterceptor implements HandlerInterceptor {
    
    private static final Logger logger = LoggerFactory.getLogger(LoggingInterceptor.class);
    
    @Override
    public boolean preHandle(HttpServletRequest request, 
                           HttpServletResponse response, 
                           Object handler) throws Exception {
        
        long startTime = System.currentTimeMillis();
        request.setAttribute("startTime", startTime);
        
        logger.info("Request URL: {} - Method: {} - Start Time: {}", 
                   request.getRequestURL(), request.getMethod(), startTime);
        
        // Authentication check example
        if (!isAuthenticated(request)) {
            response.sendRedirect("/login");
            return false; // Stop further processing
        }
        
        return true; // Continue to handler
    }
    
    @Override
    public void postHandle(HttpServletRequest request, 
                          HttpServletResponse response, 
                          Object handler,
                          ModelAndView modelAndView) throws Exception {
        
        long startTime = (Long) request.getAttribute("startTime");
        long endTime = System.currentTimeMillis();
        long executionTime = endTime - startTime;
        
        logger.info("Request URL: {} - Execution Time: {} ms", 
                   request.getRequestURL(), executionTime);
        
        // Add execution time to model for view
        if (modelAndView != null) {
            modelAndView.addObject("executionTime", executionTime);
        }
    }
    
    @Override
    public void afterCompletion(HttpServletRequest request, 
                               HttpServletResponse response, 
                               Object handler, 
                               Exception ex) throws Exception {
        
        // Cleanup resources
        if (ex != null) {
            logger.error("Request failed with exception: {}", ex.getMessage());
        }
        
        logger.info("Request completed: {} - Status: {}", 
                   request.getRequestURL(), response.getStatus());
    }
    
    private boolean isAuthenticated(HttpServletRequest request) {
        HttpSession session = request.getSession(false);
        return session != null && session.getAttribute("user") != null;
    }
}

// Another interceptor for specific functionality
@Component
public class TenantInterceptor implements HandlerInterceptor {
    
    @Override
    public boolean preHandle(HttpServletRequest request, 
                           HttpServletResponse response, 
                           Object handler) throws Exception {
        
        // Extract tenant ID from header or subdomain
        String tenantId = request.getHeader("X-Tenant-ID");
        if (tenantId == null) {
            // Try to get from subdomain
            String serverName = request.getServerName();
            tenantId = extractTenantFromDomain(serverName);
        }
        
        if (tenantId != null) {
            // Set tenant context for data isolation
            TenantContext.setCurrentTenant(tenantId);
        } else {
            response.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_BAD_REQUEST, "Tenant ID required");
            return false;
        }
        
        return true;
    }
    
    @Override
    public void afterCompletion(HttpServletRequest request, 
                               HttpServletResponse response, 
                               Object handler, 
                               Exception ex) throws Exception {
        // Clear tenant context to avoid memory leaks
        TenantContext.clear();
    }
    
    private String extractTenantFromDomain(String domain) {
        // Implementation to extract tenant from domain
        return null; // Simplified
    }
}
                            

// Configuration to register interceptors
@Configuration
public class WebMvcConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
    
    @Autowired
    private LoggingInterceptor loggingInterceptor;
    
    @Autowired
    private TenantInterceptor tenantInterceptor;
    
    @Override
    public void addInterceptors(InterceptorRegistry registry) {
        // Apply to all requests
        registry.addInterceptor(loggingInterceptor);
        
        // Apply to specific paths
        registry.addInterceptor(tenantInterceptor)
                .addPathPatterns("/api/**")
                .excludePathPatterns("/api/public/**", "/api/auth/**");
        
        // Another interceptor with order
        registry.addInterceptor(new CacheControlInterceptor())
                .addPathPatterns("/static/**")
                .order(1); // Execution order
    }
}

// Cache control interceptor example
public class CacheControlInterceptor implements HandlerInterceptor {
    
    @Override
    public void postHandle(HttpServletRequest request, 
                          HttpServletResponse response, 
                          Object handler,
                          ModelAndView modelAndView) throws Exception {
        
        if (request.getRequestURI().startsWith("/static/")) {
            response.setHeader("Cache-Control", "public, max-age=3600"); // 1 hour
        }
    }
}
